m: to burn tissue to stop bleeding or prevent infection; figuratively, to deaden feeling or stop damage
x: Field medics once had to cauterize wounds with hot iron because they had no proper surgical supplies.
The surgeon used a small electrical device to cauterize the blood vessels before closing the incision.
Our biology lecturer explained how eighteenth-century doctors would cauterize amputations with boiling oil.
Leaders moved swiftly to cauterize the scandal, firing the manager responsible and issuing a public apology.
Years of disappointment seemed to have cauterized her feelings, so she no longer cried at bad news.
tc: To stop the heavy bleeding, the doctor had to ______ the wound with a heated instrument.
'Stop the heavy bleeding' and 'heated instrument' point to burning tissue to seal it.
se: The nurse used a hot wire to ______ the small cut so that it would stop bleeding.
sear
Both 'cauterize' and 'sear' mean to burn the tissue closed, giving the same meaning.

m: famous and widely praised
x: We finally ate at the celebrated biryani house in Old Dhaka that my father has talked about for years.
Our new director was hired from a celebrated design firm in London, so expectations are high.
The professor's celebrated paper on bridge failures is still assigned to every first-year engineering student.
A celebrated violinist will perform at the city hall next month to raise money for flood victims.
Despite being a celebrated author, she felt lonely and doubted whether anyone truly understood her work.
tc: Though largely ignored during his lifetime, the painter is now ______ as one of the great masters of his era.
'Though largely ignored' signals a contrast, so the blank must mean famous and praised.
se: The museum holds several works by the ______ sculptor whose statues stand in parks across the country.
renowned
Both 'celebrated' and 'renowned' describe a famous, admired artist.

m: a feeling of complete certainty; absolute conviction that something is true
x: She spoke with such certitude about the shortcut that we all followed her, and we got completely lost.
In meetings, his certitude often silenced colleagues who had better ideas but less confidence.
Good scientists treat their conclusions as provisional rather than as matters of absolute certitude.
Voters were drawn to the candidate's certitude, even though his plans lacked any real detail.
As I grew older, the moral certitude of my teenage years gave way to doubt and humility.
tc: Unlike his hesitant colleagues, who hedged every claim, the economist stated his predictions with complete ______.
The contrast with 'hesitant' colleagues who 'hedged every claim' shows the blank means total certainty.
se: Nobody can say with ______ what the markets will do next year.
certainty
Both 'certitude' and 'certainty' mean complete sureness, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: courteous, generous and protective, especially toward women or people who are weaker
x: A chivalrous stranger on the bus gave up his seat to an elderly woman carrying heavy shopping bags.
My manager has the chivalrous habit of holding the door for everyone, whatever their rank.
The seminar examined how medieval poets idealized chivalrous knights who protected the weak.
Critics argue that some chivalrous customs, however well meant, can quietly reinforce old stereotypes about women.
She found his chivalrous manners charming at first, though she later wished he would treat her as an equal.
tc: Rather than mocking his defeated rival, the champion helped him to his feet, a gesture so ______ that it won over the crowd.
'Rather than mocking' signals the opposite of rudeness, so the blank means gallant and courteous.
se: It was ______ of him to walk her home through the dark streets after the party.
gallant
Both 'chivalrous' and 'gallant' describe courteous, protective behavior.

m: influence or power, especially in politics or business
x: My aunt has enough clout at the local school to get a meeting with the principal within a day.
As the firm's biggest client, the bank had considerable clout over our project deadlines.
Researchers with more funding often have more clout in deciding which questions the field pursues.
Small farmers lack the political clout to influence trade policy unless they form cooperatives.
After the promotion, he enjoyed his new clout a little too much, and some old friends drifted away.
tc: Although the union has many members, it has little ______, because the government rarely listens to its demands.
'The government rarely listens' shows the union lacks influence, despite its size.
se: Only a company with real ______ in the capital could have persuaded lawmakers to change the bill.
influence
Both 'clout' and 'influence' mean the power to affect decisions.

m: the quality of being clear, logical and convincing
x: Even my stubborn brother had to admit the cogency of my argument for splitting the electricity bill.
The cogency of her proposal persuaded the board to approve the budget without further debate.
Examiners reward essays for the cogency of their reasoning, not for the length of their paragraphs.
The report's cogency rests on decades of careful data rather than on dramatic anecdotes.
I admired the cogency of his apology; he explained exactly what he had done wrong and why.
tc: The lawyer's closing statement lacked ______: its points were muddled, contradictory and hard to follow.
The colon introduces a restatement; 'muddled' and 'contradictory' describe what lacking clear, convincing logic looks like.
se: Reviewers praised the ______ of the author's reasoning, which left little room for doubt.
persuasiveness
Both 'cogency' and 'persuasiveness' mean the power to convince through clear argument.

m: eager or ready to fight or argue
x: My neighbor gets combative whenever anyone mentions the parking spaces outside our building.
His combative style in meetings makes junior staff reluctant to share their ideas.
The visiting scholar gave a combative lecture attacking the field's most popular theory.
Within minutes the debate turned combative, with both candidates interrupting each other constantly.
When she is tired, she becomes combative, so we save serious conversations for the weekend.
tc: Normally calm and agreeable, the senator turned surprisingly ______ when reporters questioned his expenses.
'Normally calm and agreeable' and 'surprisingly' signal a contrast, so the blank means ready to fight.
se: The coach's ______ attitude toward referees has earned him several fines this season.
belligerent
Both 'combative' and 'belligerent' describe an aggressive, quarrelsome attitude.

m: ordinary and not unusual because it is found or happens everywhere
x: Power cuts were commonplace in our neighborhood when I was a child, especially during the summer.
Working from home, once a rare perk, has become commonplace in many offices.
Plagiarism-detection software is now commonplace in universities, so students should cite every source carefully.
Floods that once happened every few decades are becoming commonplace as the climate warms.
He wanted their anniversary to feel special, not commonplace, so he planned a surprise trip.
tc: Once a rare luxury, air travel is now so ______ that few passengers give it a second thought.
'Once a rare luxury' contrasts with the present, so the blank means ordinary and everyday.
se: Long commutes are ______ in large cities, where housing near offices is expensive.
common
Both 'commonplace' and 'common' mean widespread and ordinary.

m: comfort given to or received by someone after a loss or disappointment
x: We missed the last train, but our one consolation was a tea stall still open at the station.
As a consolation for the cancelled bonus, the company gave everyone an extra day off.
Failing the exam was painful, but she took consolation from her improved score in mathematics.
The losing team took some consolation in the fact that their young players had performed well.
After his grandfather's death, he found consolation in long conversations with his aunt.
tc: Losing the final was heartbreaking; the only ______ was that the team had played better than ever before.
After a 'heartbreaking' loss, 'the only' good thing mentioned is a source of comfort.
se: During the long months of her illness, music was her greatest ______.
solace
Both 'consolation' and 'solace' mean comfort in a time of distress.

m: to plan secretly with others to do something harmful or illegal; of events, to combine to cause trouble
x: Rain, traffic and a flat tire conspired to make me late for my own sister's wedding.
An internal audit showed that two managers had conspired to hide the losses from investors.
Historians still debate whether the generals conspired with foreign agents before the coup.
Five men were charged with conspiring to smuggle weapons across the border.
My cousins once conspired to throw me a surprise party, and somehow I never suspected a thing.
tc: The investigation revealed that the officials had met secretly for months to ______ against the president.
'Met secretly' and 'against the president' point to planning harm together in secret.
se: Prosecutors say the two executives worked together to ______ against their own shareholders.
plot
Both 'conspire against' and 'plot against' mean to plan harm secretly with others.

m: faithfulness and loyalty; the quality of staying the same over time
x: I rely on the constancy of my morning routine to stay calm on busy days.
Clients value the constancy of our service more than any flashy new feature.
Physicists were struck by the constancy of the speed of light, no matter how the observer moved.
The coach praised the constancy of the team's defense throughout a long and difficult season.
Through illness and poverty, her constancy never wavered; she stayed by his side for fifty years.
tc: Unlike her fickle friends, who changed allegiances every month, Rina was admired for her ______.
The contrast with 'fickle' friends who keep changing sides shows the blank means steady loyalty.
se: Their marriage survived decades of hardship thanks to the ______ of their devotion.
steadfastness
Both 'constancy' and 'steadfastness' mean unwavering faithfulness.

m: the spread of disease by contact; also, the spread of a harmful idea or influence
x: Washing your hands often is one of the simplest ways to reduce the risk of contagion.
Managers worried that one employee's cynicism would spread through the team like a contagion.
The study modeled how financial contagion moves from one bank to another during a crisis.
Health officials closed several schools to slow the contagion after cases of measles rose sharply.
Her laughter spread like a happy contagion, and within minutes everyone at the table was giggling.
tc: Fearing ______, the hospital isolated the patient so that the virus could not spread to others.
Isolating a patient so the virus 'could not spread' shows the fear was of disease passing by contact.
se: Doctors in the early 1800s did not yet understand how ______ passed from patient to patient.
infection
Both 'contagion' and 'infection' refer to disease being transmitted between people.

m: to make something impure or unsafe by adding a harmful or unwanted substance
x: Leaving raw chicken next to the salad can contaminate the vegetables with bacteria.
One careless line of code can contaminate an entire dataset, so we test every update.
The lab results were discarded because a dusty pipette had contaminated the samples.
Waste from nearby tanneries has contaminated the river, making its water unsafe to drink.
He let one bitter argument contaminate his memories of an otherwise happy friendship.
tc: Workers wore sealed suits so that dust from their clothes would not ______ the sterile microchips.
'Sealed suits' and 'sterile' show the goal is to avoid making the chips impure.
se: Runoff from nearby farms can ______ the wells that villagers rely on for drinking water.
pollute
Both 'contaminate' and 'pollute' mean to make water impure and unsafe.

m: existing or happening at the same time as something else; also, belonging to the present day
x: Historians compare the diary with contemporary newspaper reports to check its accuracy.
Our office is decorated with contemporary art, mostly bright abstract prints by young local painters.
Shakespeare's contemporary audiences would have understood jokes that puzzle students reading the plays today.
Contemporary accounts of the 1970 cyclone describe winds strong enough to flatten entire villages.
Letters written by people contemporary with my grandparents made their youth feel surprisingly vivid to me.
tc: Because the diary was written during the uprising itself, historians value it as evidence that is ______ rather than reconstructed decades later.
'Written during the uprising itself' and the contrast with 'decades later' show the blank means from the same time.
se: The gallery focuses on ______ design, showing furniture and posters made in the last ten years.
modern
Both 'contemporary' and 'modern' mean belonging to the present day here.

m: deliberately taking a position that opposes the popular or majority view
x: My uncle takes a contrarian view on everything, from cricket selections to the best route to the airport.
Her contrarian bet against the housing market looked foolish for years before it finally paid off.
The professor encouraged contrarian thinking, asking students to argue against the textbook's conclusions.
Some commentators adopt contrarian positions simply to attract attention on social media.
I used to find his contrarian streak exhausting, but now I appreciate how it challenges my assumptions.
tc: While most analysts urged caution, she took a boldly ______ position and bought shares just as everyone else was selling.
Buying 'as everyone else was selling' shows she deliberately went against the majority.
se: His ______ opinions, which challenged accepted wisdom, made him unpopular with the committee.
dissenting
Both 'contrarian' and 'dissenting' describe opinions that oppose the prevailing view.

m: to wear away gradually, especially by chemical action; to weaken or destroy something slowly
x: Salty air from the sea has slowly corroded the iron railings on our balcony.
Constant micromanagement can corrode trust between a manager and the team.
In the lab, we measured how quickly different acids corroded thin strips of copper.
Critics warn that widespread corruption is corroding public faith in the courts.
Years of small lies had corroded their friendship until nothing honest was left between them.
tc: Without a protective coat of paint, the steel bridge will slowly ______ in the damp, salty air.
'Without a protective coat' and 'damp, salty air' point to metal being gradually eaten away.
se: Persistent scandals can ______ voters' confidence in even the most established institutions.
erode
Both 'corrode' and 'erode' mean to wear something down gradually.

m: contrary to what common sense or intuition would lead you to expect
x: It seems counterintuitive, but a short nap after lunch actually helps me finish more work.
It sounds counterintuitive, yet adding more people to a late software project often delays it further.
Students often find probability counterintuitive, especially the famous puzzle involving three doors and a hidden car.
Researchers reported the counterintuitive finding that building wider roads can make traffic in cities like Dhaka worse.
It felt counterintuitive to give my angry friend some space, but stepping back helped us make up sooner.
tc: It may sound ______, but letting a little air out of your tires actually improves grip on sand, the opposite of what most drivers expect.
'The opposite of what most drivers expect' defines something that goes against intuition.
se: The study's most ______ result was that people who earned more reported having less free time.
paradoxical
Both 'counterintuitive' and 'paradoxical' describe a result that seems to contradict common sense.

m: having the opposite of the intended effect
x: Shouting at a crying child is usually counterproductive; it only makes the tears last longer.
Long, unfocused meetings are counterproductive because they leave less time for the actual work.
Cramming all night before an exam can be counterproductive, since tiredness hurts your memory.
Economists argue that the rent controls proved counterproductive, reducing the supply of affordable housing.
Checking on him constantly felt caring to her, but it was counterproductive and made him withdraw.
tc: Meant to boost morale, the new rules proved ______, leaving staff more frustrated than before.
Rules 'meant to boost morale' that left staff 'more frustrated' had the opposite of the intended effect.
se: Banning the book was ______, since the publicity only made more people want to read it.
self-defeating
Both 'counterproductive' and 'self-defeating' mean an action undermined its own goal.

m: a set of beliefs or principles that guides someone's actions
x: My father's credo is simple: never borrow money for anything that loses value.
Our startup's credo, printed on every mug, is to ship fast and learn from our mistakes.
Her lecture traced how the credo of free trade came to dominate economics departments.
The party's founding credo promised equal rights for every citizen, regardless of religion or language.
'Treat people as you want to be treated' has been my personal credo since my school days.
tc: The chef summed up her ______ in three words she repeated to every new cook: fresh, simple, honest.
Three guiding words repeated to every cook are the principles she works by.
se: 'Work hard and stay humble' was the ______ that guided him throughout his career.
creed
Both 'credo' and 'creed' mean a guiding statement of belief.

m: in a raw, unrefined state; roughly made and unsophisticated; also coarse or vulgar
x: When the monsoon rain started, we built a crude shelter from bamboo and plastic sheets.
The first prototype was crude, but it proved that the idea could actually work.
His crude estimate of the bridge's load turned out to be off by nearly forty percent.
Prices of crude oil rose sharply after an explosion shut down the main pipeline.
I found his crude jokes about my cousin's weight embarrassing and unkind.
tc: Compared with the sleek model on display today, the inventor's first engine was ______, held together with wire and tape.
The contrast with 'sleek' and the detail 'wire and tape' show the first engine was roughly made.
se: Using only sticks and string, the boys made fishing rods that were ______ but surprisingly effective.
rudimentary
Both 'crude' and 'rudimentary' mean simple and roughly made.

m: to develop or improve a skill, quality or relationship through deliberate effort
x: I am trying to cultivate the habit of reading for twenty minutes before bed.
Good salespeople spend years cultivating relationships with clients before asking for large orders.
The new principal wants to cultivate a culture of curiosity rather than rote memorization.
The minister carefully cultivated an image as a humble man of the people.
After moving abroad, she cultivated close friendships with her neighbors, who soon felt like family.
tc: Rather than letting their friendship fade, the two founders made an effort to ______ it with regular dinners and long calls.
'Rather than letting their friendship fade' signals deliberate effort to develop it.
se: Teachers should ______ curiosity in children rather than punishing them for asking questions.
nurture
Both 'cultivate' and 'nurture' mean to help a quality grow through care.

m: able to cure disease or heal
x: My grandmother swears by the curative power of ginger tea for every kind of cold.
Our team is testing whether the drug has curative effects or merely eases the symptoms.
Medical students learn to distinguish curative care from palliative care, which only relieves suffering.
Spa towns once attracted wealthy visitors who believed in the curative properties of mineral water.
For her, long walks by the river had an almost curative effect after the breakup.
tc: Doctors stressed that the drug was not ______; it eased the patients' symptoms but could not eliminate the disease.
The semicolon explains the blank: a drug that cannot eliminate the disease does not cure it.
se: Ancient healers believed the herb had ______ powers that could restore the sick to health.
healing
Both 'curative' and 'healing' describe powers that restore health.

m: fiercely competitive and ruthless
x: Finding a rental flat in this neighborhood is cutthroat; good places disappear within hours.
Investment banking has a cutthroat culture in which colleagues compete openly for bonuses.
Admission to the top engineering universities in Bangladesh is cutthroat, with dozens of applicants for every seat.
Cutthroat competition among airlines has pushed ticket prices down but squeezed workers' wages.
Their friendship cooled after a cutthroat rivalry over the school's top prize.
tc: Unlike the friendly local market, the city's restaurant business is ______: owners undercut and sabotage each other without mercy.
The contrast with 'friendly' and the phrase 'without mercy' show the blank means ruthlessly competitive.
se: The smartphone industry is notoriously ______, and many firms collapse after a single weak year.
ruthless
Both 'cutthroat' and 'ruthless' describe merciless competition.

m: open to question or argument; not clearly true or settled
x: Whether pineapple belongs on pizza is debatable, but my brother treats it as settled fact.
It is debatable whether the new software has actually saved our team any time.
The authenticity of the manuscript remains debatable among historians, since no earlier copies have survived.
Whether the tax cut really helped the economy is still highly debatable.
Who was really to blame for our argument is debatable, so we agreed that we would both apologize.
tc: Supporters call the policy a clear success, but its long-term benefits remain ______ among economists, who disagree sharply.
'But' and 'who disagree sharply' show the benefits are open to argument.
se: Whether the treaty actually prevented war is ______, and historians continue to argue about it.
arguable
Both 'debatable' and 'arguable' mean open to dispute.

m: to convert coded or encrypted information into a readable form
x: I forgot my password, so I could not decrypt the old files on my laptop.
Only the IT department has the keys needed to decrypt customer records.
For her thesis, she studied how wartime codebreakers decrypted enemy messages by hand.
Investigators said they could not decrypt the suspect's phone without help from the manufacturer.
Reading his vague text messages felt like trying to decrypt a secret code, so I eventually stopped trying.
tc: The message was encrypted, so without the right key nobody could ______ it.
An 'encrypted' message that needs 'the right key' must be turned back into readable text.
se: It took the analysts three weeks to ______ the intercepted messages.
decode
Both 'decrypt' and 'decode' mean to turn coded messages into plain text.

m: lacking something necessary; not good or complete enough
x: My doctor said I was deficient in vitamin D because I rarely go outside in daylight.
The audit found our safety procedures deficient in several important areas.
Reviewers rejected the paper because its methodology was deficient and its sample too small.
Soil in the region is deficient in zinc, which sharply reduces crop yields.
Growing up, she felt deficient beside her brilliant sister, though her parents never compared them.
tc: Because the diet was ______ in iron, many of the children developed anemia.
Anemia is caused by too little iron, so the diet must have lacked it.
se: Inspectors found the building's fire exits ______ and ordered immediate repairs.
inadequate
Both 'deficient' and 'inadequate' mean not good enough, which is why repairs were ordered.

m: to make someone feel less confident or excited; also, to let air out of something
x: We had to deflate the air mattress completely before it would fit into the car.
The cancelled bonus deflated morale in the office for weeks.
My supervisor's lukewarm response to my research idea deflated me, but I kept working on it.
The central bank raised interest rates to deflate the housing bubble before it burst.
One unkind comment from her brother was enough to deflate her excitement about the trip.
tc: Nothing seemed able to ______ his huge ego until he lost the election by an embarrassing margin.
A 'huge ego' finally humbled by an 'embarrassing' loss points to reducing someone's self-importance.
se: A single harsh review can ______ a young writer who has worked on a novel for years.
dishearten
Both 'deflate' and 'dishearten' mean to drain someone's confidence and enthusiasm.

m: to cheat someone out of money or property by deception
x: A man posing as a bank officer tried to defraud my uncle by asking for his PIN over the phone.
The accountant was fired for defrauding the company of nearly two million taka.
Law students analyzed several cases in which brokers had defrauded elderly investors.
The charity's founder was charged with defrauding donors by spending their money on luxury cars.
She felt more betrayed than angry when she learned her closest friend had defrauded her.
tc: The scheme was designed to ______ elderly customers by persuading them to invest in companies that did not exist.
Persuading people to invest in companies 'that did not exist' is cheating them of money by deception.
se: Prosecutors allege that the dealers tried to ______ insurers with fake accident claims.
cheat
Both 'defraud' and 'cheat' mean to take money dishonestly through deception.

m: to make a tense or dangerous situation calmer; also, to remove the fuse from a bomb
x: My father defused the argument at dinner by changing the subject to cricket.
A quick apology from the manager helped defuse the client's anger.
In our negotiation class, we practiced techniques for defusing hostile conversations.
Army experts spent three hours defusing an old bomb found at the construction site.
When she sensed her partner's frustration rising, she defused it with a joke and a hug.
tc: Instead of escalating the conflict, the mediator tried to ______ it by acknowledging both sides' grievances.
'Instead of escalating' signals the opposite action: calming the conflict.
se: The teacher told a joke to ______ the tension in the room before the exam results were announced.
ease
Both 'defuse' and 'ease' mean to reduce tension.

m: sad and low in spirits, especially after a disappointment
x: After missing the bus for the third time that week, I walked home feeling dejected.
The team looked dejected after the client rejected their proposal.
Many students feel dejected after a poor first-semester result, but most recover quickly.
Dejected fans left the stadium in silence after the home side lost in the final over.
He sounded so dejected on the phone that I drove over to keep him company.
tc: Far from celebrating, the players were ______ after their narrow loss and sat silently in the dressing room.
'Far from celebrating' and 'sat silently' after a loss show the players were downcast.
se: After the rejection letter arrived, he was too ______ to eat dinner.
despondent
Both 'dejected' and 'despondent' mean deeply discouraged and sad.

m: wildly excited; also, confused and incoherent, especially because of fever or illness
x: With a high fever, my little brother became delirious and talked about cartoon characters all night.
The whole team was delirious when the client finally signed the contract after months of negotiation.
Delirious with joy, she screamed when she saw her name on the university admission list.
Doctors say older patients can become delirious after surgery, a condition often mistaken for dementia.
Crowds in the streets were delirious after the national team's surprise victory in the final.
tc: Burning with fever, the patient was ______, mumbling nonsense and failing to recognize his own family.
'Burning with fever' and 'mumbling nonsense' describe a confused, incoherent state.
se: The fans were ______ when their team scored the winning goal in the last minute.
ecstatic
Both 'delirious' and 'ecstatic' mean wildly happy and excited here.

m: to make something easier to understand by removing its mystery or complexity
x: This cookbook aims to demystify French cooking for people with small kitchens and busy lives.
Our HR team ran a workshop to demystify the new pension scheme for staff.
Good teachers demystify calculus by linking every formula to a real problem.
The museum's new exhibition tries to demystify artificial intelligence for ordinary visitors.
Talking openly with a counselor helped demystify my anxiety, so it felt much less frightening.
tc: The author's aim is to ______ the stock market, explaining in plain language what most beginners find bewildering.
'Explaining in plain language' what is 'bewildering' restates the idea of making something less mysterious.
se: The guidebook attempts to ______ the visa application process for first-time travelers.
clarify
Both 'demystify' and 'clarify' mean to make a confusing process easier to understand.

m: to strip something of its covering, such as trees, plants or soil
x: Goats had denuded the hillside behind our village of almost every green plant.
The company was criticized for denuding the forest to build a new warehouse.
Our geography lecturer showed photographs of hills denuded by decades of logging.
Illegal logging has denuded vast areas of the rainforest, leaving the soil to wash away in heavy rains.
After the divorce, he felt denuded of the comforts and routines that had once defined his life.
tc: Within a decade, loggers had managed to ______ the once lush valley, leaving bare earth where forests had stood.
'Once lush' contrasted with 'bare earth' shows the valley was stripped of its covering.
se: A single season of locusts can ______ the fields, leaving nothing but stubble behind.
strip
Both 'denude' and 'strip' mean to remove all covering from the land.

m: to obstruct a plan or process, or throw it off course
x: A sudden fever derailed our plans for a weekend trip to Cox's Bazar.
One unhappy shareholder threatened to derail the merger at the last minute.
Personal problems almost derailed her doctorate, but she finished after an extra year.
Officials fear that renewed fighting could derail the fragile peace talks.
Don't let a single argument derail a friendship that has lasted twenty years.
tc: Negotiators worked through the night, fearing that a single misstep could ______ months of careful diplomacy.
Fearing that 'a single misstep' could ruin 'months of careful diplomacy' points to throwing the process off course.
se: Critics warned that the scandal could ______ her campaign just weeks before the election.
thwart
Both 'derail' and 'thwart' mean to stop a plan from succeeding.

m: to feel strong contempt or dislike for someone or something
x: I despise waking up early on Fridays, but the fish market only opens at dawn.
She despises office gossip and leaves the break room whenever it starts.
Many students despise group projects because one person usually ends up doing most of the work.
Voters across the political spectrum despise corruption, yet it persists in many governments.
He once despised his stepfather, but over the years he came to love and respect him.
tc: Although he praised his rival in public, in private he had come to ______ him for his dishonesty.
'Although he praised' signals a contrast, so in private he felt contempt.
se: She has always seemed to ______ people who lie to get ahead.
detest
Both 'despise' and 'detest' mean to dislike intensely.

m: to make something less stable, secure or firmly established
x: Pulling out that bottom block will destabilize the whole tower, so be careful.
Frequent changes in leadership have destabilized the department and lowered morale.
The experiment showed that small temperature changes can destabilize the protein's structure.
Rising food prices threaten to destabilize several fragile governments in the region.
Constant criticism from her parents destabilized her confidence well into adulthood.
tc: Rather than strengthening the coalition, the minister's resignation threatened to ______ it.
'Rather than strengthening' signals the opposite: making the coalition less stable.
se: Foreign agents were accused of trying to ______ the government by funding opposition militias.
undermine
Both 'destabilize' and 'undermine' mean to weaken a government's hold on power.

m: departing from accepted social, moral or normal standards
x: In our quiet neighborhood, even playing loud music after ten is treated as deviant behavior.
The audit flagged several deviant transactions that did not follow company policy.
Sociologists study why certain acts are labeled deviant in one culture but accepted in another.
Some politicians condemned the protest as deviant, while supporters called it legitimate dissent.
As a teenager he cultivated a deviant image, dyeing his hair green to shock his relatives.
tc: Behavior that one society treats as perfectly normal may be considered ______ in another with stricter norms.
The contrast with 'perfectly normal' and 'stricter norms' shows the blank means departing from accepted standards.
se: Researchers excluded the ______ data points that fell far outside the normal range.
anomalous
Both 'deviant' and 'anomalous' describe values that depart from the norm.

m: to recognize or show the difference between things
x: My grandmother can differentiate between a dozen kinds of rice just by their smell.
Our brand needs a clear message to differentiate it from cheaper competitors.
Students must learn to differentiate between correlation and causation before analyzing any data.
The new test can differentiate the virus from ordinary flu within twenty minutes.
As a child, I could never differentiate my twin cousins, which always made them laugh.
tc: Because the twins dressed identically, even their teachers struggled to ______ them.
'Dressed identically' explains why it was hard to tell the twins apart.
se: A good doctor can ______ between a harmless rash and the early signs of infection.
distinguish
Both 'differentiate between' and 'distinguish between' mean to tell two things apart.

m: to weaken something by adding water or by mixing in other elements
x: I always dilute orange juice with a little water for my young nephew.
Issuing more shares will dilute the stake held by the company's founders.
In chemistry class, we diluted the acid carefully before measuring its pH.
Critics say amendments have diluted the bill so much that it no longer protects workers.
She felt that years of living abroad had diluted her attachment to her hometown.
tc: Instead of strengthening the reforms, the committee's last-minute changes served only to ______ them.
'Instead of strengthening' signals the opposite: weakening the reforms.

weaken

m: a feeling of dissatisfaction, especially with one's situation or with those in charge

Surveys revealed widespread discontent among graduate students over the quality of supervision.
Rising prices fueled public discontent, and protests soon spread to several cities.
Behind her bright smile lay a quiet discontent with the life she had chosen.
tc: Far from being satisfied with the pay raise, workers expressed deep ______ because it failed to keep up with inflation.
'Far from being satisfied' signals the opposite feeling: dissatisfaction.
se: Years of rising rents and stagnant wages fueled widespread ______ among young voters.
dissatisfaction
Both 'discontent' and 'dissatisfaction' mean unhappiness with one's circumstances.

m: to make someone lose hope, enthusiasm or confidence

Low marks in the first quiz can dishearten students, so the tutor gives extra feedback.
The slow pace of rebuilding has disheartened residents who lost their homes in the earthquake.
Her best friend's silence after the wedding invitation disheartened her more than she admitted.
tc: Coaches must be careful not to ______ young players with harsh criticism; instead, they should encourage them.
'Instead, they should encourage them' shows the blank means the opposite of encourage.
se: Repeated rejections did not ______ the young author, who kept sending her manuscript to publishers.
discourage
Both 'dishearten' and 'discourage' mean to make someone lose hope.

m: to remove or force something or someone out of a fixed or established position
x: I used a toothpick to dislodge a small fish bone stuck between my teeth.
The challenger hopes to dislodge the company from its position as market leader.

A party entrenched for 'three decades' facing a 'weak' opposition suggests it could not be forced out.
se: Firefighters used crowbars to ______ the rock that had trapped the climber's leg.
remove
Both 'dislodge' and 'remove' mean to move the rock out of its fixed position.

m: to take something apart piece by piece; to gradually abolish a system or organization

tc: Instead of merely reforming the outdated welfare system, the new government chose to ______ it entirely.
'Instead of merely reforming' and 'entirely' point to taking the system apart completely.
se: Engineers will ______ the old bridge piece by piece and reassemble it in a museum.
disassemble
Both 'dismantle' and 'disassemble' mean to take a structure apart piece by piece.

m: to make someone confused about where they are or what is happening

tc: The dense fog was enough to ______ even experienced sailors, who lost all sense of direction.
'Lost all sense of direction' restates the meaning of being confused about one's position.
se: The sudden darkness and loud alarms were designed to ______ the intruders.
confuse
Both 'disorient' and 'confuse' mean to leave someone unsure of what is happening.

m: to refuse to acknowledge or have any connection with someone or something
x: My aunt jokingly threatened to disown me if I ever supported a rival football club.
The company quickly disowned the manager's comments, saying they did not reflect its values.

His parents disowned him when he married against their wishes, and they did not speak for a decade.

'Once proud to be linked' contrasts with cutting all ties after the scandal.
se: Party leaders were quick to ______ the extremist pamphlet, insisting they had never approved it.
repudiate
Both 'disown' and 'repudiate' mean to publicly deny any connection with something.

m: not essential; able to be done without

In your final draft, cut any dispensable sentences that do not support your main argument.
Critics say the government treats migrant workers as dispensable once a project is finished.
He sensed that he had become dispensable in her life, someone she could easily replace.
tc: During the budget crisis, the board treated the arts program as ______, cutting it first while protecting essential services.
The contrast with 'essential services' and 'cutting it first' show the program was seen as not necessary.
se: On a tight budget, luxuries such as cable television are ______ and should be cut first.
expendable
Both 'dispensable' and 'expendable' mean something you can do without.

m: to force someone or something out of its usual place; to take the place of
x: The new road displaced dozens of street vendors who had sold tea there for years.
Automation may displace thousands of factory workers over the next decade.
In physics class, we measured how much water a stone displaced when dropped into a beaker.

She worried that her new baby brother would displace her in her parents' affections.
tc: Streaming services have begun to ______ traditional television, taking over the place it once held in most homes.
'Taking over the place it once held' defines pushing something out and replacing it.
se: Wars and floods can ______ entire communities, forcing them into crowded camps.
uproot
Both 'displace' and 'uproot' mean to force people from their homes.

m: to pay no attention to; to ignore
x: Please disregard my previous email; I attached the wrong file.

The court ruled that the company had disregarded safety regulations for years.
She disregarded her friends' warnings about him and later wished she had listened.
tc: Instead of heeding the doctor's warnings, he chose to ______ them and continued smoking.
'Instead of heeding' signals the opposite: ignoring the warnings.
se: The judge instructed the jury to ______ the witness's last remark.
ignore
Both 'disregard' and 'ignore' mean to pay no attention to something.

m: to interrupt or disturb the normal course of an activity or process

Students who constantly check their phones disrupt not only their own learning but their classmates' too.

The arrival of a new baby can disrupt even the strongest couple's routines.
tc: Organizers hired extra security, fearing that protesters would ______ the ceremony by shouting during the speeches.
'Shouting during the speeches' describes interrupting the normal course of the event.
se: Noise from the building site next door continued to ______ our meetings all week.
interrupt
Both 'disrupt' and 'interrupt' mean to break into an activity and stop it running smoothly.

m: characteristic of one person or thing and so making it easy to recognize
x: You can always spot my father in a crowd because of his distinctive white cap.
Our logo needs a more distinctive color so customers notice it on crowded shelves.
Each researcher has a distinctive writing style that experienced reviewers can often recognize.
The bird's distinctive call, a sharp double whistle, helps scientists track its population.
She has a distinctive laugh that makes everyone around her smile.
tc: Unlike the bland, identical houses on the rest of the street, hers was immediately ______, with its bright blue door and round windows.
The contrast with 'bland, identical houses' shows hers stood out and was easy to recognize.
se: Experts can identify the region's wines by their ______ flavor in a single sip.
characteristic
Both 'distinctive' and 'characteristic' describe a quality typical of one thing that marks it out.

m: entertaining and amusing in a light, pleasant way
x: We spent a diverting afternoon at the street fair, sampling snacks and watching the jugglers.
Between long meetings, the Friday office quiz offered a diverting break from spreadsheets and emails.

Critics called the new film diverting but forgettable, a pleasant two hours with little substance.
On rainy monsoon evenings, my grandfather's stories were the most diverting thing in the house.
tc: Although the novel had little literary merit, it was ______ enough to make the long train journey pass quickly.
'Although' signals a contrast with 'little literary merit', and making the journey 'pass quickly' shows the book was entertaining.
se: The play was not profound, but it was ______ and kept the children laughing for an hour.
entertaining
Both 'diverting' and 'entertaining' describe something enjoyable that holds attention, as the children's laughter shows.

x: The landlord showed us a doctored receipt, and the dates clearly did not match his story.

A doctored photograph spread rapidly online before fact-checkers proved it had been manipulated.
She felt betrayed when she realized her partner had shown her doctored messages to win the argument.

Edited timestamps and removed frames show the video had been dishonestly altered.
se: Investigators proved that the bank statements were ______ to make the company look solvent.
falsified
Both 'doctored' and 'falsified' mean dishonestly changed to deceive, giving the sentence the same meaning.

Officials downplayed the flood risk until the river burst its banks during the monsoon.

Describing a 'major' breach as a 'minor glitch' shows the spokesperson was making it seem less serious.

minimize
Both 'downplay' and 'minimize' mean to make the concerns seem smaller than they are.

m: extreme and far-reaching in effect; severe

radical

dismal

Both 'dubiety' and 'skepticism' mean doubt, which the cautious questions reveal.

noticeable

se: The instructions were ______, and nobody in the office could work out how to assemble the desk.
perplexing
Both 'baffling' and 'perplexing' describe instructions too confusing to understand.

m: the way a person stands, moves or behaves; demeanor

Students noticed the visiting professor's dignified bearing before he had said a word.
Observers praised the judge's composed bearing throughout the long and tense trial.

'Calm and confident' despite chaos describes the captain's manner and the way he carried himself.

carriage
Both 'bearing' and 'carriage' refer to the way a person holds and carries the body.

advantageous

The contrast with 'perfectly normal' shows the blank means very strange.
se: The story became even more ______ when the missing parrot reappeared at a police station two hundred miles away.
strange
Both 'bizarre' and 'strange' describe the odd, unexpected turn of events.

She hated his blanket statements about women, as though all of them thought the same way.

'Rather than reviewing applications one by one' contrasts with restrictions that apply to everyone without exception.
se: Critics argued that ______ bans on protest violate the basic right to free assembly.
sweeping
Both 'blanket' and 'sweeping' describe bans that apply to all cases without distinction.

m: lacking energy, emotion or human warmth; lifeless

Critics found the textbook accurate but bloodless, with none of the drama of the actual revolution.
Reviewers dismissed the remake as a bloodless copy of the gripping original.
His apology was polite but bloodless, and she could tell he didn't really feel sorry.
tc: The actor delivered his lines correctly but without any feeling, giving a performance so ______ that the audience barely reacted.
'Without any feeling' and the audience's lack of reaction show the performance lacked life and emotion.
se: Unlike her passionate early novels, her recent books feel ______ and mechanical.
lifeless
Both 'bloodless' and 'lifeless' mean lacking the passion of her earlier work.

m: to increase or improve something
x: A strong cup of tea always boosts my energy in the middle of the afternoon.

Regular practice tests can boost students' confidence before the real exam.
The central bank cut interest rates to boost economic growth.
His kind words boosted her morale after a difficult week.
tc: Worried that low morale was hurting productivity, the manager organized team outings to ______ spirits.
Low morale is the problem, so the outings were meant to raise spirits.
se: The festival is expected to ______ tourism in the region during the off-season.
increase
Both 'boost' and 'increase' mean to raise the level of tourism.

m: to take advantage of a situation or opportunity (usually followed by 'on')

She capitalized on her internship by turning her research into a published paper.
Opposition parties tried to capitalize on public anger over rising food prices.
He capitalized on their friendship to borrow money, and she never fully trusted him again.
tc: The team failed to ______ on their opponents' early mistakes, and so they wasted a golden chance to win.
'Wasted a golden chance' shows they failed to take advantage of the mistakes.
se: The opposition was quick to ______ on the minister's careless remark, using it in every campaign speech.
seize
Both 'capitalize on' and 'seize on' mean to take eager advantage of the remark.

m: looking tired and worried because of long-lasting trouble or responsibility
x: After three nights with a sick baby, my sister looked pale and careworn.
The careworn manager had not taken a day off since the merger began.
By the end of exam season, the careworn faces in the library told their own story.
Photographs show careworn farmers waiting in line for relief after the floods.
Years of caring for her ailing husband had left her careworn but still gentle.
tc: Once cheerful and carefree, her mother now looked ______, her face lined by years of financial worry.
The contrast with 'carefree' and the face 'lined by years of worry' point to a tired, anxious look.
se: The doctor's ______ face showed how little sleep she had had during the epidemic.
haggard
Both 'careworn' and 'haggard' describe a face that looks exhausted from strain and lack of sleep.

m: the typical character, quality or appearance of something, especially of a person's mind or face
x: My father has a practical cast of mind and fixes things without reading the instructions.
Her report had a gloomy cast that worried the investors more than the actual numbers did.
Thinkers of a scientific cast of mind tend to distrust explanations that cannot be tested.
Commentators noted the increasingly nationalist cast of the party's speeches.
His face took on a melancholy cast whenever he spoke about the village he had left behind.
tc: Unlike his practical brother, he had a philosophical ______ of mind and spent hours debating questions that had no answers.
The contrast with his 'practical brother' and his love of debate describe the character of his mind.
se: Her reflective ______ of mind made her impatient with gossip and small talk.
turn
Both 'cast of mind' and 'turn of mind' mean a person's typical way of thinking.

m: including a wide variety of things; broad and wide-ranging in tastes or interests
x: My uncle has catholic tastes in food and will try anything from fermented fish to fondue.
We need a manager with catholic experience who can handle marketing, finance and logistics alike.
Her reading list is impressively catholic, ranging from Bengali poetry to quantum physics.
The festival's catholic program included jazz, folk, opera and electronic music.
He has a catholic circle of friends, from retired fishermen to university professors.
tc: Far from being narrow, his musical tastes are remarkably ______, embracing everything from Baroque opera to hip-hop.
'Far from being narrow' and the huge range of music show his tastes are wide-ranging.
se: The library's collection is genuinely ______, covering subjects from beekeeping to astrophysics.
eclectic
Both 'catholic' and 'eclectic' describe a collection drawn from a very wide range of subjects.

m: arranged in the order in which events happened
x: I keep my old photographs in chronological order, starting with my childhood in Chittagong.
Please list your work experience in reverse chronological order on your résumé.
The history course follows a chronological structure, moving from ancient empires to the modern era.
Investigators built a chronological account of the hours leading up to the crash.
She told the story of their relationship in chronological order, from first meeting to final goodbye.
tc: Rather than jumping back and forth between decades, the biography proceeds in strict ______ order, from the subject's birth to his death.
The contrast with 'jumping back and forth' and the move from birth to death show events are told in time order.
se: The letters are filed in ______ order by date, so the earliest ones are at the front.
sequential
Both 'chronological' and 'sequential' order here mean arranged one after another by date.

m: to settle or confirm something decisively, such as a deal, argument or victory
x: The free delivery offer clinched it for me, so I ordered the sofa that night.
Our team clinched the contract after a final presentation that impressed the client.
A single well-designed experiment clinched the argument in favor of her hypothesis.
Bangladesh clinched the series with a dramatic last-over win in Mirpur.
It was his kindness toward her mother that finally clinched her decision to marry him.
tc: The negotiations had dragged on for months, but a last-minute discount finally helped them ______ the deal.
After months of delay, 'finally' shows the discount settled the deal decisively.
se: A late goal allowed the home team to ______ the championship with two games to spare.
secure
Both 'clinch' and 'secure' mean to make the championship win certain.

m: to hide or disguise something
x: Thick fog cloaked the city, and we could barely see the car in front of us.
The company cloaked its price increase in a vague announcement about 'improved service'.
Early scientific discoveries were often cloaked in mystical language that confused later readers.
Officials cloaked the true purpose of the program in secrecy for decades.
He cloaked his jealousy with jokes, but his friends could tell he was hurt.
tc: To avoid alarming investors, the firm tried to ______ its losses behind optimistic language about future growth.
Wanting to avoid alarm and hiding losses 'behind optimistic language' show the firm was concealing them.
se: She tried to ______ her disappointment with a bright smile, but her eyes gave her away.
mask
Both 'cloak' and 'mask' mean to hide her true feeling behind a smile.

m: showing sound practical judgment; sensible and realistic
x: Packing an umbrella during the monsoon is the commonsensical thing to do.
Her commonsensical approach to budgeting saved the team from several costly mistakes.
Some of the professor's advice was surprisingly commonsensical: sleep well, eat breakfast, and start early.
Many voters said they wanted commonsensical solutions to rising prices rather than grand promises.
My grandmother gave commonsensical advice about love: marry someone who is kind when they are tired.
tc: The proposal was neither radical nor theoretical but thoroughly ______, the kind of plan any practical person could follow.
'Neither radical nor theoretical' and 'any practical person could follow' point to sound, sensible judgment.
se: His advice was ______: save a little each month and avoid debts you cannot repay.
sensible
Both 'commonsensical' and 'sensible' describe practical, obviously wise advice.

m: to make something more difficult or confusing
x: Heavy rain complicated our plans for a picnic in the park.
Adding another approval step will only complicate the hiring process.
Missing data complicated the analysis, so the researchers had to adjust their methods.
Rising fuel prices have complicated efforts to bring down inflation.
Her new job in another city complicated their relationship, but they decided to stay together.
tc: Instead of simplifying the tax code as promised, the new rules served only to ______ it further.
'Instead of simplifying' signals the opposite: making the code more difficult.
se: A last-minute change of venue served to ______ matters for the organizers.
confuse
Both 'complicate matters' and 'confuse matters' mean to make the situation harder to manage.

m: to weaken or put at risk, especially through carelessness or dishonorable action
x: Sharing your password with friends can compromise the security of your bank account.
Cutting corners on testing could compromise the quality of the entire product.
If the samples are not stored properly, the results of the study may be compromised.
Investigators said the leak had compromised a sensitive military operation.
He refused to compromise his principles, even when his family urged him to take the money.
tc: The journalist refused to reveal her source, knowing that doing so would ______ the safety of the informant.
Her refusal shows that revealing the source would put the informant's safety at risk.
se: Accepting gifts from suppliers could ______ an inspector's independence.
undermine
Both 'compromise' and 'undermine' mean to weaken the inspector's independence.

m: possible to imagine or believe
x: We tried every conceivable route home, but traffic was jammed in all directions.
It is conceivable that the deadline will move, but we should plan as though it won't.
Scientists once thought it barely conceivable that life could exist near volcanic vents in the deep ocean.
Experts say it is conceivable that the election will be decided by fewer than a thousand votes.
She had loved him in every conceivable way, so his silence hurt all the more.
tc: Though unlikely, it is ______ that the comet will pass close enough to be seen without a telescope.
'Though unlikely' implies the event is still possible to imagine.
se: We have considered every ______ option, and none of them solves the problem completely.
possible
Both 'every conceivable option' and 'every possible option' mean all options one could think of.

m: specific, real and definite rather than abstract or general
x: Instead of saying you'll exercise more, set a concrete goal like walking thirty minutes a day.
My manager asked for concrete examples of how the new software saves time.
The essay was full of abstractions and needed more concrete evidence to persuade readers.
Despite months of talks, the summit produced no concrete agreement on climate funding.
She wanted concrete proof that he had changed, not just another promise.
tc: The committee rejected the vague recommendations and demanded ______ proposals with clear budgets and deadlines.
Rejecting 'vague' ideas and asking for clear budgets and deadlines shows they wanted specific proposals.
se: Investors want to see ______ results before they commit more money to the project.
tangible
Both 'concrete' and 'tangible' describe real, measurable results rather than promises.

m: showing that you think you are better or cleverer than others; patronizing
x: The shop assistant gave me a condescending smile when I asked a simple question.
Her condescending tone in emails made junior staff afraid to ask for help.
Some lecturers can be condescending toward students who speak English as a second language.
Critics called the candidate's speech condescending, saying it treated voters like children.
He hated it when his older brother explained things in that slow, condescending way.
tc: Although he was trying to be helpful, his ______ explanations made his colleagues feel as though he thought they were stupid.
Making colleagues feel he thought they were stupid shows his explanations were patronizing.
se: The tour guide's ______ manner annoyed the visitors, who felt they were being treated like children.
patronizing
Both 'condescending' and 'patronizing' describe treating others as inferior, as 'treated like children' shows.

m: contradicting each other; incompatible or opposed
x: My two map apps gave conflicting directions, so I ended up asking a rickshaw driver.
Staff received conflicting instructions from two managers and didn't know whom to follow.
Studies on coffee and health have produced conflicting results over the years.
Early reports about the fire were conflicting, and the number of injured kept changing.
She felt conflicting emotions when her best friend moved abroad: pride and deep sadness.
tc: Because the witnesses gave ______ accounts, one placing the suspect at home and another at the scene, the police could not decide what had happened.
One account placing the suspect at home and another at the scene shows the accounts contradicted each other.
se: The jury struggled to reach a verdict because the experts offered ______ opinions about the cause of death.
contradictory
Both 'conflicting' and 'contradictory' describe opinions that disagree, making a verdict hard.

m: to face or deal with a difficult situation or person directly
x: I finally confronted my roommate about the dirty dishes piling up in the sink.
New managers often have to confront poor performance on their teams within weeks.
The study forces readers to confront uncomfortable facts about inequality in higher education.
Coastal cities must confront the reality of rising sea levels.
After years of avoiding the subject, he confronted his fear of losing his parents.
tc: Rather than continuing to avoid the issue, the team decided to ______ it openly at the next meeting.
'Rather than continuing to avoid' signals the opposite: facing the issue directly.
se: The new government must ______ the problem of youth unemployment head-on.
tackle
Both 'confront' and 'tackle' mean to deal with the problem directly, as 'head-on' stresses.

m: to force someone by law to serve in the armed forces
x: My great-grandfather was conscripted into the army at eighteen and never talked about the war.
Our manager jokingly conscripted three interns to help carry boxes on moving day.
Historians estimate that millions of young men were conscripted during the First World War.
The government announced plans to conscript all men aged eighteen to twenty-five for a year of service.
She was terrified that her younger brother might be conscripted while he was still at university.
tc: With too few volunteers to fill its ranks, the army began to ______ young men into compulsory service.
Too few volunteers and 'compulsory service' show the army was forcing men to serve.
se: During the war, the state had the power to ______ any able-bodied man into the army.
draft
Both 'conscript' and 'draft' mean to require someone by law to join the army.

m: cautious and moderate; (of an estimate) deliberately low to avoid exaggeration
x: At a conservative guess, we spend about three hours a day stuck in traffic.
Our finance team made a conservative forecast so the company wouldn't overpromise to investors.
Using conservative assumptions, the researchers still found a strong link between pollution and asthma.
Even by conservative estimates, the floods displaced more than a million people.
She is conservative with her money and rarely spends anything she hasn't budgeted for.
tc: The official figure of 500 deaths is almost certainly ______; independent observers believe the true number is twice as high.
A true number twice as high shows the official figure is deliberately low.
se: Investors approved of the bank's ______ lending policy, which avoided risky loans.
cautious
Both 'conservative' and 'cautious' describe a policy that avoids risk.

m: acting or done in the same way over time; also, in agreement with something
x: Going to bed at a consistent time has made me far less tired in the mornings.
Clients trust us because our quality has been consistent for twenty years.
These findings are consistent with earlier studies on sleep and memory.
The witness's testimony was consistent with the security camera footage.
He has been consistent in his support, calling her every week since she moved to Toronto.
tc: Unlike his erratic performance last season, this year his batting has been remarkably ______, with a solid score in nearly every match.
The contrast with 'erratic' and a solid score in nearly every match show steady performance.
se: Success in learning a language depends more on ______ practice than on occasional bursts of effort.
steady
Both 'consistent' and 'steady' describe regular practice, contrasted with 'occasional bursts'.

m: the circumstances or background that help explain an event, statement or idea
x: Without any context, my mother's text saying 'Call me now' made me panic.
Before the meeting, could you give me some context on why the client is unhappy?
You cannot judge an ancient text fairly without understanding its historical context.
Journalists were accused of quoting the senator out of context.
She realized his harsh comment made sense in the context of his recent divorce.
tc: Taken out of ______, his joke sounded cruel, but anyone who had heard the whole conversation knew he meant it kindly.
Hearing 'the whole conversation' changes the meaning, so the blank refers to the surrounding circumstances.
se: Students need to understand the political ______ of the 1930s to appreciate the novel fully.
background
Both 'context' and 'background' refer to the circumstances that help explain the novel.

m: disputed; the subject of disagreement or argument
x: Who gets the front seat on long drives is a hotly contested issue in our family.
Ownership of the software became a contested matter after the two founders split.
The origins of the language remain hotly contested among linguists, with three rival theories.
The contested election result led to weeks of protests and legal challenges.
Custody of their dog became the most contested point in the couple's separation.
tc: Far from being settled, the question of who first discovered the vaccine remains fiercely ______ among historians.
'Far from being settled' signals that the question is still disputed.
se: The border region has been ______ for decades, with both countries claiming it as their own.
disputed
Both 'contested' and 'disputed' describe territory that two sides argue over.

m: to act against something in order to reduce or cancel its effect
x: A squeeze of lemon can counteract the bitterness of overcooked greens.
Managers introduced flexible hours to counteract the stress of the new workload.
Researchers are testing whether exercise can counteract the effects of a high-fat diet.
Public health campaigns aim to counteract the spread of false medical information online.
Her cheerful letters helped counteract his loneliness during the long months abroad.
tc: Doctors gave her a second drug to ______ the side effects of the first, which had been causing severe nausea.
A second drug given because of the first one's side effects is meant to cancel those effects.
se: The city planted thousands of trees to ______ the heat produced by roads and buildings.
offset
Both 'counteract' and 'offset' mean to reduce the effect of the heat by acting against it.

m: to have an equal but opposite effect on something, so that a balance is kept
x: I try to counterbalance long hours of sitting with an evening walk around the neighborhood.
The firm's strong overseas sales helped counterbalance weak demand at home.
In her thesis, careful fieldwork counterbalances the more speculative theoretical chapters.
Tax cuts for businesses were counterbalanced by higher taxes on luxury goods.
His calm nature counterbalances her quick temper, which is why their marriage works so well.
tc: To ______ the dominance of the executive, the constitution gives parliament the power to block budgets.
Giving parliament power to block budgets is meant to balance the executive's dominance.
se: Gains in the technology sector helped ______ losses in manufacturing.
offset
Both 'counterbalance' and 'offset' mean the gains cancel out the losses.

m: expressed in a particular style or form of language
x: Her refusal was couched in such polite terms that it took me a moment to realise she had said no.
The manager's criticism, couched as friendly advice, still stung the new intern.
Most legal contracts are couched in language that ordinary readers find almost impossible to follow.
The government's warning was couched in vague phrases, leaving many citizens unsure what to do.
Even when couched in kindness, his comments about my cooking made me feel defensive.
tc: Although the letter was ______ in diplomatic language, its message was unmistakably a threat.
'Although' sets up a contrast between the gentle way the message was expressed and its harsh content, so the blank means expressed or phrased.
se: The proposal was ______ in such technical jargon that the board struggled to understand it.
phrased
Both 'couched' and 'phrased' describe how the proposal was expressed, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: joined or combined with something else, often to produce a particular effect
x: Heavy rain coupled with high tides caused severe flooding in the coastal villages.
His natural talent, coupled with relentless practice, made him the best player on the team.
Rising rents coupled with stagnant wages have pushed many young families out of the city.
Strong grades coupled with a thoughtful essay can make a real difference in graduate admissions.
Her honesty, coupled with a gentle sense of humour, made her easy to confide in.
tc: Neither factor alone explains the decline; it was poor management ______ with a sudden drop in demand that finally ruined the company.
'Neither factor alone' shows that two causes worked together, so the blank must mean combined.
se: Low interest rates, ______ with generous tax breaks, encouraged a surge in home buying.
combined
Both 'coupled with' and 'combined with' mean that the two factors acted together.

m: a tendency to believe things too readily, especially without proper evidence
x: The scam relied on the credulity of elderly people who trusted anyone claiming to be from the bank.
Her excuse that the dog had eaten her laptop strained the credulity of even her most patient professor.
Investors' credulity allowed the start-up to raise millions on promises it could never keep.
Online rumours spread quickly, fuelled by public credulity and a lack of basic fact-checking.
I was embarrassed by my own credulity when I realised my friend had invented the whole story.
tc: Only someone of remarkable ______ would believe that a stranger online genuinely wanted to give away a million dollars.
Believing such an obviously false offer requires a readiness to believe anything, which is credulity.
se: The fraudster's success depended entirely on the ______ of his victims.
gullibility
Both 'credulity' and 'gullibility' mean the victims' readiness to believe whatever they were told.

m: to make or become definite, clear, and fixed in form
x: After weeks of vague discussion, our holiday plans finally crystallized when we booked the tickets.
The meeting helped crystallize the team's thinking about which product to launch first.
Writing a rough outline can crystallize your argument before you begin the full essay.
Public anger crystallized into a nationwide movement after the factory collapse.
It was only after she moved abroad that her feelings for him crystallized.
tc: His ideas had been vague and scattered for months, but a single conversation with his mentor helped them ______ into a clear research proposal.
The contrast between 'vague and scattered' and 'a clear research proposal' shows the ideas became definite.
se: The long debate finally helped the committee ______ its position on the new policy.
clarify
Both 'crystallize' and 'clarify' mean the committee made its position definite and clear.

m: occurring in cycles; happening repeatedly in the same order
x: Retail jobs are cyclical, with plenty of hiring before the holidays and layoffs soon after.
Fashion is cyclical, so the wide trousers my mother wore in the eighties are popular again.
The professor explained that many economic downturns are cyclical rather than permanent.
Dhaka's flooding problems are partly cyclical, returning every monsoon season with frustrating regularity.
Their arguments seemed cyclical: a fight, a tearful apology, a few calm weeks, then another fight.
tc: Economists insist the slump is not permanent but ______, pointing out that similar downturns have come and gone every decade.
Downturns that 'have come and gone every decade' recur in cycles, so the blank means cyclical.
se: The farmers' income is ______, rising after each harvest and falling during the lean months.
periodic
Both 'cyclical' and 'periodic' describe income that rises and falls in a repeating pattern.

m: old-fashioned; belonging to an earlier time and no longer current
x: The hotel room was clean but dated, with floral wallpaper and a bulky old television.
Our office software looks so dated that new employees assume it was installed in the nineties.
Much of the textbook's data is dated, so the lecturer asked us to check recent journals instead.
Critics said the minister's views on women in the workplace were not just dated but offensive.
He kept using slang that sounded hopelessly dated, which made his teenage daughter cringe.
tc: Once considered cutting-edge, the film's special effects now seem ______ and even laughable to younger viewers.
'Once considered cutting-edge' contrasts with 'now', showing the effects have become old-fashioned.
se: The museum's displays felt ______, so the curators decided to redesign them with interactive screens.
outdated
Both 'dated' and 'outdated' mean the displays seemed old-fashioned and in need of updating.

m: settling an issue conclusively; producing a definite result
x: In the end, a generous discount was decisive in our choice of a new phone.
Her confident presentation was the decisive factor in winning the contract for the firm.
Scientists are still waiting for decisive evidence that the new drug works in humans.
The striker's late goal proved decisive, and the home side won the final.
Her mother's advice was decisive in persuading her to give the friendship another chance.
tc: Earlier battles had settled nothing, but this one was ______: the enemy surrendered within a week.
The contrast with battles that 'settled nothing' and the quick surrender show this battle produced a final result.
se: The new DNA test provided ______ evidence that the man was innocent.
conclusive
Both 'decisive' and 'conclusive' mean the evidence settled the question beyond doubt.

m: serving only to make something look attractive; ornamental rather than useful
x: The cushions on her bed are purely decorative, and she piles them on a chair every night.
In some companies, the deputy director's role is largely decorative, with little real authority.
The essay's flowery introduction was decorative but added nothing to the argument.
Critics argue that the new council is decorative, created to look democratic while changing nothing.
He felt like a decorative presence at her family gatherings, smiling politely but never really included.
tc: The fireplace in the flat is merely ______; it has been sealed for years and has never held a fire.
Since the fireplace cannot be used, it exists only for appearance.
se: The brass handles on the cabinet are ______ rather than functional, since the doors open with a push.
ornamental
Both 'decorative' and 'ornamental' mean the handles are there for looks rather than use.

m: reasoning from general principles to reach specific, logically certain conclusions
x: Using a bit of deductive reasoning, I figured out that my roommate had borrowed my umbrella again.
Auditors use deductive methods, applying general accounting rules to spot specific errors in a company's books.
Geometry teaches deductive proof, in which each step follows necessarily from the ones before it.
Philosophers distinguish deductive arguments, whose conclusions are certain, from inductive ones, which are merely probable.
Her sharp deductive mind made it almost impossible for her friends to surprise her with a party.
tc: Unlike inductive reasoning, which moves from observations to likely generalizations, ______ reasoning starts from general premises and reaches certain conclusions.
'Unlike inductive reasoning' sets up a contrast, and moving from general premises to certain conclusions defines deductive reasoning.
se: The puzzle can be solved without guessing, using purely ______ steps from the clues given.
logical
Both 'deductive' and 'logical' describe steps that follow necessarily from the clues.

m: to fix or mark the limits or boundaries of something
x: Before we start renovating, let's delimit exactly which rooms the budget will cover.
The contract clearly delimits the consultant's responsibilities, so there's no confusion about who does what.
Your thesis proposal should delimit the scope of the study rather than promise to cover everything.
A new treaty delimits the maritime boundary between the two neighbouring countries.
Setting healthy boundaries means learning to delimit what you are willing to give in a relationship.
tc: Because the original brief was so open-ended, the researchers first had to ______ the boundaries of their inquiry.
An 'open-ended' brief needs limits set, so the blank means fix the boundaries.
se: The first chapter should ______ the scope of the project so readers know what it will not cover.
define
Both 'delimit' and 'define' mean to set out the limits of the project's scope.

m: clearly able to be shown or proved; evident
x: There is a demonstrable difference in taste between fresh coffee beans and stale ones.
Candidates must provide demonstrable experience in project management, not just a certificate.
The new teaching method produced demonstrable gains in students' reading scores within a year.
The minister's claims had no demonstrable basis in fact, as journalists quickly pointed out.
His love for her was demonstrable in a hundred small acts, from cooking her dinner to fixing her bike.
tc: The supplement's makers claim it boosts memory, yet independent trials have found no ______ effect at all.
'Yet' contrasts the makers' claims with the trial results, so the blank means able to be clearly shown.
se: Investors want ______ results, not vague promises of future growth.
verifiable
Both 'demonstrable' and 'verifiable' mean results that can be clearly shown to be real.

m: serving to describe or record things as they are, rather than judging or prescribing
x: Her travel blog is so descriptive that I could almost smell the food stalls she visited.
The report was descriptive rather than analytical, listing problems without explaining their causes.
Modern dictionaries are descriptive, recording how people actually use words rather than how they ought to.
This descriptive study records voting patterns but does not try to explain why they changed.
He wrote her a long, descriptive letter about his new life, hoping she would feel part of it.
tc: Linguists insist that grammar should be ______, not prescriptive: it should record how people really speak instead of dictating rules.
'Not prescriptive' and 'record how people really speak' point to the opposite of prescriptive, which is descriptive.
se: The novel opens with a richly ______ passage about the village at dawn.
detailed
Both 'richly descriptive' and 'richly detailed' mean the passage paints a full picture of the village.

m: to officially choose or appoint someone or something for a particular role or purpose
x: We designated the spare room as a study so the children have a quiet place to do homework.
The manager designated two senior staff to train the new recruits.
The university has designated the library's top floor a silent study zone.
The government designated the mangrove forest a protected area to save its endangered tigers.
In her will, she designated her younger brother as guardian of her children.
tc: Since the founder could no longer manage the business, the board met to ______ a successor who would take over in March.
Finding someone to 'take over' requires officially choosing a successor, so the blank means appoint.
se: The committee will ______ one member to speak to the press on its behalf.
appoint
Both 'designate' and 'appoint' mean officially choosing one member for the role.

m: to identify the nature or cause of an illness or problem by examining it
x: The mechanic diagnosed the strange noise as a loose belt and fixed it in ten minutes.
Before redesigning the website, we hired a consultant to diagnose why customers were leaving.
Medical students spend years learning to diagnose diseases from a patient's symptoms and history.
Doctors in rural clinics often lack the equipment to diagnose certain infections quickly.
After many arguments, their counsellor helped the couple diagnose the real problem: neither of them truly listened.
tc: Because its symptoms resemble those of several other illnesses, the condition is notoriously hard to ______ without a blood test.
Symptoms that resemble other illnesses make the disease hard to identify, so the blank means diagnose.
se: An experienced engineer can usually ______ the fault just by listening to the engine.
identify
Both 'diagnose' and 'identify' mean working out what the fault is.

m: faint, vague, or unpromising; not bright, distinct, or clear
x: We could barely read the menu in the restaurant's dim light.
With sales falling every quarter, the company's prospects look increasingly dim.
I have only a dim recollection of the lecture, since I was half asleep for most of it.
