Hopes of finding more survivors grew dim as rescuers searched the rubble for a third day.
She had a dim sense that something was wrong between them long before he said anything.
tc: Though she had visited the village as a toddler, her memories of it were ______, little more than blurred impressions of a river and a red roof.
'Little more than blurred impressions' restates the blank, which must mean faint or vague.
se: After two failed harvests, the farmers' chances of repaying the loan looked ______.
bleak
Both 'dim' and 'bleak' mean the chances looked unpromising.

m: unwilling or reluctant to do something
x: After a long day at work, I was disinclined to cook, so we ordered pizza.
Many employees are disinclined to speak up in meetings when the boss dominates the conversation.
Students are often disinclined to read beyond the assigned chapters unless the topic really interests them.
Voters seem disinclined to trust any party that promised reform last time and failed to deliver it.
Still hurt by the argument, she was disinclined to forgive him so quickly.
tc: Having been cheated by contractors twice before, the family was ______ to hire anyone without several references.
Being cheated before explains their reluctance, so the blank means unwilling.
se: The judge seemed ______ to accept the defence's last-minute evidence.
reluctant
Both 'disinclined' and 'reluctant' mean the judge was unwilling to accept the evidence.

m: showing that you regard someone or something as unworthy of attention or consideration
x: When I asked the shop assistant for help, she gave me a dismissive wave and kept texting.
The director was dismissive of the junior analyst's warning until the numbers proved her right.
Some reviewers were dismissive of the study, calling its sample size far too small to matter.
Officials were initially dismissive of residents' complaints about the polluted river.
His dismissive tone whenever she talked about her art slowly eroded her confidence.
tc: Rather than taking her concerns seriously, the landlord was openly ______, telling her she was simply imagining the damp.
'Rather than taking her concerns seriously' signals the opposite attitude, treating them as unworthy of attention.
se: Critics were ______ of the novel at first, though it later became a classic.
disdainful
Both 'dismissive of' and 'disdainful of' mean the critics regarded the novel as unworthy of serious attention.

m: inclined or willing to do something; having a particular attitude toward someone
x: I'm not disposed to lend him money again after he failed to repay me last time.
The board seemed well disposed toward the proposal, so we expect approval next week.
Reviewers are rarely disposed to praise a first book so warmly, which made her success remarkable.
Voters in the region are favourably disposed toward candidates who promise better roads.
After his sincere apology, she felt more kindly disposed toward her brother.
tc: Usually suspicious of strangers, the old farmer was nonetheless ______ to trust the young doctor who had saved his son.
'Nonetheless' contrasts his usual suspicion with a willingness to trust, so the blank means inclined.
se: Given her past experience, she was not ______ to believe his promises.
inclined
Both 'disposed' and 'inclined' mean she was not willing to believe him.

m: (of an animal) tamed and kept by humans; (of a person) fond of home life and housework
x: Our cat is so domesticated that she panics if she is left outside for more than ten minutes.
Since moving into his own flat, Rafi has become surprisingly domesticated, even ironing his shirts on Sundays.
The farm hires workers who are experienced in handling domesticated animals such as goats and cattle.
Archaeologists are still debating when and where wolves were first domesticated.
Scientists warn that domesticated crops have lost much of the genetic variety of their wild ancestors.
tc: Unlike their ______ cousins that sleep on sofas, feral cats survive by hunting and avoid human contact entirely.
'Unlike' contrasts feral cats with cats that live comfortably among people, so the blank means tamed.
se: Goats were among the first animals to be ______ by early farmers.
tamed
Both 'domesticated' and 'tamed' mean the goats were brought under human control and kept by farmers.

m: most powerful, influential, or important; having control over others
x: In our house, the dominant smell on Sunday mornings is fresh coffee.
She quickly became the dominant voice in team meetings, which some colleagues resented.
Darwin's theory soon became the dominant explanation for the diversity of life on Earth.
A single company holds a dominant position in the country's mobile phone market, worrying regulators.
In some relationships one partner becomes dominant, making most decisions without consulting the other.
tc: Although several parties share power in the coalition, one of them is clearly ______, controlling nearly every important ministry.
Controlling nearly every important ministry shows that one party holds the most power despite the shared arrangement.
se: Fear of losing their jobs was the ______ emotion among staff during the merger.
prevailing
Both 'dominant' and 'prevailing' mean fear was the strongest and most widespread emotion.

m: to feel uncertain about something or question whether it is true or likely
x: I doubt the shop will still be open at this hour, but let's try anyway.
Nobody doubted her ability to lead the team; the question was whether she wanted the job.
My supervisor doubts that the survey results are reliable, given how few people responded.
Many experts doubt the new policy will reduce traffic jams without better public transport.
He began to doubt whether she had ever really loved him.
tc: Although the salesman sounded confident, his evasive answers made me ______ every claim he had made about the car.
'Although' contrasts his confident tone with evasive answers, which lead the listener to question his claims.
se: Some scientists ______ the accuracy of the early measurements, since the instruments were poorly calibrated.
question
Both 'doubt' and 'question' mean the scientists are uncertain whether the measurements are accurate.

m: looking tired, strained, or pale, especially from worry, pain, or illness
x: After three nights with a crying baby, my sister looked pale and drawn.
The chief executive appeared drawn and exhausted as she announced the job cuts.
By the end of exam week, the students' faces were drawn from lack of sleep.
Relatives of the missing miners waited outside, their faces drawn with worry.
He looked thin and drawn after the divorce, and his friends began to worry about him.
tc: Weeks of sleepless nights at her father's hospital bedside had left her face pale and ______.
Sleepless nights and worry leave a person looking tired and strained, which is the meaning of drawn.
se: The soldiers returned from the long campaign looking thin and ______.
haggard
Both 'drawn' and 'haggard' mean the soldiers looked exhausted and strained.

m: able to last a long time without breaking, wearing out, or weakening
x: These hiking boots are expensive, but they're durable enough to last for years.
Over time, the team built a durable working relationship with its overseas suppliers.
Engineers are testing a more durable concrete that resists cracking in extreme heat.
Negotiators hope the ceasefire will lead to a durable peace rather than a brief pause in fighting.
Their friendship proved remarkably durable, surviving distance, marriage and decades of change.
tc: Cheap plastic chairs crack within a season, whereas these teak ones are so ______ that they often outlast their owners.
'Whereas' contrasts chairs that crack quickly with ones that outlast their owners, so the blank means long-lasting.
se: Diplomats are working toward a ______ settlement that will hold for generations.
lasting
Both 'durable' and 'lasting' describe a settlement that will endure for a long time.

m: tense, nervous, or irritable
x: I always feel edgy before a dentist appointment, even for a simple check-up.
The whole office was edgy as we waited for the results of the restructuring.
Too much coffee during exam week left me edgy and unable to concentrate.
Markets remained edgy after the central bank hinted at another interest rate rise.
He gets edgy whenever she mentions her ex-boyfriend, though he pretends not to care.
tc: Normally relaxed and good-humoured, the coach grew ______ and snapped at reporters as the crucial match approached.
'Normally relaxed' contrasts with snapping at reporters, so the blank means tense or irritable.
se: Waiting for the interview results made her ______ and unable to sleep.
anxious
Both 'edgy' and 'anxious' mean she felt nervous and tense while waiting.

m: successful in producing the intended result; effective
x: Lemon and honey is a cheap but surprisingly effectual remedy for a sore throat.
The new manager introduced effectual changes that cut delivery times in half.
Researchers are looking for an effectual way to teach maths to students who fear numbers.
Critics argue that fines alone are not an effectual deterrent against illegal dumping.
She found that an honest conversation was far more effectual than sulking for days.
tc: Previous campaigns against littering had achieved nothing, but the new deposit scheme proved remarkably ______.
'But' contrasts campaigns that achieved nothing with one that worked, so the blank means effective.
se: Doctors have yet to find any treatment that is truly ______ against this rare disease.
effective
Both 'effectual' and 'effective' mean the treatment would actually produce the desired result.

m: achieved with no apparent effort; done easily and naturally
x: She speaks French with such effortless fluency that people assume she grew up in Paris.
His presentations look effortless, but he rehearses each one for hours.
With enough practice, solving these equations will eventually become almost effortless for you.
The dancer's effortless grace on stage hid years of painful, exhausting training.
Being with her felt effortless; they could talk for hours or sit in comfortable silence.
tc: The pianist's performance appeared ______, yet it was the product of decades of exhausting practice.
'Yet' contrasts the appearance of the performance with the exhausting practice behind it, so the blank means seemingly easy.
se: The champion made the steep climb look ______, barely breaking a sweat.
easy
Both 'effortless' and 'easy' mean the climb seemed to require no real effort.

m: a self-centred person who is chiefly concerned with their own interests
x: Only an egoist would take the last slice of cake without asking if anyone else wanted it.
Her boss is such an egoist that he presents the team's work as entirely his own.
In ethics class we discussed whether a pure egoist could ever act truly unselfishly.
Historians have portrayed the emperor as an egoist who waged wars mainly for personal glory.
She eventually left him, tired of living with an egoist who never asked about her day.
tc: Unlike his generous sister, who gave away most of her salary, Karim was the sort of ______ whose every decision served only himself.
The contrast with a generous sister and decisions that serve 'only himself' point to a self-centred person.
se: The novel's hero is a ruthless ______ who cares for nobody but himself.
egotist
Both 'egoist' and 'egotist' describe a self-centred person who cares only about himself.

m: relating to the most basic or simple aspects of a subject
x: Even an elementary knowledge of first aid can save a life in an emergency.
The report contained elementary mistakes that any junior accountant should have caught.
This textbook assumes only an elementary understanding of algebra.
Washing hands is an elementary precaution that greatly reduces the spread of disease.
Remembering her birthday seemed like an elementary courtesy, yet he forgot it again.
tc: The course is not for experts; it covers only the most ______ principles of economics, such as supply and demand.
'Not for experts' and the simple example of supply and demand show the blank means basic.
se: The engineer was embarrassed to have made such ______ errors in his calculations.
basic
Both 'elementary' and 'basic' describe simple errors that an expert should not make.

m: to raise to a higher position, rank, or level; to improve morally or intellectually
x: A good pair of earrings can elevate a simple dress into something special.
After ten years of loyal service, she was elevated to the position of vice president.
Great literature can elevate the mind and broaden our sympathy for others.
The scandal elevated an obscure local issue into a matter of national debate.
His kindness during her illness elevated him in her eyes from colleague to true friend.
tc: Critics once dismissed comics as cheap entertainment, but recent graphic novels have helped ______ the form to the status of serious art.
The contrast between 'cheap entertainment' and 'serious art' shows the blank means raise in status.
se: The company hopes the new design will ______ the brand above its cheaper competitors.
raise
Both 'elevate' and 'raise' mean lifting the brand to a higher level than its competitors.

m: beset by many difficulties, criticisms, or attacks
x: After the restaurant's third bad review, the embattled owner closed for renovations.
The embattled chief executive insisted he would not resign despite the accounting scandal.
The embattled professor defended her controversial study at a crowded faculty meeting.
Aid finally reached the embattled town after weeks of fighting cut off its food supply.
Feeling embattled at home and at work, he started seeing a therapist.
tc: Facing protests in the streets and a revolt within his own party, the ______ prime minister called an emergency meeting.
Being attacked both in the streets and from within his party shows he is beset by difficulties.
se: The ______ company faced lawsuits, falling sales and a hostile takeover bid all at once.
beleaguered
Both 'embattled' and 'beleaguered' describe a company under pressure from many problems at once.

m: in the process of coming into being or becoming prominent
x: Our neighbourhood has an emergent café culture, with three new coffee shops opening this year.
The firm invests in emergent technologies before they become mainstream.
Her thesis examines emergent patterns of behaviour in large online communities.
Analysts are closely watching the emergent middle class in several fast-growing Asian economies.
He was aware of an emergent fondness for her that he wasn't yet ready to admit.
tc: The field of quantum computing is still ______; only a handful of working machines exist, and their commercial uses are not yet clear.
Only a handful of machines and unclear uses show the field is just coming into being.
se: Several ______ democracies are struggling to build independent courts.
emerging
Both 'emergent' and 'emerging' describe democracies that are still developing.

m: expressing something forcefully and clearly; definite
x: When I asked if she wanted to come camping, her answer was an emphatic no.
The manager was emphatic that no one should work overtime without approval.
My professor was emphatic about citing every source, warning that plagiarism meant automatic failure.
The government won an emphatic victory, taking nearly two-thirds of the seats.
He gave an emphatic denial when his wife asked whether he had forgotten their anniversary.
tc: Far from hedging her answer, the witness was ______, declaring without hesitation that she had seen the defendant at the scene.
'Far from hedging' and 'without hesitation' show she spoke forcefully and clearly.
se: The doctor was ______ that I should rest for at least two weeks.
insistent
Both 'emphatic' and 'insistent' mean the doctor stated the advice firmly and clearly.

m: to obtain someone's help, support, or participation
x: I enlisted my brother to help me move the sofa up three flights of stairs.
The project manager enlisted two engineers from another department to meet the deadline.
The researchers enlisted hundreds of volunteers to record bird sightings across the country.
Campaigners have enlisted the support of doctors in their fight against tobacco advertising.
Desperate to win her back, he enlisted her best friend to plead on his behalf.
tc: Unable to finish the mural alone, the artist decided to ______ several local students to help with the painting.
Being unable to finish alone explains why she sought helpers, so the blank means recruit.
se: The charity hopes to ______ more young people for its literacy programme.
recruit
Both 'enlist' and 'recruit' mean bringing in new people to take part.

m: to imagine something as a future possibility
x: I never envisioned myself living in a small town, but I've grown to love it.
The founders envision a company where every employee owns shares.
Few scientists in the 1950s could envision the computing power we now carry in our pockets.
City planners envision a capital with fewer cars and many more parks and cycle lanes.
She had envisioned a quiet wedding, but her family invited four hundred guests.
tc: The architect could ______ the finished museum long before a single brick was laid, describing its galleries in vivid detail.
Describing the building before it existed shows she pictured it in her mind as a future reality.
se: It is hard to ______ a time when the internet did not exist.
imagine
Both 'envision' and 'imagine' mean forming a mental picture of that time.

m: respect and admiration for someone
x: Our family doctor is held in great esteem by everyone in the neighbourhood.
Her colleagues' esteem meant more to her than any bonus.
As a mark of esteem, the students dedicated their yearbook to their retiring headmaster.
Public esteem for politicians has fallen sharply in recent decades.
He wanted to win her esteem, not just her affection.
tc: Although she was never rich or famous, her honesty earned her the deep ______ of everyone who knew her.
Honesty earning something from others points to their respect and admiration.
se: The scientist was held in high ______ by her peers for her careful, honest research.
regard
Both 'held in high esteem' and 'held in high regard' mean her peers greatly respected her.

m: relating to moral principles; morally right and acceptable
x: We try to buy coffee from ethical brands that pay farmers fairly.
Accountants face an ethical dilemma when a client asks them to hide losses.
All research involving human subjects must be approved by an ethical review board.
Critics question whether it is ethical for companies to collect so much personal data.
Keeping quiet about his friend's cheating posed a difficult ethical question for him.
tc: Though the plan was perfectly legal, many board members felt it was not ______, since it would exploit vulnerable customers.
'Though... legal' contrasts legality with morality, and exploiting vulnerable customers is morally wrong.
se: The judge was known as a deeply ______ man who never accepted favours.
principled
Both 'ethical' and 'principled' describe a man guided by strong moral standards.

m: to describe something as larger, better, or worse than it really is
x: Don't exaggerate; the traffic jam lasted ten minutes, not an hour.
Some candidates exaggerate their experience on their CVs, hoping no one will check.
The study's authors admit that their small sample may exaggerate the drug's benefits.
Media reports often exaggerate the risks of rare diseases and cause needless panic.
She tends to exaggerate her problems, so her friends don't always take her seriously.
tc: The fisherman tends to ______ his catches: a fish he describes as huge usually turns out to be barely the length of his hand.
A 'huge' fish that is barely hand-length shows he overstates things.
se: Politicians often ______ their achievements in the months before an election.
overstate
Both 'exaggerate' and 'overstate' mean presenting the achievements as greater than they are.

m: more than is necessary, normal, or reasonable
x: Excessive screen time before bed can make it harder to fall asleep.
The company was fined for charging excessive fees to its customers.
Excessive reliance on a single source can seriously weaken a research paper.
Human rights groups condemned the police's excessive use of force against protesters.
His jealousy became excessive, and she felt she couldn't even talk to a male colleague.
tc: A little salt improves the flavour, but the cook's ______ use of it made the soup almost impossible to eat.
'But' contrasts a helpful amount with an amount that ruined the soup, so the blank means too much.
se: Critics argued that the bonuses paid to bank executives were ______ given the losses.
exorbitant
Both 'excessive' and 'exorbitant' mean the bonuses were far larger than was reasonable.

m: to deliberately leave out, keep out, or rule out
x: The price excludes breakfast, so we'll have to eat somewhere nearby.
Contract workers were excluded from the bonus scheme, which caused resentment.
The researchers excluded participants who had taken antibiotics in the previous month.
Police have not excluded the possibility that the fire was started deliberately.
She felt excluded when her friends planned a trip without telling her.
tc: The club's rules were designed to ______ newcomers, admitting only those whose parents had been members.
Admitting only members' children shows the rules were meant to keep others out.
se: The organisers decided to ______ anyone under eighteen from the competition.
bar
Both 'exclude from' and 'bar from' mean not allowing under-eighteens to take part.

m: serving to explain something or make it clear
x: The new washing machine came with an explanatory booklet in six languages.
Please attach a short explanatory note if your expense claim is unusually high.
Each chapter ends with explanatory notes that clarify difficult terms.
Scientists are still debating the explanatory power of the theory.
He sent her a long explanatory message about why he had missed dinner, but she wasn't convinced.
tc: Because the formula baffled most readers, the editor added ______ footnotes that clarified each step.
Footnotes added to clarify a baffling formula serve to explain it.
se: The textbook includes ______ diagrams that show how the heart pumps blood.
illustrative
Both 'explanatory' and 'illustrative' describe diagrams that help make the process clear.

m: done to investigate or find out more about something, often as a first step
x: We had an exploratory chat with a builder about extending the kitchen.
The two companies held exploratory talks about a possible merger.
Her exploratory study suggests a link between sleep and memory, though more research is needed.
Doctors performed exploratory surgery to find the cause of his pain.
Their first date felt exploratory, both of them trying to work out what the other wanted.
tc: These are only ______ discussions; no decision will be made until both sides have gathered more information.
'Only' and the need to gather more information show the talks are a first, investigative step.
se: The firm began ______ drilling to see whether the site contained oil.
preliminary
Both 'exploratory' and 'preliminary' describe early drilling done to investigate the site.

m: spending or using too much; going beyond what is reasonable or appropriate
x: Buying a new phone every year seems extravagant when the old one still works.
The chief executive's extravagant expense claims, including first-class flights, angered shareholders.
The paper makes extravagant claims that its limited data cannot support.
Critics condemned the extravagant wedding as tasteless while millions struggled to afford food.
He made extravagant promises to her, but rarely kept even the small ones.
tc: Her grandparents saved every coin and reused everything, so they were shocked by her ______ habit of buying designer clothes she never wore.
The contrast with grandparents who saved everything shows the blank means wastefully excessive.
se: The minister was criticised for his ______ spending on official cars and parties.
lavish
Both 'extravagant' and 'lavish' describe spending far beyond what is reasonable.

m: based on or concerned with facts; true and accurate
x: Just give me the factual details of the accident; I don't need your opinion.
The report should be factual and concise, not full of speculation.
Students must check every factual claim in their essays against reliable sources.
The newspaper apologised for a factual error in its story about the election.
Her tone was factual and calm as she told him the relationship was over.
tc: The documentary claims to be ______, yet much of it consists of invented dialogue and dramatic reconstructions.
'Yet' contrasts the claim with invented material, so the blank means based on facts.
se: The witness gave a strictly ______ account of what she had seen, avoiding any guesses.
accurate
Both 'factual' and 'accurate' describe an account that sticks to what really happened.

m: to make or shape something, especially skilfully or from limited materials
x: We fashioned a makeshift tent out of bedsheets and broom handles.
The team fashioned a workable plan from a dozen conflicting proposals.
Archaeologists believe early humans fashioned tools from stone and bone more than two million years ago.
The new constitution was carefully fashioned to protect the rights of religious and ethnic minorities.
She fashioned a new life for herself after the divorce, starting a business and making new friends.
tc: Stranded on the island without tools, the sailors had to ______ fishing hooks out of shells and bits of wire.
Having no tools and only shells and wire implies they had to make the hooks by hand.
se: The sculptor can ______ delicate birds from a single block of wood.
craft
Both 'fashion' and 'craft' mean skilfully making the birds from the wood.

m: free from any mistakes or defects; perfect
x: Her English is faultless, so people are surprised to learn it is her third language.
The event was faultless from start to finish, and the client wrote to thank us.
His faultless calculations earned him full marks on the physics exam.
Investigators later concluded that the pilot's handling of the engine failure had been faultless.
She was not looking for a faultless partner, just someone kind and honest.
tc: Although critics searched for weaknesses, they had to admit that her performance was ______, without a single wrong note.
'Without a single wrong note' restates the blank, which means perfect.
se: The gymnast's routine was ______, earning her the highest score of the evening.
flawless
Both 'faultless' and 'flawless' mean the routine had no mistakes.

m: a distinctive or characteristic part or quality of something
x: The best feature of our new flat is the large balcony overlooking the park.
The latest software update adds a feature that lets users schedule emails.
A key feature of the course is that students work on real company projects.
Monsoon flooding is a recurring feature of life in Bangladesh's low-lying districts.
Her laugh was the feature he loved most about her.
tc: Long, cold winters are the defining ______ of the region's climate; nearly every account of the area mentions them.
Something mentioned in nearly every account is a characteristic part, so the blank means feature.
se: The most striking ______ of the building is its curved glass roof.
aspect
Both 'feature' and 'aspect' refer to a distinctive part of the building.

m: capable of producing abundant crops, offspring, or ideas; richly productive
x: My grandmother grows tomatoes and chillies in the fertile soil behind her house.
The brainstorming session proved fertile, producing more ideas than we could use.
The early twentieth century was a fertile period for physics, with major discoveries in relativity and quantum theory.
The delta's fertile plains have supported large farming communities for centuries.
His fertile imagination turned every bedtime story into an adventure for his children.
tc: Unlike the barren desert to the north, the river valley is so ______ that farmers harvest three crops a year.
'Unlike the barren desert' and three harvests a year show the valley is highly productive.
se: The novelist's ______ mind produced dozens of plots and characters every year.
inventive
Both 'fertile' and 'inventive' describe a mind that produces many new ideas.

m: invented or not real; false
x: He gave the hotel a fictitious name because he didn't want anyone to know he was there.
The accountant created fictitious invoices to hide the missing money.
The novel is set in a fictitious town, though readers recognise many real landmarks.
Police say the caller reported a fictitious emergency, wasting hours of officers' time.
She realised that the exciting life he had described to her was largely fictitious.
tc: The company claimed to have hundreds of clients, but investigators found that most of them were ______ names with no real addresses.
Names with 'no real addresses', contrasted with the company's claims, show they were invented.
se: The fraudster opened several bank accounts under ______ names.
false
Both 'fictitious' and 'false' mean the names were invented rather than real.

m: having limits or bounds; not infinite
x: We have a finite amount of money for the holiday, so let's choose activities carefully.
With finite staff and time, the manager had to decide which projects to drop.
In mathematics, a finite set contains a fixed, limited number of elements.
Oil is a finite resource, and countries must prepare for a future without it.
Knowing that their time together was finite made every visit with her grandfather precious.
tc: Although many people treat clean water as if it were endless, it is actually ______ and must be carefully conserved.
'Although' contrasts 'endless' with the true state, so the blank means limited.
se: The planet has ______ resources, so unlimited growth is impossible.
limited
Both 'finite' and 'limited' mean the planet's resources will eventually run out.

m: having a fault or weakness that makes it imperfect or wrong
x: The vase was slightly flawed, so I bought it at half price.
Our sales forecast was flawed because it ignored seasonal demand.
The study's conclusions are flawed because the sample excluded women entirely.
Critics say the election system is deeply flawed and favours larger parties.
He was flawed like everyone else, but she loved him all the same.
tc: Although the argument seemed convincing at first, closer inspection showed it was ______, resting on a false assumption.
'Although' and 'resting on a false assumption' show the argument has a serious weakness.
se: The investigation was ______ from the start, because key witnesses were never interviewed.
faulty
Both 'flawed' and 'faulty' mean the investigation had a serious weakness.

m: able to change or adapt easily to new conditions; not rigid
x: My manager is flexible about working hours as long as the reports reach her by Friday afternoon.
Our university offers a flexible timetable, so students can take evening classes while working part-time.
Living in Dhaka teaches you to be flexible, because a twenty-minute trip can easily take two hours.
Economists argue that a more flexible labour market helps companies respond quickly to sudden changes in demand.
Good friendships survive because both people stay flexible and forgive each other's small habits and moods.
tc: Unlike her predecessor, who insisted that every rule be followed to the letter, the new principal was remarkably ______ when students had genuine problems.
'Unlike her predecessor, who insisted that every rule be followed to the letter' signals a contrast, so the blank must mean willing to adapt.
se: The project timeline is fairly ______, so we can move the deadline if the client needs more time.
adjustable
Both 'flexible' and 'adjustable' describe a timeline that can be changed, which the clause about moving the deadline confirms.

m: looking unfriendly, threatening or unpleasant, so that people are discouraged from approaching
x: The old house at the end of the lane looked so forbidding that children dared each other to touch its gate.
Behind his forbidding expression, our new supervisor turned out to be patient and surprisingly funny.
The professor's forbidding manner kept most students from asking questions during office hours.
Rescue teams struggled to reach the villages, as the mountain terrain was steep, icy and forbidding.
She found her fiancé's father forbidding at first, but he warmed up after a long conversation about cricket.
tc: Although the castle appeared ______ from the road, with its dark walls and narrow windows, the staff inside were warm and welcoming.
'Although' sets up a contrast with 'warm and welcoming', and the dark walls suggest the blank must mean threatening or unfriendly.
se: With its dark clouds and crashing waves, the coastline looked ______ to the tired sailors.
menacing
Both 'forbidding' and 'menacing' describe a threatening appearance, matching the dark clouds and crashing waves.

m: able to be predicted or known in advance
x: Rain delays at this time of year were entirely foreseeable, yet nobody packed an umbrella for the trip.
The manager said the office will stay closed on Saturdays for the foreseeable future.
In my research proposal, I listed every foreseeable problem and explained how I would deal with it.
Investigators concluded that the bridge collapse was a foreseeable result of years of poor maintenance.
Their breakup felt sudden to friends, but in hindsight the tensions made it quite foreseeable.
tc: The flooding was hardly a surprise; given the blocked drains and the heavy rain forecast, it was entirely ______.
'Hardly a surprise' is restated after the semicolon, so the blank must mean predictable.
se: Engineers are expected to plan for every ______ failure in the system before construction begins.
predictable
Both 'foreseeable' and 'predictable' refer to failures that can be anticipated in advance.

m: following a fixed pattern or formula; unoriginal and predictable
x: The movie was so formulaic that I guessed the ending within the first fifteen minutes.
Many cover letters sound formulaic because applicants copy the same phrases from online templates.
My writing tutor warned that formulaic essays rarely impress admissions committees, however correct the grammar is.
Critics dismissed the minister's speech as formulaic, full of familiar promises and empty slogans.
His birthday messages had become formulaic, and she longed for something that sounded personal.
tc: The band's early albums were bold and experimental, but their recent songs have become ______, repeating the same chords and themes.
'But' contrasts with 'bold and experimental', and 'repeating the same chords and themes' shows the blank must mean following a fixed pattern.
se: Reviewers praised the actors but found the script ______ and full of clichés.
unoriginal
Both 'formulaic' and 'unoriginal' describe a script lacking fresh ideas, as 'full of clichés' confirms.

m: to fail or collapse, especially after running into difficulties; (of a ship) to sink
x: Our weekend plans foundered when half the group came down with the flu.
The merger foundered after the two companies failed to agree on who would lead the new board.
Her thesis nearly foundered because the lab equipment kept breaking down in the final semester.
Peace talks foundered last week when both sides refused to compromise on the border question.
Their marriage began to founder under the strain of long working hours and constant money worries.
tc: Despite a promising start, the start-up began to ______ once its main investor withdrew funding and key staff resigned.
'Despite a promising start' signals a reversal, and the loss of funding and staff shows the blank must mean fail.
se: Without a clear plan for repayment, the project is likely to ______ within a year.
collapse
Both 'founder' and 'collapse' mean to fail completely, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: consisting of small, disconnected parts; incomplete
x: I only have fragmentary memories of my grandfather, mostly of his laugh and his old radio.
The police had fragmentary information about the theft, so they appealed to the public for help.
Historians must reconstruct the ancient city's daily life from fragmentary records and broken pottery.
Early reports from the flooded districts were fragmentary, making it hard to estimate the damage.
Her letters from abroad were fragmentary and rushed, which left her mother anxious for more news.
tc: Because only a few pages of the diary survived the fire, our picture of the writer's final years remains ______.
'Only a few pages ... survived' is the cause, so the blank must mean incomplete or in pieces.
se: The evidence against the suspect was ______, so the prosecutor hesitated to bring charges.
incomplete
Both 'fragmentary' and 'incomplete' describe evidence with gaps, which explains the prosecutor's hesitation.

m: to visit a particular place often or habitually
x: We used to frequent a small tea stall near campus that served the best singara in the neighbourhood.
Clients who frequent the downtown branch often ask for the same friendly cashier by name.
During exam season, students frequent the library until it closes at midnight.
Rare birds frequent these wetlands every winter, attracting photographers from across the region.
After the divorce, he stopped frequenting the restaurants he and his wife had loved.
tc: The café became so popular with writers that many of them would ______ it daily, spending entire afternoons at the same corner tables.
'Daily' and 'spending entire afternoons at the same corner tables' show the blank must mean visit habitually.
se: Locals who ______ the market say the prices are lowest just before closing time.
patronize
Both 'frequent' and 'patronize' mean to visit or shop at a place regularly.

m: to prevent a plan or effort from succeeding; to thwart
x: Heavy traffic frustrated our attempt to reach the airport in time for the evening flight.
Constant changes in client requirements frustrated every effort to finish the software on schedule.
A lack of reliable data frustrated the researchers' plans to publish their findings this year.
Opposition parties frustrated the government's attempt to rush the bill through parliament.
Her shyness frustrated his hopes of getting to know her better at the wedding.
tc: Although the rebels expected an easy victory, the defenders managed to ______ every attack by blocking the narrow mountain pass.
'Although' contrasts with the expected easy victory, and 'blocking the narrow mountain pass' shows the blank must mean defeat or thwart.
se: Poor weather may ______ the rescue team's efforts to reach the stranded climbers.
thwart
Both 'frustrate' and 'thwart' mean to stop an effort from succeeding.

m: feeling or causing sadness or hopelessness; pessimistic
x: He was gloomy all evening after learning that his favourite team had lost again.
Analysts gave a gloomy forecast for the third quarter, warning of falling sales and layoffs.
My supervisor was gloomy about my results until I showed her the corrected calculations.
The report paints a gloomy picture of rising sea levels along the coastline.
She tried to cheer up her gloomy brother by taking him out for ice cream.
tc: Although the economy had begun to recover, most investors remained ______, convinced that another crash was just around the corner.
'Although' contrasts with the recovery, and 'convinced that another crash was ... around the corner' shows the blank must mean pessimistic.
se: After weeks without a job offer, Rafi grew increasingly ______ about his future.
pessimistic
Both 'gloomy' and 'pessimistic' describe a hopeless outlook caused by weeks of rejection.

m: happening slowly over a long period, in small steps
x: After the surgery, my father made a gradual recovery and was walking again within a month.
The company plans a gradual shift to remote work rather than closing the office overnight.
Learning a language is a gradual process, so don't expect fluency after a few weeks.
Scientists have recorded a gradual rise in average temperatures over the past century.
The change in their friendship was so gradual that neither of them noticed when it turned into love.
tc: Unlike the sudden crash of the factory's sales, the decline in the town's population was ______, taking place over several decades.
'Unlike the sudden crash' and 'over several decades' show the blank must mean slow and step by step.
se: Doctors recommend a ______ increase in exercise rather than starting with intense workouts.
steady
Both 'gradual' and 'steady' describe an increase that builds slowly, in contrast to intense workouts from the start.

m: introducing new ideas or methods for the first time; pioneering
x: The restaurant's groundbreaking menu mixes Bengali spices with classic French cooking techniques.
Our team received an award for its groundbreaking work on low-cost water filters.
The professor's groundbreaking paper changed how engineers think about earthquake-resistant buildings.
The groundbreaking treatment could help millions of patients who do not respond to existing drugs.
She described the novel as groundbreaking, saying it changed how she viewed her own family.
tc: Far from repeating earlier studies, the young scientist's research was truly ______, opening an entirely new field of inquiry.
'Far from repeating earlier studies' and 'opening an entirely new field' show the blank must mean pioneering.
se: The architect became famous for her ______ designs, which no one had attempted before.
pioneering
Both 'groundbreaking' and 'pioneering' describe designs that were the first of their kind.

m: not based on any good reason or evidence
x: My fear that I had left the stove on turned out to be groundless.
The manager dismissed the complaints as groundless after reviewing the security footage.
Reviewers found the author's main claim groundless, since none of her sources supported it.
Health officials stressed that rumours about the vaccine's side effects were completely groundless.
Her jealousy was groundless; he had simply been planning a surprise party for her.
tc: Investigators found no evidence whatsoever to support the allegations, which they declared entirely ______.
'No evidence whatsoever to support' shows the blank must mean without basis.
se: The rumours of layoffs proved ______, and every employee kept their job.
unfounded
Both 'groundless' and 'unfounded' mean not based on fact, as everyone keeping their job shows.

m: cautious and careful not to reveal too much or commit oneself
x: When I asked about her new job, she gave a guarded reply and quickly changed the subject.
The CEO was guarded about the merger, saying only that talks were at an early stage.
Scientists offered guarded optimism about the trial results, noting that the sample was small.
Officials gave a guarded welcome to the ceasefire, warning that previous agreements had quickly collapsed.
After being hurt before, he was guarded with new people and slow to share his feelings.
tc: Rather than speaking openly about her plans, the actress gave only ______ answers, revealing almost nothing to reporters.
'Rather than speaking openly' and 'revealing almost nothing' show the blank must mean cautious and reserved.
se: The minister's comments on the budget were ______, as he did not want to commit to any figures.
cautious
Both 'guarded' and 'cautious' describe careful comments made by someone avoiding commitment.

m: practical and realistic, not influenced by emotion
x: My grandmother was a hardheaded shopper who never paid a taka more than something was worth.
We need a hardheaded assessment of the costs before we promise the client anything.
Her supervisor gave hardheaded advice: choose a thesis topic that can actually be finished in two years.
Voters wanted hardheaded solutions to inflation, not inspiring speeches about the nation's future.
Even in love, she remained hardheaded and insisted they discuss finances before getting married.
tc: Unlike his idealistic partner, who dreamed of changing the world, the investor took a ______ view, focusing only on profits and risks.
'Unlike his idealistic partner' signals a contrast, and 'focusing only on profits and risks' shows the blank must mean practical and unsentimental.
se: A ______ negotiator, she refused to let sympathy for the seller affect the price she offered.
pragmatic
Both 'hardheaded' and 'pragmatic' describe someone guided by practical considerations rather than feelings.

m: to make different things consistent or compatible; to bring into agreement
x: We tried to harmonize our holiday plans so that both families could celebrate together.
The two departments must harmonize their procedures before the new system goes live.
Researchers worked to harmonize data collected by labs in five different countries.
European nations agreed to harmonize their safety standards for electric vehicles.
After years of arguing, the siblings learned to harmonize their very different personalities.
tc: Since each branch used its own conflicting accounting rules, head office decided to ______ them into a single consistent system.
Turning 'conflicting' rules into 'a single consistent system' shows the blank must mean bring into agreement.
se: The new policy aims to ______ tax rules across the region so that businesses face the same requirements everywhere.
standardize
Both 'harmonize' and 'standardize' mean to make rules uniform, as 'the same requirements everywhere' confirms.

m: warm, enthusiastic and sincere
x: Our neighbours gave us a hearty welcome when we moved into the building.
The team received hearty congratulations from the director after landing the contract.
The proposal won hearty support from local residents, who had long demanded a new hospital.
He gave his old friend a hearty hug and a slap on the back at the airport.
She let out a hearty laugh when she saw the lopsided cake her children had made.
tc: Far from being lukewarm, the crowd's response to the singer was ______, with people cheering and clapping for several minutes.
'Far from being lukewarm' and the long cheering show the blank must mean warm and enthusiastic.
se: The host gave each guest a ______ handshake and thanked them for coming.
cordial
Both 'hearty' and 'cordial' describe a warm, friendly greeting.

m: uncertain or reluctant to act or speak
x: I was hesitant to try the street food at first, but now I eat fuchka every weekend.
Many employees are hesitant to criticize the new policy openly.
New students are often hesitant to ask questions in large lecture halls.
Banks have been hesitant to lend to small farmers since the drought.
She gave a hesitant smile, unsure whether he still wanted to be friends.
tc: Although he was usually confident in meetings, Arif was ______ about sharing his idea, fearing it might sound foolish.
'Although he was usually confident' signals a contrast, and 'fearing it might sound foolish' shows the blank must mean reluctant.
se: Investors remain ______ to commit money until the election results are known.
reluctant
Both 'hesitant' and 'reluctant' describe unwillingness to act until uncertainty is resolved.

m: to draw special attention to something; to emphasize
x: Our trip to the village highlighted how much we rely on electricity in daily life.
The quarterly report highlights the need for better customer service in our regional offices.
Your personal statement should highlight the projects where you showed leadership.
The study highlights the link between air pollution and childhood asthma in big cities.
In her toast, she highlighted the many times her sister had helped the family through hard times.
tc: Rather than hiding the flaws in the design, the engineer chose to ______ them so that the team could fix them early.
'Rather than hiding' signals the opposite action, so the blank must mean draw attention to.
se: The speaker used several examples to ______ the importance of saving for retirement.
emphasize
Both 'highlight' and 'emphasize' mean to draw special attention to the importance of something.

m: understanding of a situation or event only after it has happened
x: In hindsight, I should have left for the airport an hour earlier.
With hindsight, the manager admitted that hiring so quickly had been a mistake.
Historians benefit from hindsight that the leaders of the time simply did not have.
Hindsight shows that the warning signs of the financial crisis were visible for years.
With the benefit of hindsight, she realized their relationship had been failing for a long time.
tc: It is easy to criticize decisions using ______; at the time, nobody could have known how the crisis would unfold.
'At the time, nobody could have known' contrasts with knowledge gained later, so the blank must mean understanding after the event.
se: In ______, the decision to sell the shares so early looks like a serious error.
retrospect
'In hindsight' and 'in retrospect' both mean looking back after the event.

m: lacking real value, meaning or sincerity
x: His apology sounded hollow, because he made the same rude comment the next day.
Without the team's star engineer, the company's promises of faster delivery rang hollow.
Critics called the university's commitment to diversity hollow, since few scholarships were offered.
Winning the match on a technicality felt like a hollow victory for the players.
After the funeral, her friends' cheerful words seemed hollow and could not ease her grief.
tc: The politician's pledges to fight corruption proved ______, since he quietly protected his corrupt allies once elected.
Protecting corrupt allies contradicts the pledges, so the blank must mean insincere or empty.
se: Their promises of reform sounded ______ to voters who had heard the same words many times before.
empty
Both 'hollow' and 'empty' describe promises without real substance or sincerity.

m: to make things uniform or similar, removing differences between them
x: Supermarket chains have homogenized our diets, so the same snacks appear in every city.
Head office wants to homogenize branding so that every branch looks exactly the same.
Some teachers worry that standardized testing will homogenize the curriculum across schools.
Critics argue that global social media is homogenizing local cultures and languages.
She feared that living with his family would homogenize her tastes until she lost her own identity.
tc: Local food lovers fear that global fast-food chains will ______ regional cuisines, erasing the variety that once made each town's cooking distinctive.
'Erasing the variety' shows the blank must mean make uniform.
se: Big record labels are accused of trying to ______ popular music so that every song sounds alike.
standardize
Both 'homogenize' and 'standardize' mean to make things uniform, as 'every song sounds alike' confirms.

m: to suggest a possible explanation that has not yet been proven
x: When the cat stopped eating, we hypothesized that the new food was the problem.
The marketing team hypothesized that younger customers preferred shorter videos, so they ran a test.
In my thesis, I hypothesize that soil salinity reduces rice yields in coastal districts.
Astronomers hypothesize that a ninth planet may lie far beyond Neptune.
She hypothesized that his silence meant he was angry, but he was simply tired.
tc: Lacking any direct evidence, the scientists could only ______ about the cause of the mass extinction until new fossils were found.
'Lacking any direct evidence' shows they could only propose unproven explanations, which is what the blank means.
se: Some doctors ______ that the rash is caused by an allergy, but tests are needed to confirm it.
theorize
Both 'hypothesize' and 'theorize' mean to propose an explanation that still needs to be confirmed.

m: to regard or show something as perfect or better than it really is
x: People often idealize their childhood and forget how often they were bored or scolded.
New employees tend to idealize the company until they face their first round of budget cuts.
Some historians idealize village life, ignoring the poverty and disease that many villagers suffered.
Advertisements idealize family life, showing smiling parents who never seem tired or stressed.
It is dangerous to idealize a partner, because nobody can live up to perfection forever.
tc: Rather than ______ his late father, the biographer described the man's flaws as honestly as his achievements.
'Rather than' contrasts with describing flaws honestly, so the blank must mean portray as perfect.
se: Films often ______ rural life, ignoring the hard work and hardship it involves.
romanticize
Both 'idealize' and 'romanticize' mean to present something as better than it is, as 'ignoring the hard work' confirms.

m: helping to explain or clarify something; revealing
x: Talking to my grandmother about her youth was illuminating; I finally understood her strict rules.
The training session was illuminating, especially the part on handling difficult clients.
Her lecture offered an illuminating account of how bacteria develop resistance to antibiotics.
The report provides an illuminating look at why young voters distrust traditional parties.
Their honest conversation about money was illuminating for both of them after years of silent tension.
tc: I had always found the topic baffling, but the professor's clear and careful explanation was genuinely ______.
'But' contrasts with 'baffling', and 'clear and careful explanation' shows the blank must mean clarifying.
se: The documentary was ______, giving viewers a clear picture of how the economy really works.
enlightening
Both 'illuminating' and 'enlightening' mean helping people understand something clearly.

m: serving as an example or helping to explain something
x: Her messy desk is illustrative of how busy she has been lately.
The trainer gave several illustrative examples of poor customer service.
The textbook includes illustrative diagrams that make complex circuits much easier to follow.
The town's empty shops are illustrative of the wider decline in rural economies.
That argument was illustrative of their relationship: both wanted to win, and neither wanted to listen.
tc: The figures in this chart are not real sales data; they are merely ______, meant to show how the calculation works.
'Not real' data 'meant to show how the calculation works' shows the blank must mean serving as an example.
se: The case is ______ of a broader problem in the healthcare system.
representative
Both 'illustrative of' and 'representative of' mean that the case serves as a typical example of the wider problem.

m: having or showing creativity and new ideas
x: My niece is so imaginative that she turns cardboard boxes into castles and spaceships.
We need an imaginative solution, because the usual marketing tactics are no longer working.
The judges praised her imaginative approach to a classic engineering problem.
The city's imaginative use of old warehouses as art studios has revived the area.
He planned an imaginative proposal, hiding the ring inside a book she had always wanted.
tc: Instead of following the usual textbook methods, the teacher designed ______ lessons that turned grammar into games and puzzles.
'Instead of following the usual textbook methods' and turning grammar into games show the blank must mean creative.
se: The architect's ______ design turned a dull car park into a lively public garden.
inventive
Both 'imaginative' and 'inventive' describe a creative, original design.

m: the quality of being direct, vivid and immediate, giving a sense of urgency or involvement
x: Video calls lack the immediacy of sitting together at the same dinner table.
The immediacy of the deadline forced the whole team to work through the weekend.
Students respond well to the immediacy of hands-on experiments compared with reading about them.
Live reporting gives the news an immediacy that printed newspapers cannot match.
There was an immediacy to her grief that made everyone in the room fall silent.
tc: The photographs, taken just moments after the explosion, have a raw ______ that makes viewers feel they are standing at the scene.
'Taken just moments after' and making viewers 'feel they are standing at the scene' show the blank must mean directness or vividness.
se: The novel's first-person narration lends its war scenes a striking ______.
vividness
Both 'immediacy' and 'vividness' describe scenes that feel direct and real to the reader.

m: to force something unwelcome, such as a rule, tax or burden, on someone
x: I don't want to impose my taste in music on everyone during the road trip.
Management decided to impose a strict dress code after several complaints from clients.
The university imposes heavy fines on students who return library books late.
The government imposed a curfew after violent protests broke out in several cities.
Her parents tried to impose their choice of career on her, but she studied art anyway.
tc: To reduce traffic in the city centre, officials plan to ______ a compulsory fee on every car entering the area during rush hour.
A 'compulsory fee on every car' is something forced on drivers, so the blank must mean establish by force.
se: Parents should not ______ their own ambitions on their children.
foist
Both 'impose ... on' and 'foist ... on' mean to force something unwanted onto someone.

m: easily influenced by others, especially because young or inexperienced
x: Parents worry about what impressionable children see on social media every day.
As an impressionable new hire, I copied my boss's habits, good and bad.
Teachers have a huge influence on impressionable students in their first year of university.
Regulators want to limit junk-food advertising aimed at impressionable young viewers.
At sixteen, she was impressionable and believed everything her older boyfriend told her.
tc: Because teenagers are so ______, advertisers can easily persuade them to adopt habits they would otherwise never consider.
'Advertisers can easily persuade them' is the result, so the blank must mean easily influenced.
se: The film's violence worried parents of ______ young viewers.
susceptible
Both 'impressionable' and 'susceptible' describe viewers who are easily influenced.

m: not likely to happen or be true
x: It seems improbable that the shop will be open this late on a public holiday.
The manager thought it improbable that we would finish the project before the deadline.
Reviewers found the study's results improbable and asked the authors to repeat the experiment.
Bangladesh's improbable victory over the tournament favourites sparked celebrations across the country.
Their friendship seemed improbable, since she loved parties and he hated leaving the house.
tc: Given that the team had lost every match all season, its win in the final was so ______ that even its fans were stunned.
Losing 'every match all season' and stunning its own fans show the blank must mean unlikely.
se: It is ______ that the package will arrive before Monday, given the holiday backlog.
unlikely
Both 'improbable' and 'unlikely' mean not expected to happen, given the backlog.

m: not enough in quantity or not good enough in quality for a purpose
x: Our kitchen has inadequate storage, so pots end up piled on the floor.
Staff complained that the training was inadequate for handling the new software.
Inadequate sample sizes made it impossible to draw firm conclusions from the study.
Many hospitals still face inadequate funding and severe shortages of nurses.
He often felt inadequate next to his brilliant older brother.
tc: The old drainage system proved ______ during the monsoon, as streets flooded within minutes of the first heavy rain.
Streets flooding 'within minutes' shows the system was not good enough, which is what the blank means.
se: Relief workers warned that food supplies were ______ for the number of refugees arriving.
insufficient
Both 'inadequate' and 'insufficient' mean not enough for the need described.

m: including or welcoming everyone, without leaving out any group
x: We chose an inclusive menu with vegetarian, halal and gluten-free options for the party.
The company wants to build a more inclusive workplace where everyone feels respected.
Our school offers inclusive classrooms in which children with disabilities learn alongside their classmates.
Activists called for more inclusive policies that protect the rights of minority communities.
Her friend group is warm and inclusive, always inviting newcomers to join their weekend plans.
tc: Unlike the old club, which admitted only wealthy men, the new association is fully ______, welcoming members of every background.
'Unlike the old club, which admitted only wealthy men' and 'welcoming members of every background' show the blank must mean including everyone.
se: The festival organizers aimed to create ______ events that people of all ages and backgrounds could enjoy.
welcoming
Both 'inclusive' and 'welcoming' describe events open to everyone, as 'all ages and backgrounds' confirms.

m: not leading to a firm result, decision or proof
x: We argued for an hour about where to spend Eid, but the discussion was inconclusive.
After an inconclusive meeting, the managers agreed to meet again next week.
The experiment's results were inconclusive, so the team requested more funding for a larger trial.
The election produced an inconclusive result, with no party winning a clear majority.
After two inconclusive conversations about their future, they agreed to give each other more time.
tc: Because the tests neither confirmed nor ruled out the disease, doctors described the results as ______.
'Neither confirmed nor ruled out' shows the results gave no firm answer, which is what the blank means.
se: The debate between the two candidates was ______, and neither emerged as the clear winner.
indecisive
Both 'inconclusive' and 'indecisive' describe a contest with no clear outcome.

m: not in agreement or harmony with something; inconsistent
x: His cheerful voice was incongruent with the bad news he was delivering.
The candidate's résumé was incongruent with what she said in the interview.
When the data are incongruent with the theory, scientists must question their assumptions.
Critics say the city's luxury towers are incongruent with its promise of affordable housing.
Her words said she was fine, but her tired eyes were incongruent with that claim.
tc: The company's claim to care about the environment is ______ with its decision to dump waste into the river.
Dumping waste contradicts caring about the environment, so the blank must mean inconsistent.
se: The witness's account was ______ with the security footage, which showed a different sequence of events.
inconsistent
Both 'incongruent with' and 'inconsistent with' mean not matching, as 'a different sequence of events' shows.

m: so clear or certain that it cannot be disputed
x: It is incontestable that my brother cooks better than I do; even I admit it.
Her contribution to the project was incontestable, so she received the largest bonus.
The experiment provided incontestable proof that the drug lowered blood pressure.
Satellite images offered incontestable evidence that the forest had been illegally cleared.
His love for his children was incontestable, even if he rarely expressed it in words.
tc: The fingerprints and video footage together made the case against the thief ______; even his lawyer stopped arguing.
'Even his lawyer stopped arguing' shows the case could not be disputed, which is what the blank means.
se: Her right to the property was ______, as the deed clearly bore her name.
indisputable
Both 'incontestable' and 'indisputable' mean beyond any argument, as the clear deed confirms.

m: not exactly known, established or defined
x: The man at the door was of indeterminate age, somewhere between forty and sixty.
The project has been delayed for an indeterminate period while the budget is reviewed.
The fossil's species remains indeterminate because the skull was badly damaged.
Refugees in the camp face an indeterminate future, unsure when they can return home.
Their relationship existed in an indeterminate state, more than friendship but less than romance.
tc: Since the label had faded and no records survived, the painting's date remained ______, somewhere in the sixteenth or seventeenth century.
The faded label, missing records and range of two centuries show the date cannot be fixed exactly, which is what the blank means.
se: The meeting was postponed until some ______ date in the future.
unspecified
Both 'indeterminate' and 'unspecified' describe a date that has not been fixed.

m: serving as a sign or indication of something
x: Her messy handwriting is not indicative of carelessness; she simply writes very fast.
Rising complaints are indicative of deeper problems in our customer service department.
Low attendance may be indicative of how difficult students find the morning lectures.
Experts say the falling birth rate is indicative of wider economic anxiety.
His sudden coldness was indicative of something he wasn't ready to talk about.
tc: A persistent cough can be ______ of a serious illness, so doctors advise getting it checked.
Doctors advising a check-up shows the cough may signal illness, so the blank must mean being a sign of.
se: The long queues outside the bank were ______ of growing public panic.
symptomatic
Both 'indicative of' and 'symptomatic of' mean serving as a sign of the panic.

m: not clear or sharply defined; hard to see, hear or remember
x: Through the fog, the shapes of the buildings across the river were indistinct.
The caller's voice was so indistinct that the receptionist had to ask him to repeat himself.
The boundary between the two research fields has become indistinct in recent years.
Witnesses gave indistinct descriptions of the driver, so police released a sketch.
Memories of their first meeting had grown indistinct, but she still remembered his smile.
tc: Although the old photograph was clear in the centre, the faces at its edges were ______, blurred beyond recognition.
'Although' contrasts with 'clear', and 'blurred beyond recognition' restates the meaning, so the blank must mean not sharply defined.
se: From the next room came ______ voices, too quiet to make out any words.
faint
Both 'indistinct' and 'faint' describe voices that cannot be heard clearly.

m: favouring independent action and personal freedom over group interests or conformity
x: My uncle is so individualistic that he refuses to join any club or association.
An individualistic work style can clash with a company culture built on teamwork.
The course compares individualistic Western societies with more collective cultures in Asia.
Some sociologists blame an increasingly individualistic society for growing loneliness.
She found his individualistic attitude attractive at first, but later it felt selfish.
tc: Unlike his teammates, who always followed the coach's game plan, the striker was fiercely ______, preferring to play by his own instincts.
'Unlike his teammates, who always followed' and 'play by his own instincts' show the blank must mean independent of the group.
se: The artist was famously ______, ignoring the trends that her peers followed.
nonconformist
Both 'individualistic' and 'nonconformist' describe someone who goes her own way rather than following the group.

m: not producing the desired result
x: The cough syrup was ineffective, so I finally went to see a doctor.
Our old marketing strategy has proved ineffective with younger customers.
Cramming the night before an exam is often ineffective for long-term learning.
Experts say the new law has been ineffective at reducing air pollution.
His apologies were ineffective; she remained hurt and refused to answer his calls.
tc: Despite being expensive and widely advertised, the treatment turned out to be ______, producing no improvement in patients.
'Producing no improvement' restates the meaning, so the blank must mean not working.
se: The new pesticide was ______ against the beetles, which continued to destroy the crops.
useless
Both 'ineffective' and 'useless' mean the pesticide failed to work, as the continued damage shows.

m: lacking the ability or will to move or act; inactive
x: After the long trip, I lay inert on the sofa for most of the afternoon.
The committee had been inert for months, approving nothing while complaints piled up.
Chemistry students learn why helium and neon are inert and rarely react with other elements.
Critics accused the inert government of ignoring the housing crisis.
She felt emotionally inert after the breakup, unable to care about anything.
tc: Once a lively debating society, the club had become completely ______, holding no meetings and organizing no events for years.
'Once a lively' signals a contrast, and 'holding no meetings' shows the blank must mean inactive.
se: The economy has remained ______ for months, with almost no growth or new investment.
sluggish
Both 'inert' and 'sluggish' describe an economy with little activity, as 'almost no growth' confirms.

m: unwilling or unable to change or adapt; rigid
x: My grandfather is inflexible about meal times; dinner is always served at exactly eight.
An inflexible manager can make it hard for staff to balance work and family.
The university's inflexible rules meant I could not change my major after the first semester.
Critics say the inflexible immigration policy separates families for years.
Their relationship suffered because he was inflexible and never admitted he might be wrong.
tc: Although her colleagues suggested many reasonable compromises, the director remained ______, refusing to change a single detail of the plan.
'Refusing to change a single detail' despite compromises shows the blank must mean unwilling to adapt.
se: The landlord was ______ about the rent and would not accept even a day's delay.
unbending
Both 'inflexible' and 'unbending' describe someone who refuses to make any exception.

m: having great power to affect people, decisions or events
x: My aunt was the most influential person in my decision to study engineering.
She quickly became one of the most influential voices in the company's strategy meetings.
Darwin's book remains one of the most influential works in the history of science.
Influential business groups lobbied hard against the proposed tax on sugary drinks.
His older brother was influential in shaping his taste in music and films.
tc: Though he never held any official title, the elder was so ______ that no village decision was made without his approval.
'No village decision was made without his approval' shows great power over events, which is what the blank means.
se: The magazine became ______ in shaping public opinion on climate policy.
important
Both 'influential in' and 'important in' describe playing a major role in shaping opinion.

m: having or based on good knowledge and information
x: Before buying the car, I read reviews so I could make an informed decision.
Our consultants give clients informed advice based on years of market research.
Patients must give informed consent before taking part in any clinical trial.
A healthy democracy depends on an informed public that can judge politicians' claims.
She asked thoughtful, informed questions, which showed she had really listened to his problems.
tc: Rather than guessing, the analyst offered ______ predictions based on decades of sales data.
'Rather than guessing' and 'based on decades of sales data' show the blank must mean grounded in knowledge.
se: Voters need accurate facts in order to make ______ choices at the ballot box.
educated
Both 'informed' and 'educated' describe choices based on knowledge of the facts.

m: a new method, idea or product, or the act of introducing one
x: Ride-sharing apps were a welcome innovation for commuters stuck in Dhaka traffic.
Our company rewards innovation, so employees can spend Fridays on their own projects.
The conference showcased the latest innovations in solar panels and battery storage.
Universities are a major source of innovation in medicine and technology.
Her parents distrusted every innovation, from mobile banking to video calls with relatives abroad.
tc: The firm once led its industry, but it lost ground because it resisted every ______ and kept using decades-old methods.
'Kept using decades-old methods' contrasts with the blank, which must mean something new.
se: The electric car was hailed as the most important ______ in transport in fifty years.
breakthrough
Both 'innovation' and 'breakthrough' refer to a major new development.

m: showing a deep and accurate understanding of a person or situation
x: My little sister made an insightful remark about why our parents argue so much.
The consultant's insightful report explained exactly why our sales had dropped.
My supervisor wrote insightful comments that helped me reorganize the whole thesis.
The documentary offers an insightful look at how social media shapes young people's self-esteem.
She is insightful about people and usually knows when a friend is hiding something.
tc: Most critics only summarized the novel, but her review was genuinely ______, revealing themes nobody else had noticed.
'But' contrasts with merely summarizing, and 'revealing themes nobody else had noticed' shows the blank must mean perceptive.
se: The coach gave ______ feedback that helped each player understand their weaknesses.
perceptive
Both 'insightful' and 'perceptive' describe feedback showing deep understanding.

m: the act of demanding something firmly and refusing to accept a refusal
x: At my mother's insistence, we left home three hours before the flight.
The client's insistence on daily updates slowed the whole team down.
The professor's insistence on precise citations taught us to check every source carefully.
The union's insistence on higher wages led to weeks of difficult negotiations.
Despite his insistence that he was fine, his friends could see he was heartbroken.
tc: Despite repeated refusals, the reporter's ______ on getting an interview finally paid off when the official agreed to talk.
Continuing 'despite repeated refusals' until it 'finally paid off' shows the blank must mean firm demanding.
se: At the doctor's ______, he finally gave up smoking.
urging
Both 'insistence' and 'urging' describe the doctor's strong pressure that made him quit.

m: able to be understood; clear
x: The connection was poor, and only half of what she said was intelligible.

A good lecturer makes difficult theories intelligible to first-year students.
Scientists must make their findings intelligible to the public if they want support for research.
Through his tears, his words were barely intelligible, but she understood his apology.
tc: The professor's lectures were famously confusing, but his textbook was surprisingly ______, explaining each idea in simple terms.
'But' contrasts with 'confusing', and 'explaining each idea in simple terms' shows the blank must mean easy to understand.
se: The recording was so damaged that only a few sentences were ______.
understandable
Both 'intelligible' and 'understandable' mean able to be understood.

m: able to be exchanged or used in place of each other
x: In this recipe, butter and ghee are interchangeable, so use whichever you have.
Management treats workers as interchangeable, moving them between departments without any training.

Engineers designed the batteries to be interchangeable across all the company's power tools.
She did not want to feel interchangeable with his previous girlfriends.
tc: Because every part in the kit has exactly the same size and shape, the pieces are fully ______, and any one can replace another.
'Any one can replace another' restates the meaning, so the blank must mean able to be swapped.
se: In everyday speech, the two terms are ______, though scientists use them differently.
synonymous
Both 'interchangeable' and 'synonymous' mean the terms can be used in place of each other in everyday speech.

m: to explain or understand the meaning of something in a particular way
x: I wasn't sure how to interpret her short reply to my message.
Managers interpreted the drop in sales as a sign that prices were too high.

He interpreted her silence as anger, though she was simply exhausted.
tc: The poem is so ambiguous that readers ______ it in completely different ways, some seeing despair and others hope.
'So ambiguous' and readers 'seeing despair and others hope' show the blank must mean understand the meaning of.
se: It is easy to ______ a friend's silence as anger when they are simply busy.
construe
Both 'interpret ... as' and 'construe ... as' mean to understand something in a particular way.

m: opposite or reversed in order, direction, or effect
x: There is an inverse relationship between how late I go to bed and how productive I am the next morning.
In our sales data, the price of a product and the number of units sold showed a clear inverse correlation.
Students often confuse multiplication with its inverse operation, division, when solving word problems in a hurry.
