tc: Because demand falls whenever prices rise, economists describe the link between the two as ______.
One quantity falling whenever the other rises signals a relationship running in opposite directions.
se: The two graphs show ______ trends: as one line climbs, the other steadily drops.
opposite
Both 'inverse' and 'opposite' describe trends moving in contrary directions, giving the same meaning.

m: not based on reason or clear thinking; illogical
x: I know my fear of lifts is irrational, but I still take the stairs whenever I can.
Firing the best engineer over a minor mistake was an irrational decision that hurt the whole project.
Behavioural economists study why investors make irrational choices, such as selling good stocks in a panic.
Public debate became increasingly irrational as rumours spread faster than facts on social media.
His jealousy was completely irrational; she had never given him any reason to doubt her.
tc: Although every safety statistic shows that flying is far safer than driving, her terror of planes remains ______.
'Although every safety statistic shows' sets up a contrast, so the fear must be one that ignores reason.
se: Refusing to eat anything green because of one bad childhood meal seemed ______ to everyone but him.
illogical
Both 'irrational' and 'illogical' describe a choice not grounded in sensible reasoning.

m: not following the usual rules, pattern, or schedule; uneven or abnormal
x: Because the buses here run at irregular intervals, I always leave home twenty minutes early.
The auditors flagged several irregular payments that had been approved without proper documentation.
English has many irregular verbs, such as 'go' and 'went', that students simply have to memorize.
Doctors were concerned when the patient's heartbeat became irregular during the night.
Since he started working night shifts, his sleep has been so irregular that he feels tired all the time.
tc: Unlike his punctual sister, who ate at seven every evening, Karim kept hours that were wildly ______.
'Unlike his punctual sister' signals a contrast, so his hours must lack any fixed pattern.
se: Because the factory's output was so ______, managers could never predict how much stock they would have.
erratic
Both 'irregular' and 'erratic' mean lacking a steady pattern, which explains why output was unpredictable.

m: separate from others; occurring alone rather than as part of a wider pattern
x: The manager insisted that the late delivery was an isolated incident and would not happen again.
Living in a small village without internet, she often felt isolated from her friends in the city.
Scientists cautioned that a few isolated cases do not prove the virus is spreading in the community.
During the monsoon floods, several isolated villages in the north could be reached only by boat.
One isolated mistake should not define how you see an otherwise brilliant student.
tc: Officials claimed the attack was ______, but within a week three similar incidents had been reported across the country.
The contrast with 'three similar incidents' shows the officials had claimed it was a one-off event.
se: Police stressed that ______ break-ins like this one did not mean a crime wave was beginning.
sporadic
Both 'isolated' and 'sporadic' describe occasional events that do not form a pattern.

m: unpleasantly harsh or clashing; disturbingly out of harmony with its surroundings
x: The jarring sound of a car alarm woke me up at three in the morning.
Switching from a quiet startup to a noisy open-plan office was a jarring experience for many of us.
Critics found the film's sudden shift from comedy to violence jarring rather than clever.
The bright purple building looks jarring among the old red-brick houses on that street.
After months of kindness, his cold reply to her message was jarring and left her hurt.
tc: After the gentle piano introduction, the sudden blast of trumpets felt ______ to the audience.
The contrast between 'gentle' and 'sudden blast' shows the sound was harsh and unsettling.
se: The ______ screech of the brakes made everyone on the platform wince.
grating
Both 'jarring' and 'grating' describe a harsh, unpleasant sound that makes people wince.

m: to show or prove that something is right or reasonable
x: How can you justify spending so much money on a phone you barely use?
The manager had to justify the extra hiring costs to the finance team before they approved them.
In your thesis, you must justify your choice of research method, not just describe it.
The government struggled to justify the fuel price increase to angry commuters in Dhaka.
Nothing he said could justify the way he had spoken to his mother.
tc: The committee demanded evidence, since a budget increase that large would be difficult to ______ without clear results.
The demand for evidence shows the increase would need to be shown to be reasonable.
se: The company could not ______ its decision to close the plant, so it eventually reversed it.
defend
Both 'justify' and 'defend' mean to argue that a decision is right, and failing to do so led to the reversal.

m: having or showing a lot of knowledge or understanding of a subject
x: The guide at the museum was so knowledgeable that every question got a detailed answer.
We need someone knowledgeable about tax law to review these contracts before we sign.
My supervisor is extremely knowledgeable about fluid mechanics, so I always ask her first.
Voters tend to trust candidates who seem knowledgeable on economic issues.
My grandfather is surprisingly knowledgeable about cricket statistics going back to the 1970s.
tc: Far from being an amateur, the speaker proved remarkably ______ about every detail of medieval history.
'Far from being an amateur' signals the opposite of ignorance, so the blank means well-informed.
se: Ask Rina about wine; she is very ______ and can recommend a bottle for any meal.
well-informed
Both 'knowledgeable' and 'well-informed' mean she knows a lot, which is why she can recommend wines.

m: to make something lawful or acceptable, or to make it seem so
x: Sitting down to dinner with the man who cheated us would only legitimize his behaviour.
The new contract legitimized an arrangement that staff had been following informally for years.
Publishing the paper in a respected journal helped legitimize an approach many scholars had dismissed.
Critics warned that holding talks with the rebel group would legitimize its use of violence.
Her parents' approval seemed to legitimize the relationship in the eyes of the wider family.
tc: Opponents feared that inviting the dictator to the summit would ______ a government that had seized power illegally.
'Seized power illegally' shows the fear was that the invitation would make the regime appear acceptable.
se: The court ruling seemed to ______ a practice that many had considered unfair.
validate
Both 'legitimize' and 'validate' mean to give official acceptance to the practice.

m: to make or become smaller, weaker, or less intense
x: Drinking warm water with honey can lessen the pain of a sore throat.
Hiring two more assistants should lessen the pressure on our small team during the busy season.
Spacing your revision over several weeks will lessen the stress of the final exam period.
New flyovers were supposed to lessen traffic jams in Dhaka, but the roads remain crowded.
Time did not lessen his grief, but it taught him how to carry it.
tc: Rather than adding to his worries, her calm words helped ______ them.
'Rather than adding to' signals the opposite action, so the blank means to make smaller.
se: Wearing a seat belt can greatly ______ the risk of serious injury in a crash.
reduce
Both 'lessen' and 'reduce' mean to make the risk smaller.

m: in the same way; also
x: My father always reads before bed, and I likewise find that a book helps me fall asleep.
The sales team exceeded its target, and the support team likewise had an excellent quarter.
The first study found no link between diet and memory, and a second, larger study likewise found no effect.
Prices rose sharply in the cities, and rural areas were likewise affected by inflation.
When he apologized, she likewise admitted that she had been unfair to him.
tc: When the first guest stood up to leave, the others quickly did ______, and soon the room was empty.
The room emptying shows the others copied the first guest's action, so the blank means in the same way.
se: My brother hates spicy food, and my sister ______ refuses to eat anything with chillies.
similarly
Both 'likewise' and 'similarly' show that the sister behaves in the same way as the brother.

m: restricted in size, amount, or extent; not great or complete
x: Seats are limited, so please register for the workshop by Friday.
With a limited budget, we had to choose between new software and extra staff.
The study's findings are interesting, but their value is limited by the small sample size.
Many rural families still have only limited access to clean drinking water.
His understanding of her problems was limited, but he tried hard to listen.
tc: Because the town had only one small clinic, residents had extremely ______ access to medical care.
'Only one small clinic' explains why access to care was restricted.
se: The company's resources were ______, so it could not compete with larger rivals on advertising.
restricted
Both 'limited' and 'restricted' mean the resources were small, which explains the inability to compete.

m: progressing in a straight line or step by step from one stage to the next
x: My career has not been linear; I studied engineering, worked in sales, and now teach.
The project plan assumes a linear process, but in reality tasks often overlap.

The novel abandons linear storytelling, jumping back and forth across three decades.

tc: Unlike the film's jumbled timeline, the book tells the story in a strictly ______ order, from childhood to old age.
'Unlike the film's jumbled timeline' and 'from childhood to old age' point to a straight, step-by-step sequence.
se: The modules of this course are ______, so each one builds directly on the one before it.
sequential
Both 'linear' and 'sequential' describe modules arranged in order, each following the previous one.

m: uneven or unbalanced, with one side much larger or stronger than the other
x: The cake came out lopsided because our oven heats more on one side.

Researchers noted a lopsided gender ratio in the engineering department, with men outnumbering women five to one.
The election produced a lopsided result, giving the ruling party nearly every seat.
Their friendship had become lopsided: she always called him, but he never called her.
tc: Instead of a close contest, the final turned out to be ______, with the home side winning by forty points.
'Instead of a close contest' and a forty-point win show the match was very unbalanced.
se: The debate was rather ______, since one speaker was an expert and the other had barely prepared.
one-sided
Both 'lopsided' and 'one-sided' describe a contest where one side clearly dominated.

m: to make something appear larger or more important than it is; to enlarge or intensify
x: Staying up all night worrying will only magnify a problem that seems small in daylight.

Climate change is expected to magnify the damage caused by monsoon floods in low-lying areas.
Distance seemed to magnify her loneliness during her first winter abroad.
tc: Rather than downplaying the risks, the sensational news report tended to ______ them out of all proportion.
'Rather than downplaying' and 'out of all proportion' show the report made the risks seem bigger.
se: Tabloids often ______ small celebrity disputes into major scandals.
inflate
Both 'magnify' and 'inflate' mean to make something seem much bigger than it is.

m: to state firmly that something is true, especially when others disagree

contend
Both 'maintain' and 'contend' mean to argue firmly that something is true.

m: able to be dealt with, controlled, or done without too much difficulty

With his therapist's help over the past year, his anxiety has finally become manageable.

se: The debt is large but ______, as long as we pay a fixed amount each month.
doable
Both 'manageable' and 'doable' mean the debt can be handled without too much difficulty.

m: clearly noticeable; distinct or pronounced

After the new manager arrived, there was a marked change in the team's attitude.

'Far from subtle' and 'even strangers noticed' show the change was very obvious.
se: The price increase led to ______ declines in sales across every region.
noticeable
Both 'marked' and 'noticeable' describe declines that were clearly visible.

m: showing great skill or expertise
x: My mother's masterful handling of the wedding preparations kept everyone calm.

The professor gave a masterful lecture that made a difficult topic seem simple.
Critics praised the novel as a masterful portrait of life in a changing city.
The batsman played a masterful innings, scoring a century on a difficult pitch.

'Far from the clumsy debut' signals the opposite, so the performance showed great skill.
se: The detective's ______ questioning gradually led the suspect to confess.
skilful
Both 'masterful' and 'skilful' describe expert questioning that achieved its goal.

m: to actually happen or appear, especially as expected or promised

'Promised' contrasted with 'deeply disappointed' shows the returns never actually appeared.
se: The storm that forecasters had warned about did not ______, and the picnic went ahead.
happen
Both 'materialize' and 'happen' mean the expected storm never actually came.

m: careful, controlled, and deliberate; not hasty or extreme

Diplomats urged a measured reaction to the border incident to avoid further escalation.
She chose her words in a measured way, not wanting to hurt her friend's feelings.

'Rather than lashing out' and 'calm' point to a careful, controlled tone.
se: Her ______ reply to the angry email helped calm the situation.
restrained
Both 'measured' and 'restrained' describe a controlled reply that avoided making things worse.

m: a person or thing likely to cause harm; a threat or danger

Health officials described dengue as a serious public menace during the monsoon season.

danger
Both 'menace' and 'danger' describe something likely to cause harm on the roads.

m: to reduce to the smallest possible amount, or to make something seem less important than it is

Researchers designed the experiment carefully to minimize the influence of outside variables.
Officials were accused of trying to minimize the scale of the flood damage.

'Calling it a minor hiccup' shows the spokesperson made the crisis seem less important.
se: Good planning can ______ delays during the construction phase.
reduce
Both 'minimize' and 'reduce' mean to cut delays down as far as possible.

m: to cause someone to believe something false, through lies or a wrong impression

The advertisement misled customers into thinking the software was free.

'Technically accurate, but' signals the wording created a false impression.
se: Companies that ______ customers about the safety of their products can face heavy fines.
deceive
Both 'mislead' and 'deceive' mean to make customers believe something false.

m: to give a false or inaccurate account of someone or something
x: You misrepresented what I said; I never claimed the restaurant was bad.

tc: By quoting only half of the senator's sentence, the article managed to ______ her position entirely.

se: The critic seemed to ______ the author's argument in order to attack it more easily.
distort
Both 'misrepresent' and 'distort' mean to present the argument inaccurately.

m: the avoidance of extremes, especially in behaviour, opinions, or consumption
x: Sweets are fine in moderation, but not three times a day.
The new manager's moderation and patience calmed a team that had been arguing for months.

'Unlike his brother, who ate and drank to excess' signals the opposite of excess.
se: Doctors advise ______ rather than complete abstinence when it comes to coffee.
restraint
Both 'moderation' and 'restraint' mean limiting coffee without giving it up entirely.

m: lasting for a very short time; brief

During the exam, she felt a momentary panic but quickly remembered the formula.
The power cut caused only a momentary disruption to the hospital's systems.
His anger was momentary, and within minutes he was apologizing.

'Within seconds' shows the doubt lasted only a very short time.
se: The relief he felt was ______, as another bill arrived the next morning.
fleeting
Both 'momentary' and 'fleeting' mean the relief lasted only a short time.

m: steadily increasing, especially of something worrying
x: With mounting frustration, I watched the bus drive past without stopping.
Facing mounting pressure from clients, the agency finally hired two more designers.

The government is under mounting criticism over rising food prices.

tc: As each month brought new unpaid bills, the family's ______ debts became impossible to ignore.
'Each month brought new unpaid bills' shows the debts were steadily increasing.
se: Despite ______ criticism, the company refused to change its policy.
growing
Both 'mounting' and 'growing' describe criticism that keeps increasing.

m: having many different aspects, features, or sides
x: My grandmother is a multifaceted woman who paints, keeps bees, and runs a small charity.

Climate change is multifaceted, affecting everything from crop yields to migration patterns.
Their relationship was more multifaceted than outsiders realized; they were rivals as well as friends.
tc: Because the crisis had economic, social and environmental causes, experts called it deeply ______.
Listing three different kinds of causes shows the crisis had many sides.
se: As ______ artists, they write, sing and direct their own films.
versatile
Both 'multifaceted' and 'versatile' describe artists with many different talents.

m: felt or done by each of two or more people toward the other; shared

The two companies signed the deal because it offered mutual benefits.
Good research collaborations are built on mutual respect between senior and junior scientists.
The neighbouring countries signed a mutual defence agreement last year.
Their dislike was mutual, so they avoided each other at family gatherings.
tc: The admiration was not one-sided: the two rivals held each other in ______ esteem.
'Not one-sided' and 'each other' show the esteem was felt by both rivals.
se: The partnership survived for decades because of the ______ trust between the founders.
reciprocal
Both 'mutual' and 'reciprocal' mean each founder trusted the other.

m: limited in range, scope, or outlook; only just achieved
x: We had a narrow escape when a bus swerved into our lane on the highway near Dhaka.
The job description is too narrow; it excludes candidates with useful experience in related fields.
His research focuses on a narrow question about how ants find food in the dark.
Critics accused the court of taking a narrow view of free speech.
Living in the same small town all her life had given her a rather narrow outlook.

'Rather than taking a broad view' and 'just ten years' show the focus is limited in scope.
se: The law's definition of 'employee' is so ______ that many gig workers are left unprotected.
limited
Both 'narrow' and 'limited' describe a definition too restricted to include many workers.

m: not supporting either side in a conflict or argument; impartial
x: When my sisters argue, I try to stay neutral and let them sort it out.
HR should act as a neutral party when two employees have a dispute.
A good literature review presents competing theories in a neutral way before evaluating them.
Switzerland famously remained neutral during both world wars, refusing to join either side in the fighting.
When her parents argued about money, she refused to stay neutral and openly took her mother's side.
tc: Since the referee had no connection to either team, both coaches accepted him as completely ______.
'No connection to either team' shows the referee favoured neither side.
se: Journalists are expected to remain ______ when reporting on elections.
impartial
Both 'neutral' and 'impartial' mean not taking sides.

m: in spite of what has just been said; however
x: It was pouring with rain; nonetheless, we went out for a walk.
The deadline was tight, but the team nonetheless delivered a polished report.
The theory has several weaknesses; it remains, nonetheless, the best explanation we have.
The reforms were deeply unpopular; nonetheless, they helped stabilize the economy within two years.
He had hurt her deeply, but she forgave him nonetheless.
tc: The hike was exhausting and the views were hidden by fog; it was ______ an experience none of us would forget.
The negatives followed by a positive outcome signal a concession, meaning 'in spite of that'.
se: The plan is risky; it is ______ our only realistic option.
nevertheless
Both 'nonetheless' and 'nevertheless' mean 'in spite of the risk'.

m: relating to standards or rules about how things should be, rather than how they are
x: In our family there were strong normative expectations about who should cook and who should earn.
The company's code of conduct is a normative document that sets out how employees ought to behave.
Economists distinguish positive statements, which describe facts, from normative statements, which say what should happen.
Critics argue that the report makes normative claims about family life without supporting evidence.
She felt crushed by normative pressure to marry before thirty, even though she wasn't ready.
tc: Whereas a descriptive study simply reports how people behave, ______ analysis argues how they ought to behave.
'Whereas' contrasts describing behaviour with stating how people ought to behave, which is what normative means.
se: The guidelines are ______ rather than descriptive: they tell teachers what they should do.
prescriptive
Both 'normative' and 'prescriptive' describe rules that state what should be done.

m: the quality of judging fairly, based on facts rather than personal feelings or opinions
x: When choosing a flat, I asked a friend for advice because she could judge with more objectivity than I could.
Using a scoring sheet brings more objectivity to the hiring process.
Peer review is meant to ensure scientific objectivity, though it doesn't always succeed.
Viewers have questioned the channel's objectivity since it began running sponsored political content.
When it comes to her own son, she loses all objectivity.
tc: Because the judge was a close friend of the defendant, lawyers doubted her ______ and asked her to step aside.
A close friendship with the defendant suggests she could not judge fairly.
se: Critics praised the historian's ______ in presenting both sides of the conflict.
impartiality
Both 'objectivity' and 'impartiality' mean presenting both sides fairly without bias.

m: to cause or bring about something
x: Her sudden resignation occasioned a lot of gossip in the office.
The delay in the flight occasioned a long and uncomfortable night at the airport.
The professor's controversial paper occasioned a lively debate in the department.
The new tax on mobile phone use occasioned widespread protests across the country.
His careless remark occasioned a quarrel between the two brothers that lasted for weeks.
tc: The minor policy change seemed harmless, yet it would ______ a storm of protest that nobody had predicted.
'Seemed harmless, yet' signals that the change unexpectedly caused the protest.
se: Remarks like that are likely to ______ resentment among the staff.
provoke
Both 'occasion' and 'provoke' mean to cause the resentment.

m: hopefulness and confidence about the future or the success of something
x: Despite the rain, my father set off for the cricket match with his usual optimism.
There is cautious optimism in the office that the new contract will be signed.
Her optimism about the experiment faded after the third failed trial.
Stock markets rose sharply on Monday on renewed optimism about a trade deal between the two countries.
His quiet optimism helped her get through the hardest months of her illness.
tc: Even after three failed harvests, the farmer's ______ never faded; he was sure next year would be better.
'He was sure next year would be better' despite failures shows his hopefulness.
se: The new data gave investors reason for ______ about the economy.
confidence
Both 'optimism' and 'confidence' express a positive outlook about the economy.

m: to direct or adjust something toward a particular aim or audience; to find one's position
x: It took me a few minutes to orient myself after coming out of the metro station.
The company plans to orient its marketing more toward young professionals.
The first week of the programme is designed to orient new students to campus life.
Over the past decade, the government has oriented its economic policy toward exports and foreign investment.
After the divorce, she slowly began to orient her life around her own goals rather than his.
tc: Since most of its customers are now teenagers, the brand has decided to ______ its advertising toward a much younger audience.
The shift to teenage customers explains why the brand is aiming its advertising at the young.
se: The new curriculum aims to ______ students toward practical, job-ready skills.
direct
Both 'orient' and 'direct' mean to steer students toward a particular goal.

m: to begin or come from a particular place, source, or time
x: This recipe originated in my grandmother's village and has been passed down for generations.
The idea for the app originated in a casual conversation over lunch.
Scholars still debate exactly where and when the earliest writing systems originated.
Health officials are trying to determine where the outbreak originated.
Many of their arguments originated from small misunderstandings that neither of them cleared up.
tc: Although the song is now known around the world, few listeners realize that it did not ______ in America but in a small Irish town.
The sentence contrasts where the song is known now with the place where it first came from.
se: Most of these rumours ______ from a single anonymous account.
stem
Both 'originate' and 'stem' mean the rumours came from that source.

m: no longer useful, fashionable, or accurate because newer things or ideas exist
x: My phone is so outdated that it can't install most new apps.
The office still uses outdated software that crashes every few hours.
The textbook's statistics are outdated, so check more recent sources before citing them.
Many say the country's labour laws are outdated and fail to protect gig workers.
He still holds outdated ideas about what women should do after marriage.
tc: The map was so ______ that it showed none of the new roads built over the last decade.
Missing a decade of new roads shows the map was no longer current.
se: Many of the factory's machines are ______ and should be replaced.
obsolete
Both 'outdated' and 'obsolete' mean the machines are too old to be useful.

m: to fail to notice something; also, to ignore or excuse a fault deliberately
x: It's easy to overlook small expenses, but they add up by the end of the month.
The reviewer overlooked a serious error in the budget, and it cost the company dearly.
Earlier studies overlooked the role of diet in the disease, focusing almost entirely on genetics.
Rural women's contributions to the economy are often overlooked by policymakers.
She was willing to overlook his forgetfulness because he was so kind in other ways.
tc: The editor was so careful that she never let herself ______ even the smallest typing mistake.
'So careful' shows she never failed to notice errors.
se: Investigators are careful not to ______ any clue, however minor it seems.
miss
Both 'overlook' and 'miss' mean to fail to notice a clue.

m: more important than anything else
x: When choosing a flat, our overriding concern was how close it was to the children's school.
The overriding priority this quarter is to cut costs without losing customers.
In clinical trials, patient safety must be the overriding consideration.
The overriding issue in the election was the rising price of rice.
Her overriding emotion on hearing the news was relief that her brother was safe.
tc: All other considerations were secondary; safety was the ______ concern of the engineers designing the bridge.
'All other considerations were secondary' shows safety mattered more than anything else.
se: Profit should not be the ______ goal of a hospital.
primary
Both 'overriding' and 'primary' mean the most important goal.

m: to describe something as larger, better, or more important than it really is; to exaggerate
x: You're overstating the problem; the car only needs a new tyre.
The company overstated its profits for three years before auditors discovered the error.
It is hard to overstate the importance of sleep for students revising for exams.
Some reporters overstated the risks of the new vaccine, causing unnecessary alarm.
He tends to overstate his feelings when he's angry, so I wait until he calms down.
tc: The report did not merely describe the risks; it tended to ______ them, predicting disasters that the evidence did not support.
'Predicting disasters that the evidence did not support' shows the report made the risks seem bigger than they were.
se: Politicians often ______ their achievements during election campaigns.
exaggerate
Both 'overstate' and 'exaggerate' mean to make achievements sound greater than they are.

m: similar or corresponding; developing in a comparable way at the same time
x: My brother and I followed parallel paths: we both studied engineering and both moved abroad.
The two departments ran parallel projects without realizing they were duplicating work.
Researchers in Japan and Germany independently reached parallel conclusions about the new material.
Rising rents and parallel increases in food prices have squeezed many urban families.
Although they never met, the two women lived strikingly parallel lives, marked by the same hopes and setbacks.
tc: The two scientists, working on different continents, made ______ discoveries in the same year, each unaware of the other.
Similar discoveries made at the same time by separate people points to corresponding developments.
se: The novel tells two ______ stories, one set in the present and the other a century earlier, that mirror each other.
analogous
Both 'parallel' and 'analogous' describe stories that closely resemble each other.

m: very exacting about details or standards; hard to please
x: My aunt is very particular about how her tea is made, and only she can get it right.
Our client is particular about fonts, so check every slide before you send the deck.
Professor Rahman is particular about citations and will deduct marks for any formatting error.
Some restaurants are now so particular about sourcing that they list the farm for every ingredient.
He is particular about the people he lets into his life, so his friendships are few but deep.
tc: Unlike his easygoing roommate, who would eat anything, Imran was extremely ______ about what went on his plate.
'Unlike his easygoing roommate' signals the opposite, so Imran is fussy about food.
se: She is very ______ about cleanliness and wipes down the kitchen several times a day.
fastidious
Both 'particular' and 'fastidious' mean she has very high, exacting standards.

m: accepting what happens without active response or resistance
x: Instead of being passive, try asking the shopkeeper for a discount.
In meetings he remains passive, rarely offering ideas even when he has good ones.
Simply rereading notes is a passive way to study; testing yourself works far better.
Critics accused the regulator of taking a passive role while banks took huge risks.
She was tired of playing a passive role in the relationship and started making decisions herself.
tc: Rather than fighting back against the unfair decision, the workers remained ______ and accepted it in silence.
'Rather than fighting back' and 'accepted it in silence' show they did not resist.
se: The villagers' ______ acceptance of the new rules surprised the officials, who had expected protests.
submissive
Both 'passive' and 'submissive' describe accepting the rules without resistance.

m: waiting to be decided or settled
x: I have three pending orders on that website, and none of them has shipped yet.
Your leave request is still pending until the manager signs it.
My visa application is pending, so I can't book my flight to Canada for the semester yet.
The corruption case has remained pending before the high court for more than three years.
With the decision about their marriage still pending, they kept the news to themselves.
tc: Because the court has not yet ruled, the lawsuit is still ______.
'Has not yet ruled' shows the lawsuit is still waiting to be decided.
se: Several issues remain ______, so the contract cannot be signed today.
unresolved
Both 'pending' and 'unresolved' mean the issues have not yet been settled.

m: continuing firmly despite difficulty or opposition; lasting for a long time
x: A persistent cough kept me awake for most of the week.
Thanks to her persistent follow-up emails, the client finally paid the invoice.
Persistent students who keep practising difficult problems usually see the biggest gains.
The city has struggled with persistent water shortages for decades.
He was so persistent in asking her out that she finally agreed to coffee.
tc: Although the editor rejected her first ten stories, the young writer was ______ and kept submitting new work.
Continuing to submit despite ten rejections shows she refused to give up.
se: Only the most ______ investigators would continue the search after so many dead ends.
tenacious
Both 'persistent' and 'tenacious' describe people who keep going despite setbacks.

m: good at convincing someone to do or believe something
x: My younger sister is so persuasive that she always gets the last piece of cake.
Her persuasive pitch won the agency its biggest client of the year.
A persuasive essay needs clear evidence, not just strong opinions.
The lawyer made a persuasive case that the factory had ignored safety rules.
His apology was persuasive enough that she agreed to give him another chance.
tc: The evidence was so ______ that even the most sceptical members of the jury changed their minds.
Changing the minds of even sceptical jurors shows the evidence was convincing.
se: The report offers ______ evidence that the policy has reduced poverty.
compelling
Both 'persuasive' and 'compelling' describe evidence strong enough to convince readers.

m: causing people to divide into sharply opposing groups
x: Pineapple on pizza is a surprisingly polarizing topic at our dinner table.
The new office dress code proved polarizing, with half the staff loving it and half resenting it.
The professor's polarizing theory has both devoted followers and fierce critics.
Immigration remains one of the most polarizing issues in national politics.
Their marriage became a polarizing subject in the family, splitting relatives into two camps.
tc: Some viewers loved the film and others hated it; few works of art have been so ______.
Viewers either loving or hating the film shows it split opinion sharply.
se: The proposal to raise taxes was deeply ______, splitting the council into two hostile camps.
divisive
Both 'polarizing' and 'divisive' describe something that splits people into opposing groups.

m: appealing to ordinary people, often by setting them against a supposed elite
x: My uncle loves the populist slogans on talk radio, though he admits they rarely offer real solutions.
The company's populist pricing strategy aimed to make premium coffee affordable for everyone.
Political scientists have studied why populist movements gained ground across Europe after 2008.
The candidate ran a populist campaign, promising to take on the wealthy and the corrupt.
She grew uneasy with her friend's increasingly populist views about the 'elite' ruining the country.
tc: Claiming to speak for ordinary workers against a corrupt elite, the candidate's ______ message attracted millions of voters who felt ignored.
'Speak for ordinary workers against a corrupt elite' defines a populist appeal.
se: The party's ______ rhetoric attacked bankers and promised to return power to the people.
anti-elitist
Both 'populist' and 'anti-elitist' describe rhetoric that champions ordinary people against the powerful.

m: a person who believes that only knowledge verified by observation and science is valid
x: My uncle is a born positivist who refuses to believe in anything he cannot measure, including luck.
At the research meeting, the positivists on the team demanded hard data before accepting the new design.
Our philosophy lecturer explained how the logical positivists of the Vienna Circle rejected metaphysics as meaningless.
Critics argue that economists who behave like strict positivists ignore the values hidden inside their models.
She married a positivist, and their friendly arguments about faith and evidence have lasted twenty years.
tc: As a strict ______, she dismissed any claim that could not be tested by observation or experiment.
Dismissing claims that cannot be tested by observation defines the outlook of a positivist.
se: Being a committed ______, the professor insisted that only claims backed by observable evidence deserved serious attention.
empiricist
Both 'positivist' and 'empiricist' describe someone who trusts only knowledge grounded in observation, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: able to be done or put into practice successfully
x: Walking to work is only practicable if you live within a couple of kilometers of the office.
The engineers concluded that a second bridge across the river was not practicable within the current budget.
Our supervisor asked us to propose a research design that was practicable with the limited equipment in the lab.
During the monsoon, holding the outdoor rally on the original date was simply not practicable.
He wanted to visit his parents every weekend, but with his new job it was no longer practicable.
tc: Although the proposal looked brilliant on paper, the committee doubted it was ______, given the tiny budget and tight deadline.
'Although ... looked brilliant on paper' contrasts with doubts about whether it could actually be carried out.
se: The team searched for a cheap and ______ way to move the heavy machinery without damaging the floor.
feasible
Both 'practicable' and 'feasible' mean able to be done, so the sentence means the same either way.

m: able to be known in advance; behaving or happening in an expected, often dull, way
x: His jokes have become so predictable that the whole family can finish them before he does.
Investors prefer companies with predictable earnings to those with dramatic ups and downs.
The novel's plot was entirely predictable, and I guessed the ending by the third chapter.
Sadly, the government's response to the protests was predictable: more police and fewer explanations.
After years of chaos, she found real comfort in a calm, predictable relationship.
tc: Fans who had hoped for a surprising twist were disappointed; the film's ending was entirely ______.
Disappointment over the lack of a 'surprising twist' shows the ending was easy to foresee.
se: Given the heavy rainfall upstream, flooding in the low-lying areas was entirely ______.
foreseeable
Both 'predictable' and 'foreseeable' mean that the flooding could be expected in advance.

m: the state of being completely absorbed in thinking about something; a concern that dominates one's thoughts
x: Her preoccupation with her phone meant she completely missed her stop on the bus.
The manager's preoccupation with quarterly targets left little time for long-term planning.
Many students in Dhaka share the same preoccupation: getting into a good public university.
Historians note that national security became the government's main preoccupation after the war.
His growing preoccupation with his ex-girlfriend began to worry his friends.
tc: His ______ with the upcoming exam was so complete that he forgot his own birthday.
Forgetting his own birthday shows how completely the exam filled his thoughts.
se: Her ______ with appearances meant she never left the house without checking the mirror twice.
obsession
Both 'preoccupation' and 'obsession' describe a concern that dominates her thoughts, giving the same meaning.

m: something that must exist or be done before something else can happen
x: A valid passport is an obvious prerequisite for international travel, yet he left his at home.
Fluency in Excel is a prerequisite for almost every analyst job in the company.
Calculus is a prerequisite for the advanced physics course, so I have to take it first.
Economists argue that political stability is a prerequisite for sustained foreign investment.
Trust, she believes, is the most important prerequisite for any lasting friendship.
tc: Students cannot take Organic Chemistry II without first passing Organic Chemistry I; the first course is the essential ______ for the second.
'Cannot take ... without first passing' defines something required beforehand.
se: Peace is the basic ______ for economic development in any region.
precondition
Both 'prerequisite' and 'precondition' mean something that must come first, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to keep something in its original state or protect it from harm, loss, or decay
x: Salt and vinegar have been used for centuries to preserve fish and vegetables.
The company tried to preserve its friendly culture even after doubling its staff.
Archivists are working to preserve the fragile manuscripts in climate-controlled rooms.
Conservation groups are fighting to preserve the Sundarbans mangrove forest from industrial pollution.
Despite the divorce, they managed to preserve a warm friendship for the sake of their children.
tc: Rather than demolish the old mansion, the city chose to ______ it as a museum.
'Rather than demolish' sets up a contrast, so the blank must mean keep and protect.
se: The new law aims to ______ the city's historic buildings for future generations.
safeguard
Both 'preserve' and 'safeguard' mean to protect the buildings from loss, giving the same meaning.

m: very simple, basic, or crude; belonging to an early stage of development
x: The cabin was fairly primitive, with no electricity and a single bucket for washing.
Compared with modern software, the office's old filing system looks painfully primitive.
Biologists study primitive organisms to understand how complex life first evolved.
Health care in the remote villages remained primitive, with one clinic serving thousands of people.
Jealousy is such a primitive emotion that even sensible adults struggle to control it.
tc: Early computers were enormous and ______ compared with today's sleek, powerful laptops.
The contrast with 'sleek, powerful' modern laptops shows the early machines were crude and basic.
se: The stranded explorers had only ______ tools, made from stone and bone, to build their shelter.
crude
Both 'primitive' and 'crude' describe simple, roughly made tools, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: acting according to firm moral rules; based on clear standards of right and wrong
x: Even as a child, she was principled enough to return extra change to the shopkeeper.
Our director made a principled decision to refuse the contract because the client exploited its workers.
The professor offered a principled argument for reforming the grading system, not just a list of complaints.
Voters said they wanted a principled candidate who would not change positions simply to win votes.
I admire how principled my father is, even when honesty costs him money.
tc: Unlike his corrupt colleagues, who took bribes freely, the judge was deeply ______ and refused every gift.
'Unlike his corrupt colleagues' signals a contrast, so the blank must mean morally firm.
se: By refusing to reveal her source, the journalist showed that she was ______ and could not be pressured.
ethical
Both 'principled' and 'ethical' describe someone guided by moral rules, so the sentence means the same.

m: having special advantages, rights, or opportunities that most people do not have
x: Growing up in a privileged neighborhood, he had never had to worry about power cuts.
Only a few privileged employees had access to the executive dining room.
Researchers found that students from privileged backgrounds were far more likely to apply abroad.
Critics say the tax cuts mainly benefit the privileged few rather than ordinary workers.
She was privileged to have parents who supported her choice of career, unlike many of her friends.
tc: While most villagers struggled to pay school fees, the landlord's children enjoyed ______ lives of private tutors and foreign holidays.
The contrast with struggling villagers and the list of luxuries show the children had special advantages.
se: Children from ______ families often have access to better schools and private tutors.
advantaged
Both 'privileged' and 'advantaged' describe families with special benefits, so the meaning stays the same.

m: likely to be true or likely to happen
x: Rain is probable this afternoon, so take an umbrella when you go out.
The most probable explanation for the delay is a problem with the supplier, not our team.
The study identified smoking as the probable cause of the sharp rise in lung disease.
Analysts say a change of government is probable after next month's election.
Given how angry she was, a quick reconciliation did not seem probable.
tc: Although a full recovery was possible, the doctors did not think it was ______; most patients with this injury never walk again.
The contrast between 'possible' and the statistic that most never walk again shows the blank means likely.
se: Police said the ______ cause of the fire was an electrical fault in the kitchen.
likely
Both 'probable' and 'likely' mean the cause that is most expected to be true.

m: favoring social reform and new, liberal ideas rather than tradition
x: My aunt held surprisingly progressive views about marriage for someone of her generation.
The firm adopted progressive policies such as paid paternity leave and flexible hours.
The university is known for its progressive curriculum, which lets students design their own majors.
Progressive lawmakers pushed for higher taxes on the rich to fund free health care.
He was drawn to her progressive outlook, which challenged many of the traditions he had grown up with.
tc: Far from being ______, the party opposed every reform and longed to return to the old ways.
'Far from being' plus opposition to reform shows the blank means favoring change and new ideas.
se: The new mayor's ______ policies, including expanded rights for minorities, angered traditionalists.
reformist
Both 'progressive' and 'reformist' describe policies that push for social change, so the meaning holds.

m: corresponding in size, amount, or degree to something else; appropriately balanced
x: Your share of the bill should be proportionate to what you actually ate.
Employees received bonuses proportionate to their contribution to the project.
According to basic legal principles, a punishment must be proportionate to the offense.
Human rights groups questioned whether the army's response was proportionate to the threat.
Her anger seemed hardly proportionate to such a small mistake, and her friends were confused.
tc: Critics complained that the fine was far too large for such a minor offense; a penalty ______ to the harm caused would have been fairer.
The complaint that the fine was 'far too large' for a minor offense calls for a penalty matching the harm.
se: Each country's share of the costs will be ______ to the size of its economy.
proportional
Both 'proportionate' and 'proportional' mean matching in size, so the sentence means the same.

m: successful, wealthy, and thriving
x: After years of hard work, the family finally became prosperous enough to buy their own house.
The firm had its most prosperous year ever, with record profits in every region.
Historians describe the city as a prosperous trading port in the sixteenth century.
Money sent home by workers abroad has made some villages in Bangladesh noticeably more prosperous.
Their friends wished the newly married couple a long, happy and prosperous life together.
tc: Once a struggling fishing village, the town has become ______ thanks to tourism and new industries.
'Once a struggling' village that gained tourism and industry has become wealthy and thriving.
se: The region grew ______ as factories and new roads brought jobs and investment.
affluent
Both 'prosperous' and 'affluent' mean wealthy, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: limited or restricted in some way; not complete or absolute
x: My parents gave the trip their qualified approval: I could go, but only if I called every night.
The board's support for the merger was qualified, depending on a full audit of the other company.
The reviewer offered qualified praise, admiring the theory but questioning the small sample size.
The minister's statement was a qualified apology that blamed others for much of the damage.
She gave me a qualified yes, saying she would come if her shift ended in time.
tc: The project's success was ______ at best: it met its deadline but went far over budget.
Meeting the deadline but going over budget shows the success was only partial, not complete.
se: The critics gave the new play only ______ praise, admiring the acting but disliking the script.
guarded
Both 'qualified' and 'guarded' praise mean approval held back with reservations.

m: to measure or express the amount of something in numbers
x: It is hard to quantify how much time I waste scrolling on my phone each day.
The consultants tried to quantify the cost of each hour the factory stood idle.
In her thesis, she quantified the effect of Dhaka's air pollution on children's lung function.
Scientists are still struggling to quantify the full damage caused by microplastics in the oceans.
Love is not something you can quantify, no matter how many gifts you buy.
tc: Wanting precise figures rather than vague impressions, the researchers set out to ______ exactly how much water each household used.
'Precise figures rather than vague impressions' shows the blank means to measure in numbers.
se: Economists are trying to ______ the impact of the floods on rice production.
measure
Both 'quantify' and 'measure' mean to determine the size of the impact in numbers.

m: open to doubt about its truth, quality, or honesty; suspicious
x: The milk smelled questionable, so I poured it down the sink.
The auditors flagged several questionable payments to a company owned by the manager's cousin.
The paper's conclusions are questionable because the researchers surveyed only twelve people.
Reporters revealed a local councillor's questionable ties to a large construction firm.
He has questionable taste in friends, but he is fiercely loyal to all of them.
tc: Because the source had lied before, journalists treated his latest claims as ______ until they could be verified.
A source who 'had lied before' makes his claims open to doubt until checked.
se: The company's ______ accounting practices soon attracted the attention of regulators.
dubious
Both 'questionable' and 'dubious' mean suspicious or of doubtful honesty, so the meaning is the same.

m: to consider or judge something again, especially in light of new information
x: After the second flat tire, I had to reassess my plan to cycle across the country.
The company will reassess its hiring strategy once the new budget is approved.
New fossil discoveries forced scientists to reassess when humans first reached the region.
The government promised to reassess its flood defenses after the worst storm in decades.
Her betrayal made him reassess every friendship he thought he could trust.
tc: When the new data contradicted their earlier conclusions, the researchers had to ______ their entire theory.
New data contradicting earlier conclusions forces the researchers to judge the theory again.
se: After losing three games in a row, the coach decided to ______ his strategy.
rethink
Both 'reassess' and 'rethink' mean to consider the strategy again, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: to argue or prove that a statement or accusation is false
x: She calmly rebutted her brother's claim that she had eaten the last piece of cake.
Our lawyer prepared a detailed letter rebutting every allegation in the complaint.
In the second half of the debate, each team has three minutes to rebut the other side's arguments.
The ministry issued a statement rebutting reports that the new bridge was unsafe.
He never bothered to rebut the rumors about his marriage, which only made them spread faster.
tc: Instead of accepting the accusation, the scientist published new evidence to ______ it point by point.
'Instead of accepting' plus 'new evidence ... point by point' shows the blank means to prove false.
se: The defense attorney stood up to ______ the prosecutor's argument with fresh evidence.
refute
Both 'rebut' and 'refute' mean to show an argument is wrong, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to improve something by making small, careful changes; to remove impurities from
x: I keep refining my morning routine until it takes exactly forty minutes.
The design team spent two weeks refining the prototype based on customer feedback.
My supervisor told me to refine my research question before collecting any data.
Most of the country's crude oil is shipped abroad to be refined into petrol and diesel.
Over the years, she refined her ability to read people's moods from their faces.
tc: His first draft was rough and full of small errors, so he spent the weekend trying to ______ it.
A 'rough' draft 'full of small errors' needs to be improved through careful changes.
se: Over many months, the engineers worked to ______ their technique for welding thin steel sheets.
hone
Both 'refine' and 'hone' mean to improve a skill gradually, so the meaning stays the same.

m: thoughtful; inclined to think carefully and seriously about things
x: After the funeral, everyone was quiet and reflective on the long drive home.
Our team lead encourages reflective discussions after each project about what went wrong.
The course asks students to keep a reflective journal about what they learn each week.
On the anniversary of the disaster, the mayor gave a reflective speech admitting past mistakes.
She is a reflective person who prefers long conversations to noisy parties.
tc: Unlike his impulsive younger brother, who acted without thinking, Karim was quiet and ______.
'Unlike his impulsive ... brother, who acted without thinking' signals the opposite: thoughtful.
se: Sitting alone by the river, he grew ______ and thought about the choices he had made.
pensive
Both 'reflective' and 'pensive' describe someone lost in serious thought, giving the same meaning.

m: returning to an earlier, less advanced state; moving backward rather than forward
x: Moving back into his childhood bedroom at thirty felt oddly regressive to him.
Staff saw the new dress code as regressive, a return to the rigid rules of the 1980s.
Psychologists note that stress can trigger regressive behavior, such as thumb-sucking in older children.
Economists call a sales tax regressive because it takes a larger share of income from poorer families.
His friends found his attitude toward women embarrassingly regressive for someone his age.
tc: Far from moving the country forward, the new law was ______, restoring restrictions abolished decades ago.
'Far from moving the country forward' and 'restoring' old restrictions show the law moves backward.
se: Many activists condemned the court's ______ ruling as a return to the attitudes of the past.
retrograde
Both 'regressive' and 'retrograde' mean moving backward to an earlier state, so the meaning holds.

m: considered in comparison with something else rather than absolutely
x: After the noisy city, the small town felt like a place of relative calm.
Given the relative cost of the two laptops, the cheaper one is clearly better value for our team.
Students often misjudge the relative importance of each topic and spend too long on easy chapters.
Scientists recorded the relative humidity inside the greenhouse every hour.
Happiness is relative; what thrills one person may completely bore another.
tc: Wealth is not absolute but ______: a salary that seems huge in one country may look modest in another.
'Not absolute but' signals the opposite, and the salary example shows wealth depends on comparison.
se: The two teams enjoyed ______ success last season, though neither won a trophy.
comparative
Both 'relative' and 'comparative' mean successful only when compared with others, so the sense is the same.

m: dependence on or trust in someone or something
x: Our reliance on food delivery apps has grown since we both started working late.
The company's heavy reliance on a single supplier left it exposed when that supplier went bankrupt.
Teachers worry about students' growing reliance on AI tools to write their essays.
The country is trying to reduce its reliance on imported gas by building solar farms.
Her reliance on her sister for emotional support increased after the divorce.
tc: To achieve energy independence, the nation must reduce its ______ on foreign oil.
'Energy independence' is the opposite of the blank, which must mean dependence.
se: The region's heavy ______ on tourism made it vulnerable during the pandemic.
dependence
Both 'reliance' and 'dependence' mean needing tourism to survive, so the sentence means the same.

m: unwillingness or hesitation to do something
x: Despite my reluctance to get up early, I joined my friends for a sunrise walk.
The manager's reluctance to delegate means he works until midnight most days.
Some students show a reluctance to ask questions in class for fear of looking foolish.
The government's reluctance to raise fuel prices has created a huge budget deficit.
He understood her reluctance to talk about her childhood and never pushed her.
tc: Her ______ to join the trip surprised everyone, since she usually jumps at any chance to travel.
Her usual eagerness to travel contrasts with the blank, which must mean unwillingness.
se: Despite his initial ______ to speak in public, he gave a moving speech at his sister's wedding.
unwillingness
Both 'reluctance' and 'unwillingness' mean he did not want to speak, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: unusual or impressive enough to deserve attention; extraordinary
x: My grandfather has a remarkable memory and can still recite poems he learned as a boy.
Sales made a remarkable recovery in the final quarter after a terrible start to the year.
Her thesis made a remarkable contribution to our understanding of river erosion.
The country has made remarkable progress in reducing child mortality over three decades.
It is remarkable how quickly they became friends after years of quarreling.
tc: Most patients take months to recover from such surgery, so her return to work after only two weeks was truly ______.
Recovering in two weeks when most take months is unusual enough to be extraordinary.
se: The young pianist showed ______ talent for someone who had begun lessons only a year earlier.
exceptional
Both 'remarkable' and 'exceptional' mean unusually impressive, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: the act of making something new, fresh, or valid again; revival
x: I need to send my passport for renewal before it expires next month.
The renewal of our contract with the main client saved dozens of jobs.
Scholarship renewal depends on keeping a grade point average above 3.5 each year.
The city launched an ambitious program of urban renewal in its run-down northern districts.
For her, spring has always been a season of renewal and hope.
tc: After years of neglect and decay, the old harbor district is finally undergoing ______.
'After years of neglect and decay' sets up the opposite: being made fresh and new again.
se: The festival celebrates the ______ of life that comes with the first spring rains.
revival
Both 'renewal' and 'revival' mean life returning and becoming fresh again, so the meaning is the same.

m: to change the way something is arranged, structured, or run
x: I spent Saturday afternoon reorganizing my wardrobe and giving away old clothes.
The new chief executive plans to reorganize the sales department into three regional teams.
Our professor reorganized the syllabus so that the hardest topics come after the midterm.
After the floods, the government had to reorganize its entire relief operation.
When the baby arrived, the couple had to reorganize their lives around feeding schedules.
tc: The library's books were scattered with no clear system, so the new librarian decided to ______ them by subject.
Books 'scattered with no clear system' need to be arranged in a new way.
se: The company plans to ______ its operations to cut costs and improve efficiency.
restructure
Both 'reorganize' and 'restructure' mean to change how operations are arranged, giving the same meaning.

m: to repeat or copy something exactly, especially an experiment or its results
x: I tried to replicate my mother's fish curry, but it never tastes quite the same.
Other branches tried to replicate the head office's success, with mixed results.
Several labs have failed to replicate the study's surprising results, raising doubts about them.
Viruses replicate by hijacking the machinery of host cells and forcing them to make copies.
He tried hard to replicate the closeness he had once shared with his brother, but too much had changed.
tc: No other laboratory has managed to ______ the experiment, so most scientists remain skeptical of the original findings.
Skepticism about original findings arises when no one else can repeat the experiment.
se: Many companies have tried to ______ the startup's business model, but none has matched its growth.
copy
Both 'replicate' and 'copy' mean to imitate the model exactly, so the sentence means the same.

m: bitter anger at having been treated unfairly
x: He felt a flicker of resentment when his younger brother got the bigger bedroom.
The unequal bonuses caused deep resentment among the junior staff.
In her essay, she explored the resentment that colonized peoples felt toward their rulers.
Rising rents have fueled resentment toward wealthy newcomers in the old neighborhood.
She finally let go of her resentment toward her father and called him after ten years.
tc: Passed over for promotion yet again, the loyal employee could no longer hide his ______ toward the management.
Being unfairly passed over again explains bitter anger toward management.
se: Years of unfair treatment left the workers full of ______ toward their employer.
bitterness
Both 'resentment' and 'bitterness' describe anger at unfair treatment, so the meaning holds.

m: a doubt or feeling of uncertainty about whether something is good or right
x: I had some reservations about the hotel after reading the reviews, but it turned out to be lovely.
Several board members expressed reservations about expanding into a new market so quickly.
My supervisor accepted my proposal, though she had reservations about the sample size.
The treaty was signed despite serious reservations from environmental groups.
She married him without reservation, certain that he was the right person.
tc: She supported the plan wholeheartedly and without ______, convinced it would succeed.
'Wholeheartedly' and 'convinced' show she had no doubts at all.
se: Despite his parents' approval, he still had one nagging ______ about moving abroad.
doubt
Both 'reservation' and 'doubt' mean a lingering uncertainty, so the sentence means the same.

m: to refuse to accept or give in to something; to withstand
x: I could not resist ordering dessert, even though I had promised myself I would not.
Many employees resisted the new software at first but now cannot work without it.
This metal alloy is designed to resist corrosion, even in salt water.
Villagers resisted the government's plan to build a dam that would flood their farmland.
She resisted the urge to call him after their argument and waited for him to apologize.
tc: Instead of giving in to the pressure, the small nation chose to ______ the invaders for as long as it could.
'Instead of giving in' signals the opposite: fighting back against the invaders.
se: The older managers continued to ______ any change to the way the office was run.
oppose
Both 'resist' and 'oppose' mean to refuse to accept the change, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: separately and in the order already mentioned
x: My two sisters are eight and twelve, respectively, and they argue about everything.
Revenue and profit grew by ten and four percent, respectively, in the last quarter.
The first and second chapters of the thesis deal with theory and method, respectively.
In the local election, the two candidates won 52 and 48 percent of the vote, respectively.
My best friend and I fell for a poet and a pilot, respectively, in the same summer.
tc: Tom and Ana scored 85 and 92 on the test, ______, which means Ana did slightly better.
The conclusion that Ana did better only follows if the scores match the names in the order given.
se: The gold and silver medals went to Kenya and Ethiopia, ______.
in that order
Both 'respectively' and 'in that order' show that gold went to Kenya and silver to Ethiopia.

m: calm and controlled; not showing strong emotion or excess
x: Despite the rude waiter, my father remained restrained and simply asked for the manager.
The chief executive gave a restrained response to the news, refusing to celebrate too early.
Critics praised the novel's restrained prose, which lets the tragic events speak for themselves.
Police were praised for their restrained handling of the large but peaceful protest.
Her restrained smile told me she was pleased but did not want to show it.
tc: Whereas his brother shouted and waved his arms during arguments, Rahim always stayed calm and ______.
'Whereas' contrasts the brother's shouting with Rahim's calm, controlled manner.
se: The diplomat's ______ reply avoided any words that might inflame the crisis.
measured
Both 'restrained' and 'measured' describe a careful, controlled reply, so the meaning is the same.

m: to limit or control the size, amount, or range of something
x: My doctor told me to restrict my salt intake to protect my heart.
The company restricts access to the server room to a handful of IT staff.
The professor restricted the essay to two thousand words so that students would have to be concise.
The new law restricts the sale of plastic bags in all major supermarkets.
His jealous partner tried to restrict whom he could see and when.
tc: Rather than allow unlimited withdrawals, the bank decided to ______ them to a small amount per day.
'Rather than allow unlimited' signals the opposite: setting a limit.
se: The city plans to ______ heavy trucks to night hours to reduce daytime congestion.
limit
Both 'restrict' and 'limit' mean to allow the trucks only at night, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to change or improve something thoroughly, giving it a new form
x: We revamped our tiny kitchen with new shelves and a fresh coat of paint.
The marketing team revamped the company website to make it easier to use on phones.
The department is revamping its curriculum to include more data science courses.
The government promised to revamp the struggling public bus network before the next election.
After the breakup, she revamped her whole life, from her haircut to her career.
tc: The outdated restaurant was losing customers, so the new owners decided to ______ its menu and decor completely.
An 'outdated' restaurant losing customers needs a thorough makeover.
se: The airline plans to ______ its loyalty program to attract more frequent flyers.
overhaul
Both 'revamp' and 'overhaul' mean to change the program thoroughly, so the meaning is the same.

m: a surprising fact that is made known, or the act of making it known
x: It was a revelation to learn that my quiet neighbor had once been a rock singer.
The revelation that the accounts had been falsified shocked the entire board.
Reading the original letters was a revelation for the young historian.
Newspaper revelations about the mayor's secret payments led to his resignation.
Her revelation that she had been adopted brought the family closer together.
tc: The documents had stayed hidden for decades, so their sudden ______ caused a scandal in the capital.
Documents that had been 'hidden for decades' cause a scandal when they are suddenly made known.
se: The ______ of the minister's secret bank account forced him to resign.
disclosure
Both 'revelation' and 'disclosure' mean making the secret known, so the sentence means the same.

m: to reconsider and change something, such as an opinion, estimate, plan, or piece of writing
x: I had to revise my weekend plans when my cousins announced they were visiting.
The finance team revised its sales forecast downward after a disappointing month.
My supervisor asked me to revise the introduction so that it states the research question clearly.
Health officials revised their advice after new studies on vaccine safety were published.
Getting to know him better forced her to revise her first impression of him as arrogant.
tc: When new evidence emerged, the committee had no choice but to ______ its earlier conclusions.
New evidence forces the committee to reconsider and change its conclusions.
se: The publisher asked the author to ______ the manuscript before it went to print.
rework
Both 'revise' and 'rework' mean to change and improve the text, so the meaning holds.

m: to present something as better or more attractive than it really is
x: People who romanticize village life rarely mention the lack of hospitals and jobs.
New hires often romanticize startup culture until they face their first eighty-hour week.
The lecturer warned us not to romanticize the past simply because we did not live through it.
Critics accuse the film of romanticizing war by ignoring the suffering of civilians.
She tends to romanticize her first love, forgetting how often they fought.
tc: Rather than portraying the hardships of farm life honestly, the novel tends to ______ it as a peaceful, carefree existence.
'Rather than portraying ... honestly' signals that the novel makes farm life seem better than it is.
se: Older people sometimes ______ their childhood and forget how hard those years really were.
idealize
Both 'romanticize' and 'idealize' mean to remember something as better than it was.

m: relating to serious academic study; learned
x: My uncle is a scholarly man who reads ancient history for fun on weekends.
The consultant's report was more scholarly than practical, full of theory but short on advice.
Students must cite at least ten scholarly articles from peer-reviewed journals.
The museum's new exhibition was praised in both popular and scholarly circles.
She fell for his scholarly charm, though his long lectures at dinner sometimes bored her.
tc: Unlike his popular books written for general readers, this volume is dense and ______, intended mainly for specialists.
The contrast with books for 'general readers' and the phrase 'intended mainly for specialists' point to academic writing.
se: The professor's ______ study of medieval trade routes took ten years to complete.
academic
Both 'scholarly' and 'academic' describe serious research work, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: less important than something else; coming second in rank or value
x: For me, the price of a phone is secondary to how long the battery lasts.
The founder told staff that profits were secondary to keeping customers' trust.
In this study, the effect of age turned out to be secondary to the effect of income.
For decades, environmental concerns were treated as secondary to economic growth.
In their marriage, his career always came first and hers was treated as secondary.
tc: For the founders, profit was only ______; their primary goal was to provide clean water to poor villages.
The contrast with 'their primary goal' shows profit was of lesser importance.
se: In the new budget, defense spending is ______ to investment in health and education.
subordinate
Both 'secondary' and 'subordinate' mean ranked below in importance, so the sentence means the same.

m: carefully choosing only the best or most suitable; not accepting everything
x: I have become more selective about the people I spend my weekends with.
The firm is highly selective and hires fewer than two percent of applicants.
Top universities are extremely selective, admitting only a small fraction of those who apply.
Critics accused the minister of selective use of statistics to make the economy look stronger.
He has a selective memory and conveniently forgets every promise he makes to his wife.
tc: Rather than accepting every applicant, the program is extremely ______, admitting only twenty students each year.
'Rather than accepting every applicant' and 'only twenty students' show careful choosing.
se: She is very ______ about the books she reads and rarely starts a novel without checking the reviews.
choosy
Both 'selective' and 'choosy' mean careful about what she chooses, so the meaning stays the same.

m: presenting information in a way meant to shock or excite rather than to inform accurately
x: My aunt believes every sensational story she sees on social media.
The PR team worried that a sensational headline would distort the facts of the product recall.
Our professor warned us against citing sensational reports that offer no real evidence.
The tabloid ran a sensational account of the murder, full of rumors and gory details.
He made sensational claims about his past to impress her, most of which turned out to be false.
tc: Unlike sober, fact-based newspapers, the tabloid prefers ______ stories designed to shock its readers.
The contrast with 'sober, fact-based' papers and 'designed to shock' point to exaggerated, thrilling stories.
se: The magazine was criticized for its ______ coverage of the scandal, which exaggerated every detail.
lurid
Both 'sensational' and 'lurid' describe coverage designed to shock, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: driven by tender feelings or nostalgia, often in an exaggerated way
x: I keep my grandfather's old watch for sentimental reasons, even though it no longer works.
The manager refused to keep the old logo for sentimental reasons, saying the brand needed a fresh start.
Critics dismissed the poem as sentimental, full of tears and clichés about lost love.
Political ads often rely on sentimental images of families and flags rather than on policy.
He gets sentimental whenever he hears the songs he and his late wife used to dance to.
tc: Although the ring was worth little money, it had great ______ value because it had belonged to her mother.
'Although ... worth little money' contrasts financial worth with emotional worth tied to her mother.
se: The film's ending was so ______ that even critics who liked the story found it overly tearful.
maudlin
Both 'sentimental' and 'maudlin' describe excessive, tearful emotion, giving the same meaning.

m: following one after another in a logical or fixed order
x: The tickets have sequential numbers, so it is easy to tell if one is missing.
Our onboarding is sequential: new staff cannot start module three until they finish module two.
The textbook introduces grammar in sequential steps, moving from simple tenses to complex clauses.
Investigators studied sequential photographs to reconstruct exactly how the bridge collapsed.
Their relationship moved through sequential stages, from friendship to dating to marriage, without any rush.
tc: Rather than jumping around randomly, the instructions follow a strict ______ order, each step depending on the one before.
'Rather than jumping around randomly' and 'each step depending on the one before' describe a fixed order.
se: The apartments in the building have ______ numbers, starting at 101 on the first floor.
consecutive
Both 'sequential' and 'consecutive' mean numbered one after another, so the meaning is the same.

m: the quality of being serious, harsh, or intense
x: We did not realize the severity of the storm until the power went out across the city.
The manager underestimated the severity of the data breach and waited too long to inform clients.
Doctors grade the severity of a burn by how deeply it has damaged the skin.
Rights groups criticized the severity of the sentences handed down to the student protesters.
The severity of her tone made it clear that she was not joking about leaving him.
tc: The judge was known for the ______ of her sentences, rarely showing leniency even to first-time offenders.
'Rarely showing leniency' restates the idea of harshness.
se: Officials only grasped the ______ of the crisis when hospitals began running out of beds.
gravity
Both 'severity' and 'gravity' mean how serious the crisis was, so the sentence means the same.

m: failing to consider the long-term effects of an action; lacking foresight
x: Skipping breakfast to sleep longer is shortsighted if it leaves you exhausted by noon.
Cutting the training budget was a shortsighted decision that hurt productivity for years.
My professor said it was shortsighted to choose a thesis topic just because it seemed easy.
Environmentalists call the plan to fill in the wetlands shortsighted and dangerous.
It was shortsighted of him to lie to her; the truth always comes out eventually.
tc: Selling the forest for a quick profit was ______, since the town will now face floods for decades.
A 'quick profit' that causes 'floods for decades' shows a failure to think about the long term.
se: Economists criticized the ______ policy of borrowing heavily to fund short-term tax cuts.
myopic
Both 'shortsighted' and 'myopic' mean ignoring long-term consequences, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: important or large enough to have a noticeable effect; meaningful
x: Moving to a smaller apartment made a significant difference to our monthly expenses.
The new software led to a significant drop in customer complaints.
The researchers found no significant difference between the two groups' test scores.
Climate change poses a significant threat to low-lying coastal countries.
She gave him a significant look across the table, and he knew it was time to leave.
tc: The new drug reduced symptoms only slightly in early trials, but larger studies showed a far more ______ effect.
'Only slightly' contrasts with 'far more', so the blank means large and important.
se: The new policy led to ______ savings in fuel costs over the year.
substantial
Both 'significant' and 'substantial' mean large enough to matter, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: treating complex issues as if they were much simpler than they really are
x: It is simplistic to blame the city's traffic jams on rickshaw drivers alone.
The consultant's simplistic solution ignored the company's complicated supply chain.
My tutor said my analysis of the novel was too simplistic and ignored its historical context.
Politicians often offer simplistic answers to problems as complex as poverty and crime.
He has a simplistic view of love, believing that a good marriage requires no effort.
tc: The issue of poverty is deeply complex, so any ______ explanation that blames a single cause is bound to fail.
A 'deeply complex' issue cannot be explained by something that wrongly reduces it to 'a single cause'.
se: Critics called the documentary's account of the war ______, since it ignored most of the conflict's causes.
facile
