Both 'simplistic' and 'facile' mean oversimplified and shallow, so the sentence means the same.

m: remarkable or extraordinary; unusual enough to stand out
x: Our grandmother was a woman of singular courage who raised six children alone.
The engineer showed a singular talent for solving problems that had defeated everyone else.
The professor praised the essay as a singular achievement for a first-year student.
The total eclipse was a singular event that drew thousands of people to the coast.
She had a singular way of making everyone in the room feel welcome.
tc: Most composers of his era wrote in a similar style, but his work stood out for its ______ originality.
The contrast with composers who wrote 'in a similar style' shows his originality was extraordinary.
se: The violinist played with ______ skill, astonishing even the most experienced critics.
exceptional
Both 'singular' and 'exceptional' mean extraordinary, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to insult someone by ignoring them or treating them as unimportant
x: She felt slighted when her name was left off the wedding invitation list.
He slighted his colleagues by thanking only the boss in his farewell speech.
The young scholar felt the committee had slighted her research by giving it only a brief mention.
Diplomats worried that leaving the ambassador out of the summit would slight a key ally.
I did not mean to slight you; I simply did not see you at the party.
tc: He was careful to thank every member of the team by name, not wanting to ______ anyone who had worked on the project.
Thanking everyone by name is done to avoid making anyone feel ignored or insulted.
se: Leaving the senior professor off the guest list would ______ him in front of his colleagues.
snub
Both 'slight' and 'snub' mean to insult by ignoring, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: making one serious and thoughtful by revealing an unpleasant or worrying truth
x: Seeing my bank statement after the holidays was a sobering experience that made me cancel two subscriptions.
The quarterly report delivered a sobering message: sales had fallen for the third straight quarter.
For many first-year students, the first round of exam results is a sobering reminder that school habits no longer suffice.
A sobering new study suggests that half of the region's wetlands could disappear within a generation.
Visiting my grandfather in the hospital was sobering; I realized how little time we had spent together.
tc: Far from being cause for celebration, the census figures were deeply ______, revealing how many children still lived in poverty.
'Far from being cause for celebration' and the grim fact about child poverty show the figures made people serious and thoughtful.
se: The ______ experience of losing the final by a single run made the young team train even harder.
chastening
Both 'sobering' and 'chastening' describe an experience that humbles people and makes them more serious.

m: unity and mutual support among people who share an interest, goal or difficulty
x: Neighbors showed remarkable solidarity, taking turns to cook for the family whose house had flooded during the monsoon.
Staff in other departments wore black armbands in solidarity with the colleagues who had been laid off.
The professor argued that solidarity among nineteenth-century factory workers made the first labor laws possible.
Thousands marched through the capital to express solidarity with the striking nurses.
When my sister lost her job, I gave up eating out for a month as a small act of solidarity.
tc: Rather than turning on one another during the crisis, the villagers displayed a striking ______, sharing food and shelter freely.
'Rather than turning on one another' and 'sharing food and shelter' point to unity and mutual support.
se: The strike succeeded largely because of the ______ among workers in different factories.
unity
Both 'solidarity' and 'unity' express the workers standing together, giving the sentence the same meaning.

m: based on valid reasoning or good judgment; reliable and sensible
x: My father always says that buying a modest flat close to work is a sound investment.
Before approving the budget, the board wanted to be sure the plan was financially sound.
Her thesis was praised because each conclusion rested on sound evidence and careful analysis.
Economists questioned whether the government's new policy was based on sound economic principles.
Whenever I face a difficult choice, I ask my older brother, whose judgment has always been sound.
tc: Although the proposal seemed ambitious, the engineers found that its underlying logic was perfectly ______, with no obvious flaws.
'With no obvious flaws' restates the blank, so it must mean logically valid.
se: Every step of the argument was ______, so the committee had no reason to reject it.
valid
Both 'sound' and 'valid' mean logically correct, which explains why the committee could not reject the argument.

m: based on guesswork or theory rather than firm evidence
x: Any talk about who will win the local election is purely speculative at this stage.
My manager dismissed the sales forecast as too speculative to base a hiring plan on.
Much of the early research on dark matter was speculative, relying on indirect observations.
Reporters were warned not to publish speculative claims about the cause of the factory fire.
I know my worries about our friendship are speculative, but I can't stop imagining the worst.
tc: Because no fossils from that period have ever been found, theories about the animal's diet remain largely ______.
The absence of fossils means the theories rest on guesswork, not evidence.
se: Without hard data, the article's conclusions are entirely ______.
conjectural
Both 'speculative' and 'conjectural' mean based on guesswork, matching 'without hard data'.

m: firmly established and not likely to change, weaken or fluctuate
x: After years of freelancing, she finally found a stable job with a regular salary.
Our server has been stable since the update, with no crashes in over a month.
In the experiment, the compound remained stable even at very high temperatures.
Investors generally prefer countries with stable governments and predictable laws.
Children usually thrive when they grow up in a stable and loving home.
tc: Unlike the wildly fluctuating prices of the previous decade, rice prices this year have been remarkably ______.
'Unlike the wildly fluctuating prices' signals a contrast, so the blank must mean steady.
se: After the surgery, the patient's condition remained ______ throughout the night.
steady
Both 'stable' and 'steady' mean the condition did not change for the worse.

m: matching an oversimplified, widely held idea of what a type of person or thing is like
x: My neighbor isn't the stereotypical grumpy old man; he bakes cakes for the whole street.
The advertising team scrapped the campaign because it relied on stereotypical images of women in the kitchen.
Researchers found that children's textbooks still contained stereotypical portrayals of scientists as elderly men.
Critics said the film offered a stereotypical view of rural life that ignored its complexity.
I was hurt when my friend made a stereotypical joke about engineers having no social skills.
tc: The novel deliberately avoids ______ characters: its villain is gentle and its hero is deeply flawed.
The gentle villain and flawed hero show the novel rejects oversimplified, expected character types.
se: The sitcom was criticized for its ______ depiction of immigrants as poor and uneducated.
clichéd
Both 'stereotypical' and 'clichéd' describe an oversimplified, overused portrayal.

m: showing tension or unease; forced and not natural
x: Dinner was strained after my cousin brought up the old family property dispute.
Relations between the two departments became strained when the budget was cut.
The study notes that hospital resources were severely strained during the outbreak.
Talks between the neighboring countries remain strained over water-sharing rights.
She gave me a strained smile, and I knew immediately that something was wrong.
tc: Ever since the argument over the inheritance, conversations between the brothers have been ______, full of awkward pauses.
The argument and 'full of awkward pauses' show the conversations are tense and uneasy.
se: The atmosphere in the meeting room was ______ as everyone waited for the layoff announcement.
tense
Both 'strained' and 'tense' describe the nervous unease before bad news.

m: based on personal feelings, tastes or opinions rather than on facts
x: Whether biryani tastes better in Old Dhaka is subjective, but my uncle insists that it does.
Performance reviews can feel subjective when managers do not use clear criteria.
Grading essays is far more subjective than marking a math exam.
Judges in the competition were accused of making subjective decisions that favored local athletes.
Beauty is subjective, so I stopped worrying about what others thought of my clothes.
tc: Unlike an objective measurement such as body temperature, a patient's description of pain is inevitably ______.
'Unlike an objective measurement' signals a contrast, so the blank means based on personal feeling.
se: Because taste in music is so ______, no critic's ranking can claim to be definitive.
personal
Both 'subjective' and 'personal' mean that taste depends on the individual, so no ranking is final.

m: to come after and take the place of someone or something
x: A week of steady rain succeeded the long dry spell, and the garden finally turned green.
After twenty years in charge, the director announced that her deputy would succeed her next spring.
In history class, we traced how one empire succeeded another across the region over five centuries.
The prime minister's sudden resignation left the party scrambling to choose who would succeed him.
After the funeral, my cousin quietly accepted that he would succeed his father as head of the family.
tc: The ailing king had no children, so nobody knew who would ______ him on the throne.
Having no children raises the question of who would come next and take his place.
se: When the founder steps down, his daughter is expected to ______ him as chief executive.
replace
Both 'succeed' and 'replace' mean to take over the founder's position after him.

m: following one after another without a break
x: It rained for five successive days, and the basement flooded twice.
The company has reported losses for three successive quarters, and investors are growing nervous.
Successive generations of students have used this textbook since the 1980s.
Successive governments have promised to fix the railway, but little has changed.
After two successive breakups, he decided to spend some time on his own.
tc: The club won the title in three ______ seasons, a streak no rival had managed without a single break.
'A streak' and 'without a single break' show the seasons followed one another directly.
se: Prices have risen for four ______ months, worrying economists.
consecutive
Both 'successive' and 'consecutive' mean the months followed one after another without a break.

m: giving encouragement, help or emotional comfort
x: My parents were supportive when I decided to switch from engineering to an MBA.
A supportive manager can make even a stressful project feel manageable.
Studies show that students in supportive learning environments are more likely to ask questions.
The new law received supportive comments from both doctors and patient groups.
During my illness, my friends were incredibly supportive, visiting me almost every day.
tc: Instead of criticizing her for failing the exam, her teacher was warm and ______, helping her plan how to try again.
'Instead of criticizing' and 'helping her plan' show the teacher gave encouragement.
se: Having ______ colleagues made my first month at the new job far less stressful.
encouraging
Both 'supportive' and 'encouraging' describe colleagues who help and reassure, easing the stress.

m: able to continue over time without using up resources or causing lasting harm
x: We switched to cloth bags and a bicycle as part of a more sustainable lifestyle.
The chief executive admitted that the company's rapid growth was not sustainable without more staff.
Her dissertation examines sustainable farming practices in flood-prone regions.
Scientists warn that current fishing levels are not sustainable and could wipe out entire fish stocks.
I realized that working eighty hours a week was not sustainable if I wanted a healthy marriage.
tc: Heavy borrowing may fuel growth for a year or two, but it is hardly ______ over the long term.
The contrast between a short burst of growth and 'the long term' shows the blank means able to continue.
se: Experts doubt that the city's breakneck pace of construction is ______ for another decade.
viable
Both 'sustainable' and 'viable' mean the pace can realistically be kept up.

m: done according to a fixed plan or method; thorough and orderly
x: I take a systematic approach to cleaning, starting with the top shelves and working down.
The auditors conducted a systematic review of every invoice from the past year.
A systematic study of the data revealed a pattern that earlier researchers had missed.
The report documents systematic discrimination against women in the hiring process.
My wife is far more systematic than I am; she keeps every bill in a labeled folder.
tc: Rather than checking files at random, the investigators were thoroughly ______, examining each record in order.
'Rather than checking files at random' and 'examining each record in order' point to a methodical approach.
se: The detective was praised for her ______ search of the crime scene, which left nothing to chance.
methodical
Both 'systematic' and 'methodical' describe a careful, orderly search that leaves nothing to chance.

m: something that serves as clear evidence or proof of a fact or quality
x: The fact that this old ceiling fan still works is a testament to how well things were once made.
Her promotion after just two years is a testament to her hard work.
The thesis committee called the student's detailed fieldwork a testament to her patience.
The bridge, still standing after a century, is a testament to the skill of its engineers.
Our friendship surviving moves to three different countries is a testament to how much we care about each other.
tc: The village school, rebuilt by hand after the cyclone, is a living ______ to the community's resilience.
The rebuilt school demonstrates the community's resilience, so the blank means proof or evidence.
se: The scholarship fund she created is a fitting ______ to her late husband's love of learning.
tribute
Both 'testament' and 'tribute' describe something that honors and bears witness to his love of learning.

m: full of difficulties or controversy; hard to deal with
x: Deciding who would host Eid dinner this year turned into a surprisingly thorny family question.
The manager avoided the thorny issue of bonuses until the very end of the meeting.
Philosophers have debated the thorny problem of free will for centuries.
Immigration remains a thorny topic in the upcoming election, and both parties try to avoid it.
Talking to my parents about moving abroad was a thorny conversation that I kept putting off.
tc: The question of how to divide the land was so ______ that negotiators postponed it to a later round of talks.
Postponing the question shows it was too difficult and controversial to settle easily.
se: Data privacy is one of the most ______ problems facing technology companies today.
knotty
Both 'thorny' and 'knotty' mean complicated and hard to solve.

m: considerate of the needs and feelings of other people
x: It was thoughtful of you to bring an umbrella for me as well.
My boss sent a thoughtful note to every team member after the difficult product launch.
My roommate is thoughtful enough to study in the library whenever I have an early exam.
Volunteers made a thoughtful effort to provide halal and vegetarian meals for every guest at the shelter.
On our anniversary, my husband gave me a thoughtful gift: a book of my grandmother's recipes.
tc: Unlike his ______ sister, who always remembered birthdays, Rafiq often forgot even his mother's.
'Unlike' contrasts the sister with forgetful Rafiq, so she must be considerate of others.
se: It was very ______ of the hotel staff to leave an extra fan in our room during the heatwave.
considerate
Both 'thoughtful' and 'considerate' praise the staff for caring about the guests' comfort.

m: able to be endured or put up with, though not pleasant
x: The June heat is tolerable only if you have a ceiling fan running all day.
With noise-cancelling headphones, the open-plan office finally became tolerable.
The lecture was long, but the professor's jokes made it tolerable.
Officials said that pollution had fallen to a tolerable level for most residents.
Living with my in-laws was tolerable at first, but after a year we needed our own space.
tc: The pain was severe for the first few days, but with medication it became ______, and she could sleep again.
The contrast with 'severe' and the fact that she could sleep show the pain became bearable.
se: The long commute was only ______ because I could listen to podcasts on the bus.
bearable
Both 'tolerable' and 'bearable' mean the commute could be endured.

m: the general attitude or mood expressed in speech or writing
x: I didn't like the tone of his text message, so I called him to clear the air.
The email was polite, but its tone made it clear that the deadline was not negotiable.
In the reading passage, the author's tone shifts from admiring to skeptical.
Commentators criticized the harsh tone of the debate between the two candidates.
My mother can tell I'm upset just from my tone of voice on the phone.
tc: Although the words of her letter were polite, the cold ______ revealed how angry she really was.
The contrast between polite words and hidden anger points to the attitude conveyed by the letter.
se: The ______ of the speech was hopeful, even though it described serious problems.
mood
Both 'tone' and 'mood' refer to the overall feeling the speech conveyed.

m: causing a major and lasting change
x: Buying a dishwasher was surprisingly transformative; we suddenly had our evenings back for reading and walks.
The new software proved transformative, cutting the time spent on monthly reports by half.
Studying abroad was a transformative experience that changed how I see my own country.
Mobile banking has had a transformative effect on rural economies across South Asia.
Becoming a father was the most transformative event of his life.
tc: Far from making a minor difference, the arrival of electricity was truly ______, reshaping every aspect of village life.
'Far from making a minor difference' and 'reshaping every aspect' show the change was profound.
se: Many believe that cheap solar power will prove ______ for the global economy.
revolutionary
Both 'transformative' and 'revolutionary' mean bringing about a dramatic, fundamental change.

m: to make something seem less important or serious than it really is
x: Please don't trivialize my fear of flying by laughing it off.
The memo seemed to trivialize the staff's complaints about long working hours.
Some historians argue that popular films trivialize complex historical events.
Campaigners accused the newspaper of trivializing the issue of domestic violence.
When my friend tried to trivialize my breakup, I felt even more alone.
tc: Calling the flood a minor inconvenience would ______ the suffering of thousands who lost their homes.
Describing a disaster as 'a minor inconvenience' makes it seem far less serious than it is.
se: Critics warned that the advertisement might ______ the dangers of drunk driving.
downplay
Both 'trivialize' and 'downplay' mean to make the dangers seem less serious than they are.

m: having the usual qualities of a particular type of person or thing; characteristic
x: On a typical weekday, I leave home at seven to beat the Dhaka traffic.
A typical meeting in our office starts ten minutes late and runs over.
In a typical experiment, participants are shown images and asked to rate them.
The house is typical of the colonial buildings found in the old part of the city.
It was typical of my brother to forget my birthday and then apologize with a huge cake.
tc: Arriving an hour late and blaming the traffic was ______ of Imran, who had never been on time in his life.
'Who had never been on time in his life' shows the behavior was characteristic of him.
se: His sulky reaction was ______ of a teenager who has just been told to put away his phone.
characteristic
Both 'typical' and 'characteristic' mean the reaction is what one would expect from a teenager.

m: in the end; finally, after a long process or series of events
x: We looked at a dozen flats, but ultimately chose the one closest to my office.
The project faced many delays, but ultimately it was delivered within budget.
Ultimately, the success of the experiment depended on precise temperature control.
Lawmakers debated the bill for months before ultimately rejecting it.
Ultimately, it's your decision whether to forgive him, but I'll support you either way.
tc: After months of negotiations that seemed to go nowhere, the two sides ______ reached an agreement.
'After months of negotiations' signals that the agreement came only at the end of a long process.
se: Despite early setbacks, the startup ______ became one of the most successful in the country.
eventually
Both 'ultimately' and 'eventually' mean that success came in the end, after the setbacks.

m: plain and simple; without decoration or embellishment
x: The cafe's unadorned white walls make the colorful food stand out even more.
Her presentation was unadorned by flashy graphics, but the data spoke for itself.
The poet's unadorned style makes his verses easy for students to understand.
The memorial is an unadorned stone slab bearing only the names of the dead.
I loved his unadorned honesty when he told me exactly how he felt.
tc: In contrast to the ornate palaces of the era, the monastery was strikingly ______, with bare walls and simple wooden benches.
'In contrast to the ornate palaces' and 'bare walls' show the monastery lacked decoration.
se: She told the story in ______ language, without any of the flourishes her readers expected.
plain
Both 'unadorned' and 'plain' mean the language had no decorative flourishes.

m: natural and sincere; free of pretension or artificial behavior
x: Despite her fame in the neighborhood, she remained warm and unaffected.
Clients appreciated the new consultant's unaffected manner and plain speaking.
The professor's unaffected delight in his subject inspired even the most bored students.
Viewers were charmed by the young athlete's unaffected answers during the television interview.
What I love most about my best friend is her unaffected laugh; she never pretends.
tc: Unlike his showy, pretentious cousins, Arif was modest and ______, speaking to everyone in the same plain way.
'Unlike his showy, pretentious cousins' signals that Arif was natural and sincere.
se: Audiences loved the actor's ______ performance, which felt like watching a real person rather than a star.
natural
Both 'unaffected' and 'natural' describe a performance free of artificiality.

m: showing no prejudice for or against anyone or anything; fair and impartial
x: I asked my aunt for an unbiased opinion on which of the two dresses looked better.
The company hired an outside firm to conduct an unbiased review of its hiring practices.
Researchers use random sampling to make sure their results are unbiased.
Voters complained that it was hard to find unbiased news coverage of the election.
As your friend, I can't be completely unbiased, but I think he treated you unfairly.
tc: Because the referee had no connection to either team, both sides trusted him to be ______.
Having no connection to either team means he would favor neither side.
se: Journalists are expected to remain ______ when covering elections.
impartial
Both 'unbiased' and 'impartial' mean not favoring any side.

m: unwilling to make concessions or change one's position; firmly rigid
x: My grandmother was uncompromising about one rule: no phones at the dinner table.
Our new director has an uncompromising commitment to quality, which some staff find exhausting.
The scholar's uncompromising critique of the theory made her both admired and disliked.
The union took an uncompromising stance, refusing any deal that cut pensions.
His uncompromising honesty sometimes hurt my feelings, but I always knew where I stood.
tc: Negotiators had hoped for flexibility, but the delegation remained ______, rejecting every proposed concession.
The contrast with 'flexibility' and 'rejecting every proposed concession' indicate a refusal to give ground.
se: The coach was ______ in his demand for discipline, refusing to bend the rules even for star players.
unbending
Both 'uncompromising' and 'unbending' mean firmly refusing to relax his demands.

m: so clearly true that it cannot be denied or disputed
x: There is an undeniable charm to old bookshops, with their dusty shelves and creaky floors.
Her talent for negotiation is undeniable; she closed three major deals this quarter.
The evidence linking smoking and lung cancer is now undeniable.
The undeniable rise in sea levels has forced coastal cities to rethink their planning.
Whatever their differences, the undeniable bond between the two sisters was obvious to everyone.
tc: Even his fiercest critics had to admit that his skill as a surgeon was ______.
If even his fiercest critics had to admit it, his skill could not be disputed.
se: The benefits of regular exercise are ______, supported by decades of research.
indisputable
Both 'undeniable' and 'indisputable' mean the benefits are beyond doubt.

m: to judge something as smaller, weaker or less important than it really is
x: Never underestimate how long it takes to cross the city during rush hour.
We underestimated the cost of the project and had to ask for more funding.
Students often underestimate the amount of reading required in graduate school.
Health officials admitted that they had underestimated how quickly the virus would spread.
I underestimated how much I would miss my family after moving abroad.
tc: Many rivals were quick to ______ the young chess player, only to lose to her within twenty moves.
'Only to lose to her' shows the rivals had judged her as weaker than she really was.
se: It is easy to ______ the influence of sleep on academic performance.
underrate
Both 'underestimate' and 'underrate' mean to judge sleep's influence as less important than it is.

m: basic or fundamental, though not obvious; lying beneath the surface
x: The headaches were only a symptom; the underlying problem was poor eyesight.
Before fixing the bug, we need to understand its underlying cause.
The course teaches the underlying principles of thermodynamics rather than just formulas.
Economists say the underlying rate of inflation remains stubbornly high.
Their constant arguments about money hid an underlying lack of trust.
tc: Treating the rash alone will not help; the doctor must identify the ______ condition that is causing it.
The rash is only a surface symptom, so the blank refers to the hidden, fundamental condition.
se: The article explains the ______ causes of the financial crisis, not just its visible effects.
fundamental
Both 'underlying' and 'fundamental' refer to the basic causes beneath the visible effects.

m: to value or rate something lower than it deserves
x: People underrate the joy of a simple cup of tea on a rainy afternoon.
Many managers underrate the value of clear documentation until something breaks.
Critics long underrated the novelist, but scholars now consider her a major figure.
Analysts warn that investors underrate the risks of rising interest rates.
I always underrated my own cooking until my friends started asking for my recipes.
tc: Coaches tended to ______ the small striker, assuming that his size would keep him from scoring.
Assuming his size would stop him from scoring means the coaches valued him too low.
se: Many historians ______ the role that women played in the independence movement.
underestimate
Both 'underrate' and 'underestimate' mean to judge the women's role as less important than it was.

m: presented in a subtle, restrained way; not showy
x: She has always preferred understated jewelry, usually just a thin gold chain and small earrings.
The office has an understated design, with neutral colors and simple furniture.
The author's understated prose makes the tragic ending all the more powerful.
The mayor's understated style contrasted sharply with that of his flamboyant predecessor.
His understated way of saying 'I missed you' meant more to me than any grand gesture.
tc: Instead of the flashy decorations everyone expected, the wedding hall was elegant and ______.
'Instead of the flashy decorations' signals the opposite of showy.
se: The hotel's ______ elegance appealed to guests who disliked flashy luxury.
restrained
Both 'understated' and 'restrained' describe elegance that avoids showiness.

m: to fail to recognize the true worth or importance of something
x: Don't undervalue your old textbooks; second-year students will pay good money for them.
Many companies undervalue the experience that older workers bring.
Academic culture tends to undervalue teaching compared with research.
Some economists argue that the market undervalues the country's currency by as much as twenty percent.
She felt undervalued at home, where nobody noticed how much she did.
tc: Nurses often feel that hospitals ______ their work, paying them far less than their skills deserve.
'Paying them far less than their skills deserve' shows their worth is not recognized.
se: Society tends to ______ the work of caregivers, even though it is essential.
underrate
Both 'undervalue' and 'underrate' mean to treat essential work as less important than it is.

m: more than is reasonable or appropriate; excessive
x: Please don't put undue pressure on your little brother before his exams.
The manager was accused of showing undue favor to his relatives when hiring.
Researchers must ensure that no undue influence affects how participants answer.
The inquiry concluded that the police had used undue force during the protest.
I didn't want to cause my parents undue worry, so I didn't tell them about the accident.
tc: The court ruled that holding the suspect for six months without charge caused ______ hardship, far beyond what the law permits.
'Far beyond what the law permits' shows the hardship was excessive.
se: Parents should avoid placing ______ pressure on children to win every competition.
excessive
Both 'undue' and 'excessive' mean more pressure than is reasonable.

m: having no basis in fact or evidence
x: My fears about the new neighbors proved unfounded; they turned out to be very kind.
The rumor that the company was closing turned out to be completely unfounded.
Her study shows that the popular concerns about the vaccine's safety are unfounded.
The minister dismissed the corruption allegations as unfounded and promised to cooperate with any inquiry.
His jealousy was unfounded, but no amount of reassurance could calm him.
tc: Investigators found no evidence whatsoever to support the accusation, which proved entirely ______.
'No evidence whatsoever to support' means the accusation had no factual basis.
se: The parents' worries about the new teacher turned out to be ______.
groundless
Both 'unfounded' and 'groundless' mean the worries had no basis.

m: not planned or meant to happen
x: Leaving the window open had the unintended effect of letting mosquitoes in all night.
The new policy had the unintended consequence of making staff work longer hours.
Scientists are studying the unintended effects of the pesticide on bees.
Rent controls can have unintended consequences, such as a shortage of housing.
My joke caused unintended offense, and I apologized to her the next day.
tc: The ban was meant to reduce plastic waste, but it had the ______ result of increasing paper use.
'Was meant to... but' shows the result was not what anyone had planned.
se: The tax cut produced some ______ side effects, including a sharp rise in housing prices.
unforeseen
Both 'unintended' and 'unforeseen' describe side effects nobody planned for.

m: not shown to be right, fair or reasonable
x: Charging extra for tap water in a restaurant seems totally unjustified to me.
Employees protested the unjustified dismissal of their colleague.
The reviewer said the paper's conclusions were unjustified given its small sample.
Human rights groups condemned the unjustified detention of several journalists.
I realized my anger at my sister was unjustified, so I called to apologize.
tc: Since the tenant had paid every bill on time, the landlord's sudden demand for a larger deposit was completely ______.
The tenant's perfect record means there was no good reason for the demand.
se: The editor felt that the harsh criticism of the young author was ______.
unwarranted
Both 'unjustified' and 'unwarranted' mean the criticism had no fair basis.

m: having no equal; better or greater than anything else of its kind
x: The view from the rooftop is unparalleled, especially at sunset.
The firm offers unparalleled expertise in cross-border tax law.
The university library has an unparalleled collection of medieval manuscripts and early printed maps.
The country has enjoyed a period of unparalleled economic growth over the past decade.
Her kindness during my illness was unparalleled; no one else did nearly as much.
tc: No other batsman of his generation came close to his record; his consistency was truly ______.
'No other batsman... came close' shows his consistency had no equal.
se: The museum offers ______ access to rare documents that no other institution can provide.
unrivaled
Both 'unparalleled' and 'unrivaled' mean no other institution can match it.

m: achieving little or nothing useful; producing few results
x: I spent an unproductive afternoon scrolling on my phone instead of cleaning the flat.
Long, unproductive meetings are one of the main complaints in our office.
My first week of thesis writing was unproductive because I kept rereading the same papers.
After years of drought, many farmers abandoned the unproductive land and moved to the cities.
Arguing over who was right proved unproductive, so we agreed to start fresh.
tc: After three hours of talks in which neither side moved an inch, both delegations admitted the session had been ______.
'Neither side moved an inch' shows the talks achieved nothing.
se: The search for a vaccine was ______ for years before scientists finally made a breakthrough.
fruitless
Both 'unproductive' and 'fruitless' mean the search produced no results until the breakthrough.

m: accepting something completely, without doubt or hesitation
x: My little brother has an unquestioning belief that our father can fix anything.
The new hire's unquestioning acceptance of every instruction worried her mentor.
Good scholarship requires healthy skepticism, not unquestioning faith in authority.
Like most cults, the group demanded unquestioning loyalty and cut members off from their families.
Her unquestioning trust in me made me determined never to let her down.
tc: The general demanded ______ obedience; soldiers who asked why an order had been given were punished.
Punishing soldiers who asked why shows he wanted obedience without any doubt or question.
se: The dictator's followers showed ______ loyalty, never doubting any of his orders.
blind
Both 'unquestioning' and 'blind' describe loyalty given without any doubt.

m: ordinary; not particularly interesting, unusual or surprising
x: From the outside, the restaurant looks unremarkable, but the food is excellent.
His first year at the company was unremarkable, but his second year won him a promotion.
The results of the trial were unremarkable, showing no difference between the two drugs.
The town is unremarkable except for the annual boat race on the river.
She thought her life was unremarkable until she read her grandmother's diary.
tc: Though the house looked ______ from the street, inside it held one of the finest art collections in the country.
'Though' contrasts the plain exterior with the extraordinary collection inside.
se: Apart from one memorable chapter, the novel was ______.
ordinary
Both 'unremarkable' and 'ordinary' mean the rest of the novel was nothing special.

m: causing anxiety, unease or a sense of disturbance
x: There was an unsettling silence in the house when I came home late.
The sudden resignation of three senior managers was unsettling for the whole team.
The study's findings about memory loss are unsettling for anyone over fifty.
Reports of an unsettling rise in hate crimes prompted a government inquiry.
It's unsettling when someone you trust suddenly stops answering your messages.
tc: The calm music of the film's opening contrasts with the ______ images that follow, which leave viewers uneasy.
The contrast with 'calm' and 'leave viewers uneasy' show the images are disturbing.
se: Waking up in a strange hotel room gave me a deeply ______ feeling.
unnerving
Both 'unsettling' and 'unnerving' describe a feeling of unease.

m: not supported or proven by evidence
x: My aunt shared an unsubstantiated claim in the family chat group that lemon water cures diabetes.
HR refused to act on unsubstantiated complaints that came without supporting documents.
The paper was rejected because its central argument rested on unsubstantiated assumptions.
The newspaper apologized for printing unsubstantiated allegations against the mayor.
I hated that he believed unsubstantiated gossip about me instead of asking me directly.
tc: Because no witness or document backed up the accusation, the judge dismissed it as ______.
'No witness or document backed up the accusation' means it lacked supporting evidence.
se: The report was criticized for relying on ______ claims from anonymous sources.
unverified
Both 'unsubstantiated' and 'unverified' mean the claims had not been backed by evidence.

m: confirmed or supported a decision, principle or law that had been questioned (past of uphold)
x: My parents upheld the family tradition of eating together every Friday night.
The board upheld the manager's decision to cancel the supplier's contract.
The university upheld the student's appeal and allowed her to retake the exam.
The Supreme Court upheld the lower court's ruling in the long-running land dispute.
Throughout their marriage, they upheld their promise never to go to bed angry.
tc: Instead of overturning the verdict as the defense had hoped, the appeals court ______ it.
'Instead of overturning' signals the opposite, so the court confirmed the verdict.
se: The tribunal ______ the original decision, rejecting the company's request to reverse it.
affirmed
Both 'upheld' and 'affirmed' mean the tribunal confirmed the decision rather than reversing it.

m: to support, maintain or confirm a principle, law or decision
x: We try to uphold the rule that nobody uses phones during dinner.
Every employee is expected to uphold the company's code of conduct.
Researchers must uphold strict ethical standards when working with human subjects.
The police have a duty to uphold the law, even when it is unpopular.
I promised my late grandfather that I would uphold the values he taught me.
tc: Instead of abandoning their principles under pressure, the journalists vowed to ______ them at any cost.
'Instead of abandoning' signals the opposite, so the blank means to maintain and defend.
se: Judges are sworn to ______ the constitution, whatever their personal views.
defend
Both 'uphold' and 'defend' mean to protect and maintain the constitution.

m: completely and absolutely
x: After the twelve-hour flight from Toronto, I was utterly exhausted and slept until noon.
The proposal was utterly unrealistic given our budget and timeline.
The professor found the student's excuse for missing the exam utterly unconvincing.
Residents said they felt utterly abandoned by the authorities after the floodwaters rose.
I was utterly heartbroken when my best friend moved to another country.
tc: The plan was not just slightly flawed; it was ______ hopeless from the start.
'Not just slightly' signals that the blank must mean completely.
se: The defense lawyer's argument was ______ convincing, and the jury needed only an hour to decide.
completely
Both 'utterly' and 'completely' mean the argument was convincing in every respect.

m: the quality of being logically sound, well-founded or legally acceptable
x: I checked the validity of my passport before booking the flight.
The auditor questioned the validity of several expense claims.
Peer review helps establish the validity of a study's findings.
Opposition parties challenged the validity of the election results in court.
My friend never doubted the validity of my feelings, even when I couldn't explain them.
tc: Because the survey included only twenty people, critics questioned the ______ of its sweeping conclusions.
A tiny sample makes sweeping conclusions doubtful, so critics questioned their soundness.
se: Philosophers continue to debate the ______ of the argument for free will.
soundness
Both 'validity' and 'soundness' refer to whether the argument is logically correct.

m: able to be checked or proved true
x: When selling the car, I made sure every claim about its history was verifiable through receipts.
Job applicants should list verifiable achievements rather than vague strengths.
Scientific theories must make verifiable predictions that other researchers can test independently.
The website promises to publish only verifiable facts, not rumors.
I want verifiable proof that you've changed, not just more promises.
tc: The editor rejected the article because its claims, however interesting, were not ______ from any reliable source.
'From any reliable source' shows the problem was that the claims could not be checked.
se: Courts accept only claims that are ______ through documents or witnesses.
provable
Both 'verifiable' and 'provable' mean the claims can be shown to be true.

m: causing annoyance, frustration or worry; difficult to solve
x: Finding parking near the market on a Friday afternoon is a vexing problem.
The most vexing part of the project was a bug that appeared only on certain phones.
Scientists have long found the origin of the moon a vexing question.
Traffic congestion remains one of the most vexing issues facing city planners.
It was vexing that my roommate kept borrowing my things without asking.
tc: The puzzle had baffled mathematicians for a century, making it one of the most ______ problems in the field.
Having baffled mathematicians for a century shows the problem was frustrating and hard to solve.
se: The constant delays were ______ for passengers who had connecting flights.
exasperating
Both 'vexing' and 'exasperating' mean the delays were deeply annoying.

m: almost or nearly as described, but not completely or officially
x: Without a road, our village becomes a virtual island during the monsoon.
The week-long strike brought production at the garment factory to a virtual standstill.
The new edition of the textbook is a virtual copy of the old one, with only the cover changed.
The two candidates are in a virtual tie, according to the latest poll.
After years apart, my childhood friend had become a virtual stranger to me.
tc: Though rivals technically exist, the firm's dominance gives it ______ control of the market.
'Though rivals technically exist' shows the control is nearly total in practice but not official.
se: In the remote village, the old headman exercised ______ control over every decision, though he held no official post.
effective
Both 'virtual' and 'effective' mean he had control in practice though not officially.

m: justified or necessary given the circumstances
x: Given the heavy rain forecast, cancelling the picnic was warranted.
A full investigation is warranted after so many customer complaints.
The reviewer felt that further experiments were warranted before publication.
Officials said the evacuation was warranted given the strength of the cyclone.
Her anger was warranted; he had broken his promise for the third time.
tc: Given the serious safety risks the inspectors uncovered, shutting the factory down was entirely ______.
'Given the serious safety risks' supplies the reason that makes the shutdown justified.
se: Considering how much she contributed, her promotion was fully ______.
deserved
Both 'warranted' and 'deserved' mean the promotion was justified by her contribution.

m: unsteady in resolve or opinion; uncertain and changing between choices
x: Polls suggest that wavering voters in the coastal districts could decide the outcome of the election.
Her manager's wavering commitment to the project left the whole team unsure whether to keep working on it.
Despite his parents' wavering confidence, Rafi stuck to his plan of studying engineering abroad.
Scientists worry that wavering public support will make it harder to fund long-term climate research.
I could hear the wavering resolve in his voice as he promised, once again, to quit smoking.
tc: Unlike her ______ colleagues, who changed their minds with every new rumor, Nadia never doubted that the merger was a good idea.
The restatement 'changed their minds with every new rumor' defines the blank as indecisive.
se: The senator's ______ stance on the tax bill frustrated allies who wanted a firm commitment.
vacillating
Both 'wavering' and 'vacillating' describe a position that keeps shifting, the opposite of the 'firm commitment' the allies wanted.

m: important and serious; having great significance or influence
x: Choosing a university is a weighty decision, so don't let anyone rush you into it.
The board spent the entire afternoon on weighty matters such as layoffs and the company's future.
Her thesis tackles the weighty question of how inequality shapes access to clean water.
Legal experts say the court's ruling carries weighty implications for press freedom across the region.
He felt the weighty responsibility of caring for his younger siblings after their father fell ill.
tc: The meeting was supposed to deal with ______ issues like the budget crisis, but it was wasted on trivial complaints about parking.
The contrast word 'but' and the opposite 'trivial' show the blank must mean serious and important.
se: Whether to move abroad for an MBA is a question too ______ to be settled over a single cup of tea.
momentous
Both 'weighty' and 'momentous' mean highly important, which is why the question cannot be settled casually.

m: in contrast with the fact that; while on the other hand (used to link two contrasting statements)
x: My brother loves spicy food, whereas I can barely handle a little black pepper.
Whereas the old system took weeks to process refunds, the new software handles them in a day.
Some students learn best by reading, whereas others need to see problems worked out on the board.
Rural districts saw their populations shrink, whereas the capital grew by nearly two million people.
She remembers every birthday and anniversary, whereas her husband needs constant reminders on his phone.
tc: In some cities the monsoon floods the streets for weeks, ______ in desert cities rain is a rare event.
The two clauses describe opposite situations, so the blank must be a word that introduces a contrast.
se: Older employees tend to prefer phone calls, ______ younger staff usually prefer messaging apps.
while
Both 'whereas' and 'while' link two contrasting facts and give the sentence the same meaning.

m: found or happening over a large area or among many people
x: There was widespread relief in the office when the manager cancelled the Saturday meeting.
Power cuts were widespread across the city after the storm brought down dozens of lines.
Widespread cheating on the entrance exam forced the university to hold the test again.
Doctors are alarmed by the widespread misuse of antibiotics, which is fuelling drug-resistant infections.
Her novel won widespread praise from critics, but she cared most about her mother's opinion.
tc: Far from being confined to a few villages, the disease had become ______ across the entire district.
'Far from being confined to a few villages' signals the opposite of limited, so the blank means spread over a large area.
se: Corruption was so ______ in the agency that almost every contract involved a bribe.
pervasive
Both 'widespread' and 'pervasive' mean present almost everywhere, matching 'almost every contract'.

m: deserving respect, attention, or support; having good qualities
x: Every year the club donates its surplus to a worthy cause chosen by the members.
After months of hard work, she proved herself a worthy successor to the retiring head of sales.
His research is certainly worthy of publication, though the reviewers asked for a few revisions.
Few politicians are worthy of the trust that voters place in them on election day.
I never felt worthy of her friendship, yet she stood by me through every difficult year.
tc: Despite a few minor errors, the judges felt the essay was ______ of the top prize because of its striking originality.
'Because of its striking originality' gives the reason the essay deserved the prize, so the blank means deserving.
se: Volunteers raised money for several ______ causes, including a school for blind children.
deserving
Both 'worthy' and 'deserving' describe causes that merit support, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: a very large quantity of something; plentifulness
x: Our garden produced such an abundance of tomatoes that we gave bags of them to the neighbors.
There is no shortage of talent here; if anything, we have an abundance of qualified applicants.
Scientists were surprised by the abundance of marine life around the newly discovered reef.
During the monsoon, the abundance of water in the fields contrasts sharply with the dry winter months.
She has an abundance of patience, which makes her a wonderful teacher for young children.
tc: In sharp contrast to the scarcity of the previous year, this year's harvest brought food in ______.
'In sharp contrast to the scarcity' tells us the blank means the opposite of scarcity, a large quantity.
se: Visitors were amazed by the sheer ______ of fresh fruit at the market, from mangoes to lychees.
profusion
Both 'abundance' and 'profusion' mean a very large amount, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: up in the air; high above the ground
x: The winning captain held the trophy aloft as the crowd roared in celebration.
Kites stayed aloft for hours over the rooftops of Old Dhaka during the winter kite festival.
Waiters carried trays aloft as they squeezed through the crowded wedding hall.
Hot air balloons stay aloft only as long as the air inside them is warmer than the air outside.
Our pilot explained that the plane would remain aloft for another forty minutes before landing.
tc: Though the engine sputtered and the passengers held their breath, the small plane somehow stayed ______ until it reached the runway.
'Though the engine sputtered' suggests the plane might fall, so the contrast tells us it stayed up in the air.
se: The glider remained ______ for nearly an hour, riding the warm currents above the hills.
airborne
Both 'aloft' and 'airborne' mean up in the air, so the sentence means the same with either.

m: to attack persistently, especially with a stream of questions, information, or criticism
x: Every evening my phone is bombarded with messages from three different family group chats.
New employees are often bombarded with policies, passwords and training videos during their first week.
Students are bombarded with so much information before exams that it is hard to know what matters.
Reporters bombarded the spokesperson with questions about the factory fire.
After the breakup, she bombarded him with apologies until he finally agreed to meet her for coffee.
tc: Rather than give the guest a moment to settle in, the eager hosts began to ______ him with questions about his life abroad.
'Rather than give the guest a moment' shows the hosts did the opposite, flooding him with questions.
se: Whenever a new phone is released, companies ______ consumers with advertisements on every platform.
inundate
Both 'bombard' and 'inundate' mean to overwhelm with a constant stream, so the meaning is the same.

m: to research or examine something deeply and thoroughly
x: Before buying the flat, we delved into the building's history and found several unpaid tax bills.
The auditor delved deep into the accounts and uncovered a pattern of small, suspicious payments.
In her second year at university, she began to delve into the philosophy of science.
The documentary delves into the causes of the river erosion that has displaced thousands of families.
He rarely delves into his feelings, so his honest letter to his sister surprised everyone.
tc: The first report merely skimmed the surface, so the committee hired an expert to ______ into the root causes of the collapse.
The contrast with 'merely skimmed the surface' shows the blank means to examine deeply.
se: The new biography doesn't just list his achievements; it tries to ______ into the motives behind them.
dig
Both 'delve into' and 'dig into' mean to examine something deeply, so the sentence means the same.

m: to dislike someone or something intensely
x: I detest waking up early on weekends, but the dog doesn't care what day it is.
Most of the staff detest the new open-plan office because it is impossible to concentrate there.
Many students detest group projects in which one person ends up doing all the work.
Voters across the political spectrum detest the idea of paying higher fuel taxes.
She detested her stepfather at first, but over the years they grew surprisingly close.
tc: Tanvir claims to ______ crowded shopping malls; he will happily drive across town just to avoid one.
Going out of his way to avoid malls restates the blank, which must mean to dislike intensely.
se: Most cats seem to ______ baths, struggling and yowling whenever they are put in water.
loathe
Both 'detest' and 'loathe' mean to hate strongly, which the struggling and yowling illustrate.

m: removing suspicion, hostility, or tension; winning people over by charm or frankness
x: The waiter's disarming smile made it impossible to stay annoyed about the long wait.
During the negotiation, her disarming honesty about the company's weaknesses won the investors' trust.
Our professor has a disarming habit of admitting when he doesn't know the answer to a question.
Journalists used to evasive replies were surprised by the minister's disarming candor at the press conference.
There was something disarming about the way he laughed at his own clumsy proposal.
tc: I arrived ready to argue, but his ______ frankness about his own mistakes left me with nothing to be angry about.
'Ready to argue, but ... nothing to be angry about' shows his frankness removed my hostility.
se: The candidate's manner was so ______ that even the sternest interviewers soon relaxed.
charming
Both 'disarming' and 'charming' describe a manner that wins people over and puts them at ease.

m: extremely happy and excited
x: We were elated when the rain stopped just in time for the outdoor wedding.
The whole team was elated after landing the biggest contract in the company's history.
Sara was elated to learn that she had scored in the top percentile on the GRE.
Fans poured into the streets of Dhaka, elated by the cricket team's last-ball victory.
She felt elated and nervous at the same time when he finally asked her to dinner.
tc: Expecting rejection, Nabila was ______ when the acceptance letter arrived, dancing around the room and calling everyone she knew.
Dancing around the room and calling everyone shows she was overjoyed, not merely surprised.
se: The players were ______ after the victory, hugging one another and singing in the dressing room.
jubilant
Both 'elated' and 'jubilant' mean full of great joy, as the hugging and singing show.

m: to make someone nervous, confused, or agitated
x: Don't let the long queue fluster you; the counter usually moves quickly after lunch.
Nothing seems to fluster our office manager, even when the printer and the internet fail at once.
Tricky follow-up questions from the examiners flustered the student, and she lost her train of thought.
The sudden announcement flustered officials, who had not prepared any statement for the press.
He gets flustered whenever she compliments him, turning red and quickly changing the subject.
tc: The interviewer deliberately tried to ______ the applicant with rapid-fire questions, but she remained calm and composed throughout.
The contrast 'but she remained calm and composed' shows the blank means to make nervous or confused.
se: Hecklers in the crowd tried to ______ the speaker, but she kept calmly to her script.
rattle
Both 'fluster' and 'rattle' mean to make someone nervous and lose composure.

m: done or acting too quickly, without enough thought or care
x: Don't make a hasty decision about the flat; let's see a few more before signing anything.
The manager later regretted his hasty dismissal of the intern's idea, which turned out to be brilliant.
Hasty conclusions drawn from a small sample can undermine an otherwise careful study.
Critics say the hasty passage of the law left no time for public debate.
I sent her a hasty reply in anger and spent the rest of the evening wishing I could take it back.
tc: The judge urged jurors to weigh every piece of evidence carefully rather than reach conclusions that were ______.
'Rather than' sets up a contrast with 'carefully', so the blank means made too quickly.
se: Investors who made ______ decisions during the panic often sold their shares at the worst possible moment.
rash
Both 'hasty' and 'rash' describe decisions made too quickly without thought, leading to bad results.

m: having a modest view of one's own importance; not proud or arrogant
x: Despite his wealth, my uncle is humble enough to sit on the floor and eat with the workers.
A humble manager admits mistakes openly, which makes the whole team more willing to take risks.
The visiting professor was remarkably humble, crediting her graduate students for most of the discoveries.
Researchers should stay humble about their models, since the climate system still holds many surprises.
She remained humble about her achievements, never mentioning her scholarship unless someone asked.
tc: For all his fame, the actor was surprisingly ______, insisting that luck rather than talent explained his success.
'For all his fame' sets up a contrast, and crediting luck rather than talent shows he was modest.
se: Even after winning the award, she stayed ______ and thanked everyone who had helped her.
modest
Both 'humble' and 'modest' mean not proud of oneself, which fits thanking others after a success.

m: to beg someone earnestly or desperately to do something
x: My mother implored me to call her as soon as my flight landed in Toronto.
The staff implored management to reconsider the pay cuts before the holiday season.
Our supervisor implored us to back up our data after one student lost an entire chapter of her thesis.
Aid agencies implored wealthy nations to send emergency food to the drought-stricken region.
He implored her to stay, but she had already packed her bags and called a taxi.
tc: Desperate to save his shop, the owner went to the bank to ______ the manager to give him one more month, practically on his knees.
'Desperate' and 'practically on his knees' show he was begging earnestly.
se: Health officials continue to ______ residents to stay indoors during the worst of the heatwave.
beg
Both 'implore' and 'beg' mean to ask urgently and earnestly, so the meaning is the same.

m: to mock someone or shout rude, scornful remarks at them
x: Some boys on the bus jeered at the young couple, but they simply ignored them.
When the manager announced the cancelled bonuses, a few employees jeered from the back of the hall.
Students jeered the visiting speaker until the dean stepped in and asked for respect.
Protesters jeered as the minister's car drove past the parliament gates.
He still remembers how his classmates jeered at his stammer, and it made him a kinder adult.
tc: Instead of cheering their struggling striker, the fans began to ______ every time he missed the goal.
'Instead of cheering' signals the opposite reaction, so the blank means to mock loudly.
se: Opposition members began to ______ when the finance minister claimed that prices were falling.
heckle
Both 'jeer' and 'heckle' mean to shout mocking remarks at a speaker.

m: to shock someone suddenly, often into awareness or action; to jerk abruptly
x: The alarm jolted me awake at five, long before I was ready to face the day.
Losing our biggest client jolted the company out of years of complacency.
A failing grade on the midterm jolted him into taking his studies seriously.
The earthquake jolted residents from their beds and sent thousands into the streets.
Her sudden diagnosis jolted the family into spending more time together.
tc: Years of comfortable profits had made the firm complacent, and it took a sudden crisis to ______ its leaders into action.
A 'sudden crisis' ending complacency shows the blank means to shock into action.
se: Only a serious health scare could ______ him out of his unhealthy habits.
shake
Both 'jolt him out of' and 'shake him out of' mean to shock him into changing.

m: relaxed, gentle and easygoing, often through age or experience
x: We spent a mellow evening on the rooftop, drinking tea and listening to old songs.
Our once fiery boss has become far more mellow since his children were born.
In music class we learned why the cello has such a deep, mellow tone.
After weeks of heated debate, the mood in parliament turned surprisingly mellow before the holiday recess.
She grew mellow with age, forgiving old quarrels she had once refused even to discuss.
tc: Once famous for his temper, the coach has become noticeably ______ in recent years, rarely raising his voice even after a defeat.
The contrast with 'famous for his temper' and 'rarely raising his voice' shows he has become calm and easygoing.
se: Grandfather was always ______ after his afternoon nap, happy to tell stories to anyone who would listen.
genial
Both 'mellow' and 'genial' describe a relaxed, friendly mood, so the meaning is the same.

m: the beginning of something, especially something unpleasant
x: With the onset of winter, street vendors in our neighborhood start selling steaming bhapa pitha.
Productivity in the office tends to drop sharply with the onset of the holiday season.
The study tracks patients from the onset of symptoms until their full recovery.
Economists disagree about the exact onset of the recession, but agree that it began last year.
Every Sunday evening he noticed the onset of anxiety as the working week approached.
tc: Doctors stressed that treatment works best if it begins at the ______ of the illness rather than weeks later.
The contrast with 'weeks later' shows the blank means the very beginning.
se: Residents stocked up on firewood before the ______ of winter.
start
Both 'onset' and 'start' mean the beginning of winter, so the sentence keeps its meaning.

m: to defeat or gain an advantage over someone by being cleverer
x: Our cat somehow manages to outwit every child-proof lock we put on the cupboard.
The small startup outwitted its larger rivals by spotting the trend a year before anyone else.
In the novel we are studying, the young detective outwits the villain with a simple trick.
Bacteria constantly evolve new ways to outwit the antibiotics designed to kill them.
My little sister loves to outwit me at chess and then remind me of it for days.
tc: Lacking the strength to fight the giant, the hero had to rely on cunning to ______ him.
'Rely on cunning' instead of strength shows the blank means to defeat by cleverness.
se: The prisoner hoped to ______ the guards by hiding in the laundry cart.
outsmart
Both 'outwit' and 'outsmart' mean to beat someone through cleverness.

m: extremely dry, especially from heat or lack of rain; very thirsty
x: After the long walk in the sun, I was parched and drank two bottles of water at once.
By the end of the three-hour meeting, everyone was parched because someone had forgotten to order water.
Our geography lecture examined how farmers in parched regions are adapting to falling groundwater levels.
Months without rain have left the fields parched and cracked, threatening the entire harvest.
Her parched lips and sunken eyes told the nurse she had not been drinking enough.
tc: After months without a drop of rain, the once lush valley was so ______ that the soil cracked under people's feet.
'Months without a drop of rain' and cracked soil point to extreme dryness.
se: Travelers crossing the ______ plains carried as much water as their camels could bear.
arid
Both 'parched' and 'arid' mean extremely dry, which explains the need to carry water.

m: full of danger or risk
x: The road to the hill station becomes perilous after heavy rain, so we postponed our trip.
The company is in a perilous financial position after losing its two biggest customers.
Early explorers made perilous voyages across uncharted seas with only crude maps.
Thousands of migrants attempt the perilous sea crossing each year in overcrowded boats.
Telling her the truth felt perilous, but hiding it any longer seemed even worse.
tc: The guide refused to lead anyone across the glacier in winter, calling the route far too ______ for inexperienced climbers.
Refusing to lead inexperienced climbers shows the route was dangerous.
se: Rescuers made their way along the ______ cliff path, roped together in case anyone slipped.
treacherous
Both 'perilous' and 'treacherous' describe a dangerous path, which is why the rescuers were roped together.

m: having high status and widely admired or respected
x: My cousin could not stop boasting about his new job at a prestigious law firm.
Working for a prestigious consultancy looks impressive on a résumé, but the hours can be brutal.
Getting into a prestigious university like BUET requires months of intense preparation.
The scientist received the most prestigious award in her field for her work on malaria vaccines.
He cared less about a prestigious title than about having time to watch his children grow up.
tc: Only the most ______ journals, those read and respected by every expert in the field, rejected the institute's papers.
The restatement 'read and respected by every expert' defines the blank as highly esteemed.
se: She turned down offers from several ______ banks in London to start her own company.
renowned
Both 'prestigious' and 'renowned' describe banks with high status and reputation.

m: to tremble or shake slightly, often from emotion, cold, or fear
x: The puppy quivered in the rain until we wrapped it in a warm towel.
His hands quivered as he handed the quarterly report to the furious director.
Under the microscope, the tiny organisms quivered and darted across the slide.
Trees along the coast began to quiver as the first winds of the cyclone arrived.
Her voice quivered with emotion as she thanked her parents at the graduation ceremony.
tc: Though she tried to appear confident before the panel, her lower lip began to ______, betraying her nerves.
'Though she tried to appear confident' and 'betraying her nerves' show the lip was trembling.
se: The child's chin started to ______ and tears welled up in his eyes.
tremble
Both 'quiver' and 'tremble' mean to shake slightly with emotion.

m: to think or suppose; to calculate or estimate
x: I reckon the rain will stop by evening, so let's leave the umbrellas at home.
Analysts reckon the merger will save the company about ten million dollars a year.
Historians reckon that the manuscript was written sometime in the twelfth century.
Until the recent wave of burglaries, the town was reckoned among the safest in the country.
She reckoned she could forgive him, but the hurt returned whenever he raised his voice.
c: a force to be reckoned with
tc: Without exact figures, the engineer could only ______ that the bridge would need another two years of repairs.
'Without exact figures' means he could only make a rough judgment, so the blank means estimate.
se: Experts ______ that the population of the city will double within twenty years.
estimate
Both 'reckon' and 'estimate' mean to judge a figure approximately.

m: to restore to life, consciousness, strength, or popularity
x: A cup of strong tea was enough to revive me after the long bus ride.
The new editor plans to revive the struggling magazine by moving it entirely online.
Scholars are working to revive interest in forgotten women poets of the nineteenth century.
The government hopes the tax cuts will revive the economy before next year's election.
A week together in Cox's Bazar helped revive a marriage that had grown distant over the years.
tc: After decades of neglect, the old craft seemed doomed to vanish, until a group of young artisans set out to ______ it.
'Doomed to vanish, until' signals a reversal, so the blank means to bring back to life.
se: Paramedics worked for twenty minutes to ______ the drowning victim.
resuscitate
Both 'revive' and 'resuscitate' mean to restore someone to consciousness or life.

m: having a rough, uneven surface; strongly built and able to withstand hard conditions
x: We needed rugged boots for the trek through the hills of Bandarban.
Field engineers prefer rugged laptops that can survive dust, heat, and the occasional drop.
Geologists mapped the rugged coastline to understand how centuries of storms had shaped it.
Rescue teams struggled to reach villages scattered across the rugged mountain terrain.
She was drawn to his rugged good looks, but it was his gentle humor that won her heart.
tc: Unlike the smooth, sandy beaches to the south, the northern coast is ______, with jagged cliffs and rocky inlets.
The contrast with 'smooth, sandy' and the detail 'jagged cliffs' show the blank means rough and uneven.
se: Only four-wheel-drive vehicles can handle the ______ mountain roads in winter.
rough
Both 'rugged' and 'rough' describe uneven, difficult roads.

m: smooth, glossy and elegantly streamlined in appearance
x: Her cat has a sleek black coat that shines in the afternoon sun.
The company unveiled a sleek new office with glass walls and minimalist furniture.
Engineering students designed a sleek, aerodynamic car body for the national solar race.
Dolphins have sleek bodies that let them glide through water with very little resistance.
He looked sleek and confident in his new suit, nothing like the nervous boy I remembered.
tc: Gone was the clunky old phone; in its place was a slim, ______ device that slipped easily into a shirt pocket.
The contrast with 'clunky' and the word 'slim' show the blank means smooth and elegant.
se: The new train has ______ lines that cut down on air resistance at high speeds.
streamlined
Both 'sleek' and 'streamlined' describe a smooth shape that reduces air resistance.

m: to burn slowly without flame; (of feelings) to exist in a suppressed, hidden form
x: The campfire was still smoldering in the morning, so we poured a bucket of water over it.
Resentment smoldered among the staff for months after the unfair promotions.
Historians argue that tensions had smoldered for decades before finally erupting into civil war.
Firefighters warned that the ruins of the factory could keep smoldering for days.
His anger smoldered quietly through dinner until he finally exploded over dessert.
tc: Although the protests had ended, discontent continued to ______ beneath the surface, ready to flare up again at any moment.
'Beneath the surface' and 'ready to flare up' show the feeling was hidden but still burning.
se: Anger over the land seizures continued to ______ in the villages long after the officials had left.
simmer
Both 'smolder' and 'simmer' describe anger that persists quietly without bursting out.

m: an indirect or passing reference to something
x: The comedian's joke contained an allusion to a famous old film that only the older audience understood.
In her email, the director made a vague allusion to budget cuts but gave no details.
Because the poem is full of allusions to Greek mythology, the footnotes are essential.
Commentators noted the speech's thinly veiled allusion to the scandal in the finance ministry.
He made no allusion to their quarrel, but his tone told her he had not forgotten it.
tc: Rather than naming the rival company outright, the chairman made only a subtle ______ to 'certain competitors overseas.'
'Rather than naming ... outright' tells us the blank is an indirect reference.
se: The novel's title contains a clever ______ to a line from Shakespeare.
reference
Both 'allusion' and 'reference' mean a mention of something else, here a line from Shakespeare.

m: to walk or move about on foot
x: After hip surgery, my grandmother was encouraged to ambulate around the ward twice a day.
Part of a nurse's job is helping post-operative patients ambulate safely without falling.
The study measured how far elderly participants could ambulate without assistance in six minutes.
Robotic exoskeletons now allow some paralyzed patients to ambulate with the help of crutches.
Once the cast came off, he could ambulate again, though he still limped when he was tired.
tc: Bedridden for weeks after the accident, he was finally strong enough to ______ down the corridor on his own.
The contrast with 'bedridden' and 'down the corridor' shows the blank means to walk.
se: Doctors want surgical patients to ______ as soon as possible to prevent blood clots.
walk
Both 'ambulate' and 'walk' mean to move about on foot, so the meaning is unchanged.

m: the ancient past, especially before the Middle Ages; great age
x: Visitors to the museum's new gallery can see coins and pottery from classical antiquity.
My grandfather's wooden chest is of such antiquity that no one knows who first owned it.
Our seminar compares ideas about democracy in antiquity with those of the modern world.
Archaeologists believe the ruins at Mahasthangarh date back to antiquity, perhaps the third century BCE.
Since antiquity, people have looked to the stars for guidance in love and war.
tc: Far from being a modern invention, the practice dates back to ______, when Greek and Roman doctors already described it.
'Far from being a modern invention' and the mention of Greek and Roman doctors point to the ancient past.
se: The philosophers of ______ debated many of the questions that still puzzle us today.
yore
Both 'philosophers of antiquity' and 'philosophers of yore' mean thinkers of the ancient past.

m: an open and firm declaration or admission of something
x: Her avowal that she would never touch sweets again lasted exactly until dessert arrived.
The chief executive's public avowal of responsibility for the data leak calmed angry shareholders.
The philosopher's essay opens with a frank avowal of his own doubts about free will.
Despite the government's repeated avowals of transparency, key documents remain classified.
His sudden avowal of love, delivered in a crowded café, left her speechless.
tc: Far from concealing his membership in the group, the writer made it the subject of a public ______ in his memoir.
'Far from concealing' signals the opposite, an open declaration.
se: The treaty opens with a solemn ______ of peace between the two nations.
declaration
Both 'avowal' and 'declaration' mean a formal, open statement.

m: to deprive someone of a loved one, especially through death
x: The accident bereaved three families in our small town in a single afternoon.
Our company gives two weeks of paid leave to employees who have been bereaved.
The study examines how children bereaved of a parent cope with schoolwork and friendships.
The war bereaved thousands of mothers, many of whom never learned where their sons were buried.
Recently bereaved, she found comfort in her late husband's garden and the roses he had planted.
tc: In the nineteenth century, a single cholera outbreak could ______ a family of several children within a week.
A deadly outbreak taking 'several children' shows the blank means to deprive of loved ones by death.
se: Wars ______ countless parents of their sons and daughters.
deprive
Both 'bereave' and 'deprive' mean to take loved ones away from someone.

m: to feel irritated or impatient, especially because of restrictions
x: Teenagers often chafe at curfews their parents set, even when the rules are reasonable.
Experienced engineers chafed under the new manager's rule that every decision needed his approval.
Graduate students chafe at funding rules that forbid them from taking part-time jobs.
Small businesses have long chafed under regulations designed for large corporations.
She chafed at her in-laws' constant advice about how to raise her baby.
tc: Used to making his own decisions, the former entrepreneur began to ______ at the endless approvals required in his new government job.
'Used to making his own decisions' explains why the approvals irritated him.
se: Many athletes ______ at the strict diets their coaches impose.
bristle
Both 'chafe at' and 'bristle at' mean to feel irritated by restrictions.

m: an absurd pretense meant to give a false appearance of something
x: Their polite smiles at dinner were a charade; they had been arguing all afternoon.
Everyone knew the job interview was a charade, since the director had already chosen his nephew.
The professor called the journal's peer review a charade that approved every paper submitted.
Observers dismissed the election as a charade designed to give the regime a veneer of legitimacy.
She was tired of keeping up the charade of a happy marriage for the sake of her relatives.
tc: Everyone saw through the ______: the decision had been made in private weeks before the so-called public consultation.
'So-called' and the decision already made in private show the consultation was a pretense.
se: After years of pretending, they finally ended the ______ and told their friends the truth about their marriage.
pretense
Both 'charade' and 'pretense' mean a false show, which ended when they told the truth.

m: tending to stick closely to one's own group and exclude outsiders
x: The neighbors on our street are a bit clannish, so it took years before we were invited to their parties.
New hires complained that the senior staff were clannish and rarely shared useful information.
Some university departments are notoriously clannish, rarely collaborating with outside researchers.
Sociologists argue that clannish politics can weaken public trust in national institutions.
His family was so clannish that his wife never felt fully accepted, even after ten years.
tc: The villagers were so ______ that outsiders who had lived there for twenty years were still treated as strangers.
Treating long-time residents as strangers shows the villagers excluded outsiders.
se: Newcomers found the school's teachers ______, always eating lunch together and ignoring anyone new.
cliquish
Both 'clannish' and 'cliquish' describe a group that keeps to itself and shuts out others.

m: making up for a loss, deficiency, or injury
x: The airline offered us compensatory meal vouchers after our flight was delayed by six hours.
Employees who work on public holidays receive compensatory leave later in the month.
Some researchers argue that the brain develops compensatory strategies after a stroke.
