The court awarded compensatory damages to families whose homes were destroyed by the oil spill.
He showered his children with gifts, a compensatory gesture for all the evenings he spent at the office.
tc: Having lost much of his hearing, the musician developed ______ skills, learning to feel the rhythm through the floor.
New skills developed to make up for lost hearing show the blank means making up for a loss.
se: To soften the pension cuts, the company introduced ______ increases in health benefits.
offsetting
Both 'compensatory' and 'offsetting' describe increases meant to balance out a loss.

m: to make stronger or more secure; to combine several things into one
x: We decided to consolidate our three bank accounts into one to make budgeting easier.
The firm plans to consolidate its regional offices into a single headquarters in Chittagong.
Reviewing your notes each evening helps consolidate what you learned in class.
After the election, the ruling party moved quickly to consolidate its control over the media.
Their trip together helped consolidate a friendship that had begun only a few months earlier.
tc: Having won the first battle, the general chose not to advance but to ______ his gains, fortifying the towns he had already taken.
'Fortifying the towns he had already taken' restates the blank as making his position secure.
se: The new champion will need several more victories to ______ her position at the top of the rankings.
strengthen
Both 'consolidate' and 'strengthen' mean to make her position more secure.

m: to trick or deceive someone, usually to get something from them
x: The street vendor tried to cozen tourists by charging double for fake silk scarves.
The finance officer was fired for cozening suppliers into accepting late, partial payments.
In the play, a clever servant cozens his greedy master out of a fortune.
Investigators say the scheme cozened thousands of pensioners out of their savings.
She felt cozened by a man who had charmed her with stories that turned out to be lies.
tc: The con artist used flattery and false promises to ______ the old widow out of her savings.
'Con artist' and 'false promises' show the blank means to trick or cheat.
se: He was the kind of salesman who would ______ his own grandmother if it meant a bigger commission.
cheat
Both 'cozen' and 'cheat' mean to deceive someone for gain.

m: to select or gather from a large quantity or from various sources
x: I culled a few favorite recipes from my mother's old notebooks for the family cookbook.
The editor culled the best quotes from hundreds of interviews for the anniversary issue.
For her literature review, she culled relevant studies from over two thousand search results.
The report culls data from forty countries to show how inequality has changed since 1990.
Before moving abroad, he culled his belongings, keeping only the books and letters that mattered most.
tc: From thousands of applications, the committee had to ______ just twenty finalists for the scholarship.
Choosing 'just twenty' from 'thousands' shows the blank means to select.
se: The producers will ______ the most striking footage from more than three hundred hours of film.
select
Both 'cull' and 'select' mean to pick out the best from a large amount.

m: extremely serious, urgent, or dreadful
x: After the long drive, we were in dire need of a hot shower and a decent meal.
The company is in dire financial straits and may not survive another year.
Researchers issued dire warnings about the state of the region's groundwater.
Aid workers describe the situation in the flooded districts as dire, with food running out fast.
Her parents predicted dire consequences if she married him, but they have been happy for twenty years.
tc: Without immediate rain, experts warned, the drought would have ______ consequences, including widespread famine.
'Widespread famine' shows the consequences would be extremely serious.
se: The hospital's staffing shortage has become so ______ that patients now wait hours in the corridors.
grave
Both 'dire' and 'grave' mean extremely serious, as the long waits show.

m: a state of shame or disgrace; loss of respect
x: In many families, failing an exam was once treated as a dishonor to the whole household.
The officer chose to resign rather than face the dishonor of a public investigation.
Historians have documented how soldiers who surrendered were often treated as a dishonor to their nation.
The scandal brought dishonor on a university that had always prided itself on academic integrity.
He would rather lose everything than bring dishonor on his late father's name.
tc: For the old warrior, defeat itself was acceptable, but fleeing the battlefield meant ______ that could never be erased.
The contrast between acceptable defeat and fleeing shows the blank means lasting shame.
se: The athlete's doping scandal brought ______ on the entire national team.
disgrace
Both 'dishonor' and 'disgrace' mean shame brought on the team.

m: to make someone lose enthusiasm, hope, or confidence
x: Three days of constant rain dispirited the campers, who packed up early and went home.
Repeated budget cuts have dispirited even the most loyal members of staff.
Don't let one poor exam result dispirit you; there is still plenty of time to improve.
The team's early batting collapse dispirited fans who had travelled all the way to Chattogram for the match.
Her parents' silence about her achievements dispirited her more than any criticism could have.
tc: The coach worried that another heavy defeat would ______ his young players, who were already losing confidence.
'Already losing confidence' shows the blank means to discourage further.
se: Constant rejection can ______ even the most determined job seekers.
dishearten
Both 'dispirit' and 'dishearten' mean to make someone lose hope.

m: extremely and often uncritically loving and fond of someone
x: Her doting grandparents spoil her with sweets every time she visits.
A doting father of twins, he leaves the office at five sharp every day.
Doting parents who do their children's homework may actually harm their learning.
Researchers found that doting owners often overfeed their pets, contributing to rising obesity in dogs.
She was a doting wife, though she sometimes wished her husband noticed her efforts more.
tc: Far from being strict, Aunt Rina was so ______ that she forgave her nephews' every mischief and showered them with gifts.
'Far from being strict' and showering gifts show she was excessively fond.
se: The ______ mother kept every drawing her children had ever made.
adoring
Both 'doting' and 'adoring' describe a mother full of fond love.

m: a flowering or blossoming; a period of rich development, especially in art or culture
x: Each spring, the hillside bursts into an efflorescence of wild yellow flowers.
The design studio's creative efflorescence in the 1990s produced its most famous products.
Scholars describe the Bengal Renaissance as an efflorescence of literature, music and social reform.
The decade saw an efflorescence of independent newspapers after censorship was lifted.
Falling in love triggered an unexpected efflorescence of poetry from the shy engineer.
tc: After centuries of stagnation, the city enjoyed a sudden cultural ______, producing great painters, poets and architects within a single generation.
The contrast with 'stagnation' and the burst of great artists show the blank means a flowering.
se: The end of the war brought a remarkable ______ of new theaters, galleries and literary magazines.
flowering
Both 'efflorescence' and 'flowering' mean a burst of creative growth.

m: to come out or spread from a source
x: A wonderful smell of frying onions emanated from the kitchen next door.
Confusion seemed to emanate from head office, where no one could agree on the new policy.
In physics class we learned how radiation emanates from unstable atomic nuclei.
Officials are investigating reports that toxic fumes emanated from the factory before the explosion.
Calm seemed to emanate from her, and everyone in the waiting room relaxed a little.
tc: Investigators finally traced the strange humming to the basement, where it seemed to ______ from an old generator.
Tracing the sound to its source shows the blank means to come out from.
se: Warmth and confidence seemed to ______ from the new teacher, putting even the shyest pupils at ease.
radiate
Both 'emanate' and 'radiate' mean to flow outward from a person.

m: to make someone feel bitter or resentful
x: Years of noisy neighbors had embittered him against apartment living altogether.
Being passed over for promotion twice embittered the senior accountant, who started arriving late and leaving early.
Rejection after rejection can embitter young researchers, pushing some to leave academia entirely.
The disputed election embittered relations between the two parties for a generation.
A painful divorce had embittered her, but new friendships slowly softened that resentment.
tc: Instead of softening him, decades of injustice served only to ______ the old man, leaving him resentful toward everyone.
'Leaving him resentful' restates the blank as making someone bitter.
se: Losing the family land in the lawsuit would ______ her for the rest of her life.
sour
Both 'embitter' and 'sour' mean to make someone resentful and bitter.

m: serving as a symbol or typical example of something
x: The rickshaw has become emblematic of Dhaka's colorful, chaotic street life.
Her quick promotion is emblematic of the company's new focus on rewarding results.
The essay argues that the novel's crumbling mansion is emblematic of a declining aristocracy.
Long queues for bread became emblematic of the country's economic crisis.
For him, that small café was emblematic of the carefree years they had shared as students.
tc: The empty factory, once the town's largest employer, has become ______ of the region's industrial decline.
The empty factory stands for the wider decline, so the blank means symbolic of.
se: The olive branch is ______ of peace in many cultures.
symbolic
Both 'emblematic of' and 'symbolic of' mean serving as a symbol of peace.

m: to give someone the courage or confidence to do something
x: Winning the first two matches emboldened the team to try a more attacking style of play.
Positive feedback from her manager emboldened Rina to pitch her own project at the next meeting.
Encouraged by his supervisor, the shy student felt emboldened to challenge a claim in the textbook.
Critics warned that a weak response from the authorities would only embolden smugglers operating along the border.
His gentle reassurance emboldened her to finally tell her parents she wanted to study abroad.
tc: Rather than deterring the protesters, the government's harsh threats only served to ______ them further.
'Rather than deterring' signals a contrast, so the blank must mean the opposite: to make them bolder.
se: The surprisingly strong early poll numbers seemed to ______ the candidate, who began speaking far more forcefully.
hearten
Both 'embolden' and 'hearten' mean to give confidence, which explains why the candidate grew more forceful.

m: to make a bill or proposal officially into law
x: Parliament enacted a new data protection law after months of heated debate.
Our company enacted a strict no-smoking policy across all its offices last year.
In our history seminar, we studied how Congress enacted civil rights legislation in the 1960s.
Many cities have enacted bans on single-use plastic bags to reduce waste in rivers and drains.
Once the reforms are enacted, single parents like my sister will find it easier to claim child support.
tc: Although the bill had broad public support, the deadlocked legislature failed to ______ it before the session ended.
The words 'bill' and 'legislature' show that the blank means to make it law, which the deadlock prevented.
se: Lawmakers hope to ______ the new tax code before the end of the fiscal year.
pass
Both 'enact' and 'pass' mean to make a proposed law official.

m: to cause someone to be loved, liked, or favored by others
x: Her habit of remembering everyone's birthday endeared her to the whole neighborhood.
His willingness to stay late and help colleagues quickly endeared him to the team.
The professor's dry humor endeared him to students who usually dreaded statistics.
The mayor's decision to double parking fees did little to endear him to local shopkeepers.
What endeared my grandmother to everyone was the way she fed every guest as if they were family.
tc: His arrogance and constant complaints did nothing to ______ him to his new colleagues, who soon began avoiding him.
Arrogance and complaining led colleagues to avoid him, so the blank must mean to make him liked.
se: Her modesty and quiet competence will surely ______ her to the selection committee.
commend
To 'endear' or 'commend' her to the committee both mean to make her appealing and favored in their eyes.

m: to make someone or something weak or feeble
x: Weeks of high fever had enfeebled him so much that he could barely climb the stairs.
Constant restructuring has enfeebled the department, leaving it with too few experienced staff.
Some historians argue that endless wars enfeebled the empire long before its final collapse.
Years of corruption have enfeebled public institutions and eroded trust in the courts.
She refused to let grief enfeeble her, and she returned to work within a month of the funeral.
tc: Far from strengthening the army, the long siege served only to ______ it, as hunger and disease spread through the ranks.
'Far from strengthening' and the spread of hunger and disease show the blank means to weaken.
se: Doctors feared that another round of chemotherapy would further ______ the already frail patient.
weaken
Both 'enfeeble' and 'weaken' mean to make the frail patient weaker still.

m: to surround and cover something completely; to overwhelm
x: Within minutes, flames engulfed the old wooden warehouse by the river.
During the monsoon, floodwaters can engulf entire villages in northern Bangladesh overnight.
A wave of panic engulfed the office when the server crashed on the day of the product launch.
Researchers modeled how rising seas might engulf low-lying coastal cities by the end of the century.
After her father's death, a deep sadness engulfed her for months, and she rarely left the house.
tc: The small fishing boat was no match for the storm; huge waves threatened to ______ it completely.
'No match for the storm' and 'completely' show the waves would swallow the boat entirely.
se: Officials feared that the civil war would soon ______ the entire region.
overwhelm
Both 'engulf' and 'overwhelm' mean the war would spread over and swamp the whole region.

m: to arouse or stir up a feeling, interest, or passion
x: A single inspiring teacher can enkindle a lifelong love of reading in a child.
The new manager's enthusiasm seemed to enkindle fresh energy in the tired sales team.
Her lecture on black holes enkindled a curiosity that eventually led him to study physics.
The leaked documents enkindled public anger against the officials who had hidden the report.
His letters from abroad enkindled in her a longing to travel that she had never felt before.
tc: Where years of dull textbooks had left her indifferent to history, one gifted lecturer managed to ______ her interest in the subject.
The contrast with 'indifferent' shows the lecturer did the opposite: aroused her interest.
se: The rousing speech was designed to ______ patriotic feeling among the crowd.
ignite
Both 'enkindle' and 'ignite' mean to set a strong feeling alight.

m: to make something more lively, interesting, or cheerful
x: A few bright cushions and plants can enliven even the dullest living room.
She enlivened the quarterly report presentation with short video clips from happy customers.
The lecturer enlivened his talk on economics with stories from his village childhood.
Colorful street murals have enlivened once-neglected neighborhoods across the city.
His surprise visit enlivened what had been a long, lonely week for his grandmother.
tc: The dinner party had been dull and awkward until Karim arrived; his jokes and stories helped ______ the evening.
The party was 'dull and awkward' until his jokes, so the blank means to make it lively.
se: The organizers hired a live band to ______ the otherwise formal ceremony.
brighten
Both 'enliven' and 'brighten' mean to make the stiff ceremony more cheerful.

m: to give someone or something greater dignity or moral worth
x: Hard, honest work, she believed, ennobles a person more than any university degree.
Our mentor insisted that serving customers well ennobles even the most routine office job.
Many Victorian novels portray suffering as something that ennobles the human spirit.
Writers often claim that the struggle for justice ennobles those who take part in it.
Caring for his ailing father never felt like a burden; if anything, it seemed to ennoble him.
tc: Some argue that poverty only degrades people, but the novelist insists that hardship can ______ those who endure it with courage.
'But' sets up a contrast with 'degrades', so the blank must mean to raise in dignity.
se: The film suggests that genuine sacrifice can ______ even a deeply flawed character.
elevate
Both 'ennoble' and 'elevate' mean to raise the character morally.

m: to catch someone or something in a trap, or as if in a trap
x: Fishermen complain that discarded nets ensnare turtles and dolphins along the coast.
The fraudsters ensnared dozens of small businesses with fake invoices that looked completely genuine.
Students can easily get ensnared in the habit of memorizing answers instead of understanding concepts.
The corruption investigation ensnared several senior officials who had accepted bribes.
He felt ensnared in a relationship that he no longer wanted but did not know how to leave.
tc: The spider waits patiently at the edge of its web, ready to ______ any insect careless enough to land there.
A spider waiting by its web is ready to trap insects, so the blank means to catch.
se: Investigators set up a fake website to ______ online fraudsters.
trap
Both 'ensnare' and 'trap' mean to catch the fraudsters through a trick.

m: to catch in a trap; to trick someone into doing something wrong, especially a crime
x: Hidden clauses in the contract were designed to entrap unwary customers in long, costly subscriptions.
Our law lecturer explained the difference between legitimate undercover work and illegally entrapping a suspect.
The documentary showed how poachers use simple wire snares to entrap deer in the forest.
Critics said the sting operation entrapped people who would never have committed the crime otherwise.
She felt entrapped by her own lies and could no longer tell her family the truth.
tc: The defense lawyer argued that undercover officers had deliberately tried to ______ his client into a crime he would never have planned on his own.
'Into a crime he would never have planned on his own' shows the officers tricked him, which is what entrap means.
se: The scammers used promises of quick profits to ______ inexperienced investors.
ensnare
Both 'entrap' and 'ensnare' mean to catch the investors through deception.

m: to demand and obtain something from someone, often by force or pressure
x: The local gang exacted protection money from every shop on the street.
The project's impossible deadlines exacted a heavy toll on the team's health and morale.
Preparing for the GRE while working full-time exacted a heavy price on his sleep.
After the war, the victorious powers exacted harsh reparations from the defeated nation.
She vowed to exact revenge on the friend who had betrayed her trust.
tc: Determined to make the rebels pay for their betrayal, the king set out to ______ a terrible revenge.
'Determined to make the rebels pay' shows the king wants to inflict and obtain revenge, which is to exact it.
se: The occupying forces used threats to ______ heavy taxes from the villagers.
extort
Both 'exact' and 'extort' mean to force payment out of the villagers.

m: to dig out or uncover something, especially buried remains, by removing earth
x: Workers spent a month excavating the foundation for a new apartment block on our street.
Our engineering firm was hired to excavate the site before construction of the metro station could begin.
Archaeologists have excavated a Buddhist monastery at Paharpur that is more than a thousand years old.
For her thesis, she excavated old court records that no historian had examined in decades.
Therapy helped him excavate painful memories he had buried since childhood.
tc: Before the ancient tomb could be studied, the team had to carefully ______ tons of sand and rubble that had buried it for centuries.
Sand and rubble burying a tomb must be dug out, which is what excavate means.
se: Scientists hope to ______ the fossil without damaging its fragile bones.
unearth
Both 'excavate' and 'unearth' mean to dig the fossil out of the ground.

m: intensely painful; almost unbearably uncomfortable or embarrassing
x: After twisting my ankle on the stairs, I was in excruciating pain all night.
Sitting through a three-hour budget meeting with no agenda was absolutely excruciating.
Waiting for the admission results felt excruciating, especially with relatives calling every day to ask.
Patients with the disease often suffer excruciating headaches that ordinary painkillers cannot relieve.
There was an excruciating silence after he accidentally called his girlfriend by his ex's name.
tc: Although the injury looked minor, the pain was ______, leaving him unable to sleep or even stand.
'Although the injury looked minor' sets up a contrast, and being unable to sleep or stand shows the pain was extreme.
se: In the days before anesthesia, surgery was ______ for patients, who were often held down by assistants.
agonizing
Both 'excruciating' and 'agonizing' describe pain so intense it is almost unbearable.

m: to dig up a buried body; to bring something back from neglect or obscurity
x: Our marketing team exhumed an old slogan from the 1980s and gave it a modern twist.
The historian exhumed long-forgotten letters that shed new light on the war.
Forensic experts exhumed the body to determine the true cause of death.
A court has ordered the authorities to exhume the remains for DNA testing.
Looking through old photo albums, she exhumed memories of childhood summers in her grandparents' village.
tc: Doubts about the official cause of death led the family to ask the court for permission to ______ the body and order a second autopsy.
A second autopsy on a buried person requires digging up the body, which is what exhume means.
se: Investigators obtained a warrant to ______ the remains for DNA analysis.
disinter
Both 'exhume' and 'disinter' mean to dig a body out of its grave.

m: to disturb or unsettle someone so that they lose their composure
x: Nothing seems to faze my mother, not even Dhaka traffic at rush hour.
The tough questions from the board did not faze the new finance director at all.
She was not fazed by the difficult viva because she had prepared thoroughly for every topic.
Angry shouts from the crowd did not faze the veteran reporter, who calmly kept filming.
His harsh words fazed her more than she was willing to admit.
tc: The young chess player was remarkably composed; even her opponent's aggressive opening failed to ______ her.
'Remarkably composed' signals that nothing could unsettle her, so the blank means to disturb.
se: The interviewer's hostile tone did not ______ the candidate, who answered every question calmly.
fluster
Both 'faze' and 'fluster' mean to make someone nervous or confused, which the calm candidate avoided.

m: something that seems real but exists only in the imagination
x: The ghost in the corridor turned out to be a figment of a tired security guard's imagination.
Our manager insisted the budget problem was no figment; the numbers clearly showed a shortfall.
Philosophers have long asked whether free will is real or merely a figment of the mind.
The reported weapons program proved to be a figment invented by a rival intelligence agency.
Her fear that everyone disliked her was a figment of her anxiety, not a reflection of reality.
tc: The monster that the boy swore lived under his bed was not real at all; it was merely the ______ of an overactive imagination.
'Not real at all' and 'imagination' show the blank means something imagined.
se: The so-called conspiracy turned out to be the ______ of a few bloggers with too much time on their hands.
invention
Both 'figment' and 'invention' describe something made up rather than real.

m: to wave or swing about wildly; to struggle without making progress
x: The toddler lay on the floor, flailing his arms and screaming for more sweets.
After the merger, the new management seemed to flail without any clear strategy.
Without a study plan, he flailed through his first semester and nearly failed two courses.
Economists warned that the government was flailing as inflation rose month after month.
She flailed through her first weeks abroad, homesick and unsure of what to do.
tc: Unable to touch the bottom, the panicked boy began to ______ wildly in the water instead of floating calmly as he had been taught.
'Panicked', 'wildly' and the contrast with 'floating calmly' show the blank means to thrash about.
se: Without experienced leadership, the young company began to ______ as its competitors moved ahead.
flounder
Both 'flail' and 'flounder' mean to struggle helplessly without direction.

m: to force someone to accept something unwanted or of poor quality
x: My aunt tried to foist her old, sagging sofa on us when she moved house.
Management foisted the extra workload on junior staff without asking for their input.
Students resent having outdated and overpriced textbooks foisted on them by the university.
Critics accused the government of foisting an unpopular tax on small farmers.
He felt that his parents had foisted their dream of medicine on him when he loved engineering.
tc: The salesman tried to ______ an overpriced warranty on us, even though we had clearly said we didn't want one.
'Even though we had clearly said we didn't want one' shows he was pushing something unwanted on them.
se: Residents complained that the council was trying to ______ an unwanted waste plant on their neighborhood.
impose
Both 'foist' and 'impose' mean to force something unwelcome on people.

m: to give special emphasis or prominence to something
x: In her wedding speech, she foregrounded her parents' sacrifices rather than her own achievements.
The new annual report foregrounds customer satisfaction instead of simply listing sales figures.
Recent scholarship foregrounds the role of women in the independence movement.
The campaign deliberately foregrounded climate change, an issue the other parties had largely ignored.
In our arguments, he always foregrounds his own hurt and never acknowledges mine.
tc: Whereas earlier histories pushed ordinary workers to the margins, this new study chooses to ______ their experiences.
'Whereas' contrasts with 'pushed to the margins', so the blank means to give prominence.
se: The museum's new exhibition aims to ______ the contributions of local artists.
highlight
Both 'foreground' and 'highlight' mean to draw special attention to the artists' work.

m: to break or crack; to split a group or system into separate parts
x: He fractured his wrist when he slipped on the wet bathroom floor.
Disagreements over pay and promotions fractured the once close-knit design team.
The professor showed how tiny defects can cause steel beams to fracture under repeated stress.
The ruling coalition fractured after two smaller parties withdrew their support.
Their twenty-year friendship fractured after a bitter argument over money from a failed business.
tc: Once united behind a single leader, the party began to ______ into rival factions after his death.
The contrast between 'once united' and 'rival factions' shows the blank means to split apart.
se: The dispute over the inheritance threatened to ______ a family that had always been close.
split
Both 'fracture' and 'split' mean to break the close family into divided parts.

m: lack of seriousness; silly, light-hearted behavior when seriousness is expected
x: After a week of exams, the dorm was full of laughter and frivolity.
The CEO had no patience for frivolity in meetings and expected every minute to count.
Our supervisor warned that any frivolity in a research proposal would cost us marks.
Critics condemned the lavish party as an act of frivolity in the middle of a national crisis.
She loved his frivolity at first but later wished he would take their future seriously.
tc: The somber occasion called for gravity, so the mourners were shocked by his ______ as he joked loudly throughout the funeral.
His joking contrasts with the 'gravity' the occasion required, so the blank means unseriousness.
se: The judge, irritated by the lawyer's ______, reminded him that a man's freedom was at stake.
levity
Both 'frivolity' and 'levity' mean inappropriate lack of seriousness.

m: refined, polite manners and the respectability associated with a higher social class
x: My grandmother served tea in her best china, insisting on a certain gentility even at home.
The old law firm cultivated an air of gentility, with oak-paneled offices and hushed voices.
Her dissertation examines how nineteenth-century novels portray the fading gentility of country families.
Behind the gentility of the wealthy suburb lay serious problems with drugs and debt.
He admired her quiet gentility, which never seemed forced or snobbish.
tc: Despite the family's fallen fortunes, they clung to an outward ______, dressing formally for dinner and never raising their voices.
Dressing formally and never raising their voices describe refined manners, which is gentility.
se: The hotel's elegant lounge preserved the ______ of a bygone era.
refinement
Both 'gentility' and 'refinement' describe the polished elegance of an earlier age.

m: to bite or chew steadily; to trouble or worry someone persistently
x: Our dog spent the afternoon gnawing a bone under the dining table.
A sense that she had missed something important gnawed at her throughout the audit.
Doubts about his chosen major gnawed at him during his entire first year.
Investigators found that rats had gnawed through the electrical wiring, causing the fire.
Guilt over the way he had treated his younger brother gnawed at him for years.
tc: Though he tried to dismiss the warning, a persistent worry continued to ______ at him long after the meeting.
'Persistent' and 'continued' show the worry kept troubling him, which is what gnaw at means.
se: Regret over the job offer she had turned down continued to ______ at her for months.
nag
Both 'gnaw at' and 'nag at' mean to trouble someone persistently.

m: to irritate or annoy, especially through repetition; to make a harsh, rasping sound
x: The squeak of chalk on the board always grates on my nerves.
His habit of interrupting everyone in meetings began to grate on his colleagues.
Her roommate's loud music grated on her while she was trying to revise for finals.
Many voters found the minister's smug tone grating, especially in the middle of a crisis.
Little things he once found charming, like her constant humming, now grated on him.
tc: At first his cheerful whistling seemed harmless, but after weeks of sharing an office, it began to ______ on her nerves.
'At first ... seemed harmless, but' signals that it later became irritating.
se: The tuneless singing from the flat next door began to ______ on her nerves.
jar
Both 'grate on' and 'jar on' someone's nerves mean to irritate them.

m: causing horror or disgust, especially because it involves death or violence
x: My brother loves reading grisly crime novels before bed, then complains that he can't sleep.
The insurance investigator had to examine grisly photos from the accident scene.
The anatomy class began with a grisly demonstration on a cadaver that made two students faint.
Police described it as one of the most grisly murder cases in the city's history.
She could never forget the grisly details her uncle told her about the war.
tc: The documentary was not for the faint-hearted; it showed ______ footage of the battlefield, with bodies scattered across the mud.
'Not for the faint-hearted' and bodies in the mud show the footage was horrifying.
se: Hikers were badly shaken by the ______ discovery of human remains near the trail.
gruesome
Both 'grisly' and 'gruesome' describe something horrifying involving death.

m: to argue or bargain persistently over the price or terms of something
x: My mother can haggle with a rickshaw puller for ten minutes over just five taka.
Our procurement team haggled with the supplier for weeks before agreeing on a price.
Graduate students sometimes haggle with their supervisors over deadlines for thesis chapters.
Negotiators from both countries haggled late into the night over the trade agreement.
Even after years of marriage, they still haggle over whose turn it is to cook.
tc: In the bazaar nobody pays the first price quoted; buyers are expected to ______ until both sides agree on a fair deal.
Not paying the first price and arguing until a deal is reached describes bargaining.
se: Tourists who don't know how to ______ often end up paying twice the normal price.
bargain
Both 'haggle' and 'bargain' mean to argue for a lower price.

m: to cause someone great distress or mental suffering
x: The drive through the mountain pass in thick fog was harrowing for every passenger.
Managers were harrowed by weeks of uncertainty about whether the factory would close.
The book's harrowing account of life in a refugee camp is assigned in many sociology courses.
Survivors gave harrowing testimony about the factory collapse, describing hours trapped under rubble.
She was harrowed by guilt after missing her father's final days in hospital.
tc: Reporters were warned that the survivors' stories of torture would ______ even the most hardened listener.
Stories of torture affecting 'even the most hardened listener' point to causing deep distress.
se: Images of starving children are meant to ______ viewers and move them to donate.
distress
Both 'harrow' and 'distress' mean to cause emotional pain to viewers.

m: a loud, confused noise made by many people; a commotion
x: We could barely hear each other over the hubbub of the crowded café.
The constant hubbub in the open-plan office makes it hard to concentrate on detailed work.
When the professor walked in, the hubbub in the lecture hall died down at once.
The announcement of the new tax caused a hubbub in parliament that lasted for days.
Amid the hubbub of the wedding, she slipped away to sit quietly with her grandmother.
tc: After the noisy ______ of the marketplace, the quiet courtyard of the mosque felt like another world.
'Noisy' and the contrast with the 'quiet courtyard' show the blank means a loud commotion.
se: The ______ in the stadium grew louder as the players walked onto the field.
din
Both 'hubbub' and 'din' mean a loud, confused noise from a crowd.

m: deceptive or insincere talk or behavior; nonsense meant to mislead
x: My grandfather dismissed most of the diet advice on television as pure humbug.
The consultant's report was full of jargon, and most of us suspected it was humbug.
The professor exposed the so-called miracle cure as scientific humbug.
Voters are tired of political humbug and want honest answers about rising prices.
She could tell that his tearful promises to change were just humbug.
tc: Behind the politician's lofty talk of serving the poor lay nothing but ______; he had quietly cut every welfare program.
His lofty talk is contradicted by his cutting welfare, so the blank means hypocritical nonsense.
se: Critics dismissed the advertisement's claims of instant weight loss as ______.
nonsense
Both 'humbug' and 'nonsense' describe misleading claims that should not be believed.

m: not lasting or enduring forever; temporary
x: The sandcastle we built was impermanent, washed away by the next high tide.
Many tech jobs now feel impermanent, with contracts renewed only six months at a time.
Buddhist teachings stress that all things, including the self, are impermanent.
Experts warn that the ceasefire may prove impermanent unless the core disputes are resolved.
Grief taught her that even the closest relationships are impermanent and should be cherished.
tc: Unlike the stone temples that have stood for centuries, the bamboo shelters were ______, built to last only a single season.
'Unlike' contrasts with buildings that last centuries, and 'only a single season' confirms the blank means temporary.
se: The monk reminded us that wealth and fame are ______ and will eventually fade.
transient
Both 'impermanent' and 'transient' mean not lasting, which fits 'will eventually fade'.

m: to fix something firmly in the mind or memory; to stamp a mark on a surface
x: The company imprints its logo on every pen, mug and notebook it gives away.
Our trainer used vivid stories to imprint the safety rules on every new worker's mind.
Repeating new vocabulary aloud each morning helps imprint the words in your long-term memory.
Images of the burning tower were imprinted on the nation's memory for a generation.
The day her brother left for Canada is imprinted on her memory in painful detail.
tc: Moments of intense fear tend to ______ themselves on our memory so deeply that we can never forget them.
'So deeply that we can never forget them' shows the blank means to fix firmly in memory.
se: Good teachers know how to ______ key ideas on students' minds through vivid examples.
impress
Both 'imprint' and 'impress' ideas on the mind mean to fix them there firmly.

m: a sudden invasion or attack into another's territory; an unwelcome intrusion
x: Our vegetable garden suffered regular incursions from the neighbor's hungry goats.
The company's costly incursion into the smartphone market ended after just two years.
Scientists are tracking the incursion of salt water into rice fields in coastal Bangladesh.
Border guards reported several armed incursions into the territory last month.
She resented her mother-in-law's frequent incursions into her private life.
tc: The ceasefire collapsed after a brief armed ______ across the border by rebel fighters.
An armed crossing of the border that breaks a ceasefire is a sudden invasion.
se: The small country formally protested its neighbor's ______ into its territory.
intrusion
Both 'incursion' and 'intrusion' mean an unwelcome entry into another's territory.

m: treatment or circumstances that cause someone shame or a loss of self-respect
x: He suffered the indignity of being searched in front of other passengers at the airport.
After twenty years at the firm, she faced the indignity of reapplying for her own job.
Graduate students resented the indignity of having their phones confiscated like schoolchildren.
Refugees described the daily indignities of queuing for hours just to receive water.
Being treated as a servant in her in-laws' house was an indignity she refused to accept.
tc: Already demoted and stripped of his office, he then had to endure the further ______ of training his own replacement.
'Already demoted' and 'further' signal another humiliating experience.
se: Elderly patients should not have to suffer the ______ of waiting on hospital trolleys for hours.
humiliation
Both 'indignity' and 'humiliation' describe treatment that strips people of self-respect.

m: to inspire someone with an intense but foolish and usually short-lived passion
x: My little sister is completely infatuated with a Korean pop singer.
The new manager seemed infatuated with every fashionable buzzword he read about online.
Young scholars sometimes become so infatuated with a grand theory that they ignore contrary evidence.
Investors were so infatuated with the start-up that they ignored its mounting losses.
He was infatuated with her from the moment they met, but she barely noticed him.
tc: Flashy new gadgets seem to ______ him completely for a week, after which he loses interest entirely.
An intense attraction that vanishes after a week is a foolish, short-lived passion.
se: Charming strangers seemed to ______ her easily, though the feeling never lasted long.
captivate
Both 'infatuate' and 'captivate' mean to fill her with strong attraction.

m: a slight suspicion or vague idea about something
x: I had no inkling that my friends were planning a surprise party for me.
Nobody in the office had the slightest inkling that the company was about to be sold.
After the first lecture, she had an inkling that organic chemistry would be her hardest course.
Before the new study, scientists had only an inkling of how the virus spread between bats.
He had an inkling that she was unhappy, but he never asked her directly.
tc: Her parents had not the faintest ______ of her plans to elope; they found out only when she phoned from the airport.
They found out only at the last moment, so they had no suspicion at all; 'faintest' points to a slight idea.
se: None of the investors had the slightest ______ that the firm's accounts were fraudulent.
suspicion
Both 'inkling' and 'suspicion' mean a faint idea that something is true.

m: an official investigation, especially one into the cause of a death
x: After the cricket team's shock defeat, fans held their own inquest on social media.
The board ordered an internal inquest into why the product launch had gone so badly.
The medical students attended an inquest to learn how coroners determine the cause of death.
An inquest into the factory fire revealed that the emergency exits had been locked.
After their breakup, she spent weeks conducting a painful inquest into what had gone wrong.
tc: Because the cause of the patient's sudden death remained unclear, the coroner opened a formal ______ into the circumstances.
An unclear cause of death and a coroner point to an official investigation.
se: Families of the victims demanded a public ______ into the stadium disaster.
inquiry
Both 'inquest' and 'inquiry' mean an official investigation into what happened.

m: too unpleasant, arrogant, or annoying to bear
x: The heat on the crowded bus was insufferable by midday, and nobody could open the jammed windows.
Since his promotion, Rafiq has become insufferable, lecturing everyone about leadership.
Our seminar leader's insufferable arrogance discouraged many students from speaking up.
Critics described the film's narrator as smug and insufferable, which hurt its box-office sales.
Her brother was insufferable after winning the family quiz, reminding everyone about it for days.
tc: His constant boasting about his salary and his car made him so ______ that even his oldest friends stopped inviting him out.
Friends stopping their invitations because of his boasting shows he had become unbearable.
se: The noise from the construction site next door had become ______, so we moved out for a week.
unbearable
Both 'insufferable' and 'unbearable' mean too unpleasant to endure.

m: a person who takes part in a conversation, or who speaks for others in talks
x: At the dinner, my interlocutor turned out to be a retired diplomat with fascinating stories.
The firm used a local consultant as its main interlocutor with government officials.
In Plato's dialogues, Socrates questions his interlocutors until their contradictions become clear.
Western governments see the moderate faction as a credible interlocutor in the peace talks.
She was a patient interlocutor, always letting him finish his thoughts before she replied.
tc: Because she spoke both languages fluently, she became the main ______ between the foreign investors and the village elders.
Speaking both languages and standing 'between' two groups describes someone who conducts dialogue for them.
se: The ambassador was regarded as a trusted ______ between the two rival governments.
intermediary
Both 'interlocutor' and 'intermediary' describe someone who carries on talks between two sides.

m: an indirect hint or suggestion that something is true or will happen
x: There was no intimation in her cheerful text message that anything was wrong.
The first intimation of trouble at the company came when salaries were paid late.
Early experiments gave only faint intimations of the discovery that was to come.
Officials dismissed every intimation of a cover-up as baseless rumor.
His sudden coldness was the first intimation that their marriage was in trouble.
tc: Though he never said so directly, his gloomy remarks at the meeting were the first ______ that he planned to resign.
'Never said so directly' shows his remarks were an indirect hint.
se: The minister's speech contained a clear ______ that taxes would rise next year.
hint
Both 'intimation' and 'hint' mean an indirect signal of what is coming.

m: a short trip taken for pleasure
x: On Friday we took a quick jaunt to Cox's Bazar to escape the city heat.
The team's weekend jaunt to the hills was paid for by the company as a reward.
During study leave, he allowed himself only one short jaunt to the lake with friends.
Critics accused the mayor of spending public money on overseas jaunts disguised as business trips.
Their spontaneous jaunt to the countryside reminded them why they had fallen in love.
tc: It wasn't a serious business trip at all, just a brief ______ to the coast to enjoy a day of sunshine.
'Not a serious business trip', 'brief' and 'enjoy' describe a short pleasure trip.
se: On Sunday, the family went on a short ______ to the countryside for a picnic.
outing
Both 'jaunt' and 'outing' mean a short trip for pleasure.

m: similar in nature, character, or origin; related
x: Finding someone who loves old Bengali songs as much as I do felt like meeting a kindred spirit.
Engineers and designers share kindred goals, even if they speak different professional languages.
Linguists have shown that English and German are kindred languages descended from a common ancestor.
Activists from kindred movements around the world met to coordinate their campaigns.
They knew within minutes of meeting that they were kindred souls.
tc: Although they grew up on different continents, the two poets recognized each other as ______ spirits, sharing the same tastes and fears.
'Sharing the same tastes and fears' despite different origins shows they were alike in nature.
se: Chemistry and physics are ______ disciplines that share many basic principles.
related
Both 'kindred' and 'related' mean closely connected in nature.

m: a brief failure of concentration, memory, or judgment
x: A momentary lapse of concentration caused him to miss the exit on the highway.
One lapse in data security can cost a company millions and destroy its reputation.
A brief lapse in attendance cost him the scholarship he had worked so hard to win.
The official report blamed the accident on a serious lapse in safety procedures.
She forgave his lapse in judgment but warned him it must never happen again.
tc: The otherwise flawless pilot was suspended after one careless ______ that nearly caused a collision.
'Otherwise flawless' and 'careless' show the blank means a brief failure.
se: Forgetting the client's name was a rare ______ for such an organized manager.
slip
Both 'lapse' and 'slip' mean a small, uncharacteristic mistake.

m: lack of strictness, care, or attention to rules
x: The laxity of our building's security means almost anyone can walk in.
Auditors sharply criticized the laxity of the bank's lending rules over the past decade.
Some teachers worry that laxity in grading is steadily lowering academic standards.
Regulators were blamed for the laxity that allowed unsafe factories to keep operating.
Her parents' laxity about bedtimes was a running joke among her cousins.
tc: The new principal, known for her strictness, vowed to end the ______ that had let students skip classes without consequence.
Her 'strictness' contrasts with letting students skip classes, so the blank means lack of strictness.
se: Inspectors blamed the outbreak on ______ in the kitchen's hygiene standards.
slackness
Both 'laxity' and 'slackness' mean a careless failure to keep standards.

m: mercy or gentleness, especially when punishment would be expected
x: Our landlord showed rare lenity when we paid the rent a week late during the floods.
The manager's lenity toward latecomers began to frustrate staff who arrived on time.
The professor was known for her lenity in granting extensions to struggling students.
The judge's lenity toward the young offender sparked a debate about juvenile justice.
She pleaded for lenity, explaining that her brother had acted out of desperation.
tc: Instead of the harsh sentence everyone expected, the judge showed surprising ______, releasing the first-time offender with a warning.
'Instead of the harsh sentence' and release with a warning show the blank means mercy.
se: The defense lawyer asked the court to show ______ to a young mother who had never broken the law before.
clemency
Both 'lenity' and 'clemency' mean mercy in punishment.

m: to officially impose and collect a tax, fee, or fine
x: The building committee levied an extra charge on every flat to repair the broken lift.
Our company levies a small fee on clients who cancel appointments at short notice.
Many universities levy additional fees on international students for visa services.
The government plans to levy a new tax on sugary drinks to fight rising obesity.
Every time he forgot their anniversary, his wife levied a 'penalty' of dinner at her favorite restaurant.
tc: To pay for the new bridge, the council decided to ______ a toll on every vehicle crossing the river.
Paying for a bridge with a toll on vehicles means officially imposing a charge.
se: The government will ______ a heavy tax on imported luxury cars.
impose
Both 'levy' and 'impose' a tax mean to officially require its payment.

m: containing false written statements that damage someone's reputation
x: My cousin deleted his angry post after a lawyer warned him it could be libelous.
Our legal team reviews every press release to make sure nothing in it is libelous.
The journalism course spends a week on how to report allegations without being libelous.
The newspaper paid damages after a court ruled that the article was libelous.
She was deeply hurt by the libelous rumors her former friend posted online about her.
tc: The magazine was forced to withdraw the story after the actor proved that its false claims about his finances were ______.
Published false claims that damage someone and force a withdrawal are libelous.
se: The senator sued the blogger, claiming the post was ______ and had damaged his reputation.
defamatory
Both 'libelous' and 'defamatory' describe false statements that harm a reputation.

m: to run with long, relaxed, bounding strides
x: Our dog loped across the field to greet us as soon as we got out of the car.
Every morning the young intern loped up the office stairs two at a time.
Biologists filmed wolves loping across the snow for hours without seeming to tire.
The marathon leader loped along at an easy pace, far ahead of the pack.
He loped over to her table with a shy grin and asked if the seat was free.
tc: Unlike the short-legged terrier, which scampered frantically, the greyhound seemed to ______ effortlessly with long, easy strides.
'Long, easy strides' in contrast with frantic scampering define the blank as loping.
se: The tall athlete began to ______ around the track, barely appearing to make an effort.
jog
Both 'lope' and 'jog' mean to run at a relaxed, easy pace.

m: money or profit, especially when gained in a greedy or dishonest way
x: My grandmother used to joke that she married for love, not for filthy lucre.
Colleagues accused the partner of abandoning his principles for lucre when he joined the tobacco firm.
Medieval scholars often condemned moneylending as the sinful pursuit of lucre.
Critics say the sports league now cares more about lucre than about its loyal fans.
He insisted he had become a doctor to help people, not for the lucre.
tc: The once idealistic artist was accused of selling out, abandoning his principles for the sake of ______.
'Selling out' and 'abandoning his principles' point to greedy pursuit of money.
se: The corrupt official was willing to betray his country for ______.
money
Both 'lucre' and 'money' name the financial gain he betrayed his country for.

m: to make a sudden, unsteady movement; to move erratically from one state to another
x: The bus lurched forward suddenly, and half the passengers lost their balance.
The company has lurched from one crisis to another since its founder retired.
The research project lurched along for months because nobody could agree on the methodology.
Global stock markets lurched lower after the central bank's surprise announcement on interest rates.
Her heart lurched when she saw his name appear on her phone after months of silence.
tc: Unable to walk steadily after the long voyage, the sailor began to ______ from side to side as he stepped onto the dock.
'Unable to walk steadily' and 'from side to side' show the blank means to move unsteadily.
se: As the ship hit the huge wave, passengers felt the deck ______ beneath their feet.
pitch
Both 'lurch' and 'pitch' describe a sudden, violent tilting movement of the deck.

m: having a soft, glowing shine; glossy
x: Regular oiling keeps my mother's long black hair thick and lustrous.
The jeweler polished the pearls until they were lustrous enough to display in the window.
In the lab, students compared the lustrous surface of pure silver with dull, tarnished samples.
Archaeologists uncovered lustrous glazed pottery that had survived for centuries underground.
She looked up at him with lustrous eyes, full of tears and gratitude.
tc: After years of neglect, the old silver tray looked dull and black, but a careful polish left it ______ once more.
'But' contrasts with 'dull and black', and polishing makes it shine, so the blank means shining.
se: The horse's ______ coat gleamed in the morning sun.
glossy
Both 'lustrous' and 'glossy' describe a shiny surface that gleams.

m: to ruin or badly damage something, such as a text or object, by twisting, crushing, or careless handling
x: The printer jammed again and mangled the only copy of my boarding pass.
Our new intern mangled the client's name in the email, so I had to send an apology.
The professor complained that the translation mangled the poet's subtle imagery beyond recognition.
The car was so badly mangled in the crash that rescuers needed hours to free the driver.
He mangled his apology so thoroughly that she ended up angrier than before.
tc: Rather than conveying the author's meaning faithfully, the hasty translation managed only to ______ it.
'Rather than conveying ... faithfully' signals a contrast, so the blank must mean to distort or ruin.
se: Nervous on live television, the reporter began to ______ the names of the foreign delegates.
butcher
Both 'mangle' and 'butcher' mean to pronounce or handle something so badly that it is ruined.

m: tending to interfere in other people's affairs without being asked
x: Our meddlesome neighbor keeps telling us where to park and when to water the plants.
A meddlesome manager who rewrites every report will soon lose the trust of the team.
Researchers found that meddlesome reviewers often slowed publication without improving the papers.
Critics accused the government of being meddlesome in matters best left to local councils.
Her meddlesome aunt in Chittagong had already chosen three possible grooms before she finished university.
tc: Though he insisted he only wanted to help, his constant, uninvited advice about our wedding plans struck everyone as ______.
'Uninvited advice' about someone else's plans shows the blank must mean interfering.
se: The committee resented the ______ regulator, who demanded weekly updates on decisions that were none of its concern.
interfering
Both 'meddlesome' and 'interfering' describe someone who involves himself in matters that are not his business.

m: to hand out or allot something, especially punishment, usually used in the phrase 'mete out'
x: My grandmother meted out sweets to the children only after they had finished their homework.
The new director meted out blame for the failed project before hearing anyone's side of the story.
One study suggests that judges mete out harsher sentences when they are tired and hungry.
The referee meted out three yellow cards in the first twenty minutes of the match.
She felt the silent treatment he meted out after every argument was crueler than shouting.
tc: Unlike his lenient predecessor, the new headmaster was quick to ______ out severe punishments for even minor offenses.
The contrast with 'lenient' and the phrase 'out severe punishments' show the blank means to hand out.
se: The court has the authority to ______ out heavy fines to companies that pollute the river.
deal
'Mete out' and 'deal out' both mean to hand out or distribute, so the sentence keeps the same meaning.

m: to annoy or offend someone slightly, often over something minor
x: I was a little miffed when the cafe gave away the table I had reserved.
It miffed the senior engineers that the intern's suggestion was adopted instead of theirs.
Several students were miffed to learn that the deadline had been moved forward without notice.
Local shopkeepers were miffed by the council's decision to close the street for a festival.
He seemed miffed that his oldest friend had forgotten his birthday yet again.
tc: Although the snub was too minor to cause real anger, it was enough to ______ the guest of honor.
'Too minor to cause real anger' tells us the blank means to annoy only slightly.
se: Being left off the email chain was a small thing, but it was enough to ______ the department head.
irk
Both 'miff' and 'irk' mean to annoy mildly, which fits 'a small thing'.

m: to soften or restrain one's words to avoid offending, usually in the phrase 'not mince words'
x: My father never minces words when he thinks I am wasting money.
The auditor did not mince words: the company's accounts were a complete mess.
In her report on the thesis, the external examiner minced no words about its weak methodology.
The inquiry minces no words in blaming poor planning for the city's flooding every monsoon.
I value friends who don't mince words, even when their honesty stings.
tc: Known for her bluntness, the coach did not ______ words when she told the team their performance had been disgraceful.
'Known for her bluntness' shows she did not soften her words, so the blank means to restrain or soften.
se: The editorial refused to ______ its words, calling the new policy a reckless gamble.
soften
Refusing to 'mince' or 'soften' its words both mean the editorial spoke harshly and directly.

m: a wrong, wicked, or illegal act
x: As a child, I confessed every small misdeed to my mother before she could find out.
An internal audit uncovered years of financial misdeeds by the former accounts manager.
Historians are still debating how much the colonial administrators knew about the misdeeds of their officials.
The minister resigned after a newspaper exposed the misdeeds of his closest advisers.
She forgave his past misdeeds, but she made it clear she would not forget them.
tc: The company's annual report praised its charitable work but said nothing about the ______ that had led to three lawsuits.
The contrast with 'charitable work' and the link to 'lawsuits' show the blank means a wrongful act.
se: The priest urged him to confess every ______, however small, before seeking forgiveness.
transgression
Both 'misdeed' and 'transgression' mean a wrong act that needs confessing and forgiving.

m: a complicated, confusing situation that is hard to escape from; originally a swamp
x: Trying to get a refund pulled me into a morass of phone menus and broken links.
The merger left the company stuck in a morass of conflicting policies and duplicate departments.
My first year of doctoral study felt like wading through a morass of contradictory literature.
Reformers promised to rescue the agency from its bureaucratic morass, but little changed.
After the divorce, he sank into a morass of self-pity and unpaid bills.
tc: Far from being simple, the new tax code turned out to be the kind of ______ in which even experienced accountants became hopelessly lost.
'Far from being simple' and 'hopelessly lost' show the blank means a confusing, trapping situation.
se: The once-promising reform got bogged down in the ______ of regulations and competing interests.
quagmire
Both 'morass' and 'quagmire' describe a messy situation in which progress gets stuck.

m: to gather or summon something, such as courage, support, or people
x: I finally mustered the courage to ask my landlord to fix the leaking roof.
The project lead struggled to muster enough support from other departments to meet the deadline.
Despite weeks of revision, she could barely muster any enthusiasm for the organic chemistry exam.
The opposition failed to muster the votes needed to block the controversial bill.
He mustered a weak smile when his ex-girlfriend walked into the party with her new partner.
c: all the strength she could muster
tc: Exhausted after the long campaign, the candidate could barely ______ the energy to deliver her final speech.
'Exhausted' and 'barely' show the blank means to summon or gather energy with difficulty.
se: Though terrified of heights, he managed to ______ the nerve to climb the ladder.
summon
To 'muster' or 'summon' the nerve both mean to call up courage despite fear.

m: willing and eager to help or to do favors for others
x: The obliging shopkeeper let us leave our bags behind the counter while we explored the market.
Our IT technician is so obliging that people call him even for problems they could fix themselves.
An obliging librarian stayed late to help me find the old journals I needed for my thesis.
Visitors often describe the town's residents as warm, obliging, and quick to offer directions.
Being too obliging with her friends left her little time for her own plans.
tc: Expecting a grumpy official, we were surprised to find the clerk so ______ that he filled out the forms for us himself.
The contrast with 'grumpy' and the fact that he did the forms for them show the blank means eager to help.
se: The hotel staff were remarkably ______, rearranging our rooms twice without a single complaint.
accommodating
Both 'obliging' and 'accommodating' describe people who willingly meet others' requests.

m: a strange or peculiar person, thing, or trait
x: Among the souvenirs in her flat was one real oddity: a stuffed crocodile wearing a hat.
In an office where everyone wore suits, his colorful sandals were seen as an oddity.
The astronomer noticed an oddity in the data that later led to the discovery of a new planet.
Electric cars were once a rare oddity on our roads, but now they seem to be everywhere.
She loved him for his oddities, including his habit of naming every houseplant.
tc: In a village where nearly everyone farmed rice, people regarded the full-time poet as the local ______.
The contrast between the poet and a village where 'nearly everyone farmed' shows the blank means a strange or unusual person.
se: Researchers dismissed the strange reading as a statistical ______ until it appeared in three more experiments.
anomaly
Both 'oddity' and 'anomaly' mean something unusual that does not fit the expected pattern.

m: to stare at someone or something in a rude, lustful, or greedy way
x: It is rude to ogle strangers on the bus, and most people find it deeply uncomfortable.
The new office policy makes clear that ogling colleagues counts as harassment.
Tourists ogled the gleaming sports cars parked outside the luxury hotel.
Campaigners argue that women in crowded public spaces should not have to put up with being ogled.
My little brother stood at the bakery window, ogling the chocolate cakes he couldn't afford.
tc: Rather than glancing politely, the men on the corner continued to ______ every woman who walked past, making them visibly uneasy.
'Rather than glancing politely' and 'visibly uneasy' show the blank means to stare rudely.
se: The hungry children pressed their faces to the shop window to ______ the rows of sweets.
eye
Both 'ogle' and 'eye' here mean to look at something with obvious desire.

m: an official rule or law, especially one made by a city or local authority
x: A city ordinance forbids playing loud music in residential areas after ten at night.
Our building manager posted a copy of the new fire ordinance beside the lift.
Her dissertation compares noise ordinances in five Asian megacities, including Dhaka and Manila.
The council passed an ordinance banning single-use plastic bags from all supermarkets.
We argued for weeks about whether the parking ordinance applied to our own driveway.
tc: Because the local ______ prohibits building above four stories, the developer had to scrap plans for a tower.
'Prohibits building' shows the blank is an official local rule.
se: Residents were fined under a new municipal ______ that bans burning leaves in backyards.
bylaw
Both 'ordinance' and 'bylaw' mean a rule made by a local authority.

m: to exceed or surpass; to grow faster or do better than something else
x: Our grocery bills have outstripped our salaries ever since prices began to soar.
Demand for the new phone quickly outstripped supply, and stores ran out within hours.
By her second year, the young researcher had outstripped her supervisor in publications.
In many cities, population growth has outstripped the construction of affordable housing.
He felt a pang of jealousy when his younger brother outstripped him in almost everything.
tc: Although the company started as a tiny regional player, its sales soon began to ______ those of its largest rival.
'Although ... tiny' signals a contrast, so the blank must mean to surpass.
se: Experts warn that the city's water use will soon ______ the capacity of its aging reservoirs.
exceed
Both 'outstrip' and 'exceed' mean to go beyond a limit or amount.

m: like a palace in size and splendor; very large, grand, and luxurious
x: My cousin's new flat in Gulshan is so palatial that we got lost looking for the kitchen.
The startup moved into palatial offices that its modest revenue could hardly justify.
The university's palatial new library has more marble than books, some students joke.
Reporters toured the palatial residence that the official had built with public funds.
After years in a cramped hostel room, even a modest apartment felt palatial to her.
tc: Unlike the cramped cottages of the villagers, the landlord's mansion, with its forty rooms and grand ballroom, was truly ______.
The contrast with 'cramped cottages' and the 'forty rooms' show the blank means grand and palace-like.
se: The couple's ______ villa, complete with marble floors and a private cinema, was the envy of their friends.
opulent
Both 'palatial' and 'opulent' describe a home of great luxury and splendor.

m: to make something extremely dry, especially through heat or lack of water
x: After the long hike, I was so parched that I drank three bottles of water.
The scorching sun parched the cricket pitch, which had cracked badly by the third day.
Our office air conditioning parches my throat, so I keep a flask of tea at my desk.
Scientists warn that longer droughts will parch farmland across much of the region.
Weeks of relentless heat had parched the garden she and her late husband had planted together.
tc: With no rain for months, the relentless summer sun began to ______ the fields until the soil cracked.
'No rain for months' and 'the soil cracked' show the blank means to dry out severely.
se: Farmers feared that another week of heat would ______ the young rice plants beyond saving.
scorch
Both 'parch' and 'scorch' mean to damage plants by heat and dryness.

m: by necessity; because circumstances leave no other choice
x: We missed the last bus, so we perforce walked home through the rain.
The budget was cut in half, so the team perforce dropped two of its planned features.
Because the archives were closed, the historian perforce relied on secondhand accounts.
With the bridge washed away by the floods, villagers perforce crossed the river by boat.
Living abroad alone, she perforce learned to cope with loneliness and to cook for herself.
tc: Since there was no other qualified surgeon in the hospital that night, the young resident ______ performed the operation herself.
'No other qualified surgeon' shows she acted out of necessity, so the blank means by necessity.
se: The discussion must ______ be brief, since we have only ten minutes before the hall closes.
necessarily
Both 'perforce' and 'necessarily' mean that circumstances force the discussion to be short.

m: overly fussy about small details; also needing very precise, careful handling
x: My pernickety roommate insists that the towels be folded in thirds, never in half.
Our editor is pernickety about commas, but her care makes the reports much clearer.
Calibrating the microscope is a pernickety task that takes the lab assistant most of the morning.
Some voters found the new rules on campaign posters absurdly pernickety.
He loved her deeply, though her pernickety habits at the dinner table drove him slightly mad.
tc: Unlike his relaxed predecessor, the new supervisor was so ______ that he rejected reports for using the wrong font size.
The contrast with 'relaxed' and rejecting reports over font size show the blank means overly fussy.
se: My grandfather is ______ about his tea: the water must be boiled exactly once and the cup warmed first.
fussy
Both 'pernickety' and 'fussy' describe someone who insists on small details being exactly right.

m: to annoy someone with frequent, persistent requests or interruptions
x: My little sister pestered me all afternoon to take her to the new ice cream shop.
Please stop pestering the accounts team; they will process your claim by Friday.
Students who pester professors for extra marks rarely get what they want.
Journalists pestered the hospital spokesperson for updates throughout the night.
He pestered her with messages for weeks until she finally agreed to meet for coffee.
tc: Tired of being asked every five minutes, the parents finally gave in when their children continued to ______ them for a puppy.
'Being asked every five minutes' shows the blank means to annoy with repeated requests.
se: Salespeople kept calling to ______ him about upgrading his phone plan.
badger
Both 'pester' and 'badger' mean to bother someone with repeated requests.

m: a deadly, fast-spreading epidemic disease; also anything highly destructive
x: Old village stories describe a pestilence that killed half the cattle in a single summer.
In the meeting, she joked that the office flu was spreading like a medieval pestilence.
Historians link the decline of the medieval city to war, famine, and pestilence.
Public health officials once feared cholera as a pestilence that followed every monsoon flood.
To the grieving family, the war seemed a pestilence that had swallowed everything they loved.
tc: Within months, the ______ had emptied whole villages, killing more people than the war itself.
'Emptied whole villages' and 'killing more people than the war' show the blank means a deadly epidemic.
se: Ancient chroniclers blamed the ______ that swept through the city on the anger of the gods.
plague
Both 'pestilence' and 'plague' mean a deadly disease spreading through a population.

m: to walk slowly and heavily, or to work slowly and steadily at something dull
x: We plodded home through ankle-deep water after the evening downpour.
She plodded through two hundred invoices before finally taking a lunch break.
Instead of skimming, he plodded through every chapter of the statistics textbook twice.
Negotiations plodded on for months without producing any real agreement.
Their marriage plodded along without passion until a holiday reminded them why they had fallen in love.
tc: Unlike the sprinters who raced ahead, the exhausted hikers could only ______ slowly up the muddy hill.
The contrast with 'raced ahead' and the words 'exhausted' and 'slowly' show the blank means to walk heavily.
se: Weighed down by their heavy packs, the soldiers began to ______ through the snow.
trudge
Both 'plod' and 'trudge' mean to walk slowly and with effort.

m: a long column of smoke, dust, gas, or water rising into the air; also a large feather
x: A plume of smoke rose from the neighbor's kitchen window, and we ran to help.
From our office window, we watched a huge plume of dust drift over the construction site.
Satellite images showed a plume of volcanic ash stretching hundreds of kilometers across the ocean.
Investigators traced the toxic plume in the river back to a leaking factory pipe.
She wore a hat with a bright red plume to her sister's wedding, delighting the guests.
tc: After the explosion, residents miles away could see the towering ______ of black smoke rising above the refinery.
'Of black smoke rising' shows the blank means a tall column of smoke.
se: A thick ______ of steam rose from the geyser every ten minutes, drawing gasps from the tourists.
column
Both 'plume' and 'column' describe a tall stream of steam rising upward.

m: to study or read something very closely and attentively, usually in the phrase 'pore over'
x: I pored over the menu for ten minutes and still ordered the same dish as always.
Lawyers pored over the contract late into the night, searching for loopholes.
Before the GRE, he pored over word lists every morning on the bus to campus.
Investigators are poring over flight data to understand why the plane lost altitude.
She pored over his old letters, looking for any sign that he had once loved her.
tc: Rather than skimming the report, the auditor chose to ______ over every line of the accounts.
The contrast with 'skimming' shows the blank means to study closely.
se: The students spent an hour trying to ______ over the difficult passage, reading each sentence again and again.
puzzle
'Pore over' and 'puzzle over' both describe studying something intently to understand it.

m: to groom oneself carefully, or to show smug pride and self-satisfaction
x: He spent ten minutes preening in front of the mirror before we could leave for dinner.
After landing the big contract, the sales manager preened in front of the whole department.
The visiting professor preened as students praised his latest book during the seminar.
Officials preened at the ribbon-cutting ceremony, though the bridge had opened two years late.
She found his habit of preening whenever someone complimented him rather unattractive.
c: preen in front of the mirror
tc: Instead of thanking his team for the victory, the self-satisfied manager stood on stage to ______ before the applauding crowd.
'Self-satisfied' and 'instead of thanking his team' show the blank means to show off smugly.
se: As soon as the photographers arrived, the winning captain began to ______ for the cameras.
strut
Both 'preen' and 'strut' mean to show off proudly in front of an audience.

m: to make small, fussy adjustments to one's appearance, hair, or clothes
x: My brother primps for half an hour before every family dinner, fixing his hair again and again.
Before the interview, she slipped into the restroom to primp and check her collar.
Some students spend more time primping for graduation photos than preparing for their finals.
A survey found that more commuters now primp on trains, applying makeup on the way to work.
He teased her for primping before their video call, but he had changed his shirt twice.
tc: While her friends dressed in minutes, Nadia needed an hour to ______ in front of the mirror before any party.
The contrast with friends who 'dressed in minutes' shows the blank means to fuss over one's appearance.
se: The actors had only five minutes to ______ before the curtain rose.
preen
Both 'primp' and 'preen' mean to tidy and adjust one's appearance.

m: to investigate or examine something thoroughly, especially to uncover hidden facts
x: My mother gently probed until I admitted that I had failed my driving test.
During the interview, the panel probed her reasons for leaving her previous job.
Her thesis probes the links between childhood nutrition and later school performance.
A parliamentary committee will probe allegations of bribery in the port contract.
He didn't like it when friends probed into his past, so he quickly changed the subject.
tc: Not satisfied with the official explanation, the journalist decided to ______ further into the company's finances.
'Not satisfied with the official explanation' shows the blank means to investigate more deeply.
se: Police have been asked to ______ the circumstances surrounding the fire at the warehouse.
investigate
Both 'probe' and 'investigate' mean to examine the facts thoroughly.

m: to poke with a finger or pointed object; to urge or stir someone into action
x: I had to prod my roommate three times before he finally switched off his alarm.
Our manager keeps prodding the team to submit timesheets on Friday instead of Monday.
A good supervisor prods doctoral students to publish without crushing their confidence.
Public outrage prodded the government into tightening building safety rules.
She prodded him to call his father, knowing they both regretted the argument.
tc: The committee was reluctant to act, and it took months of public pressure to ______ it into reforming the law.
'Reluctant to act' and 'public pressure' show the blank means to push someone into action.
se: Without a deadline, he would never finish the report, so his boss had to ______ him every few days.
nudge
Both 'prod' and 'nudge' mean to remind or push someone to act.

m: to declare openly, often claiming a quality, belief, or feeling one may not truly have
x: He professes to love spicy food, yet he always orders the mildest curry on the menu.
The consultant professed expertise in supply chains but couldn't answer basic questions about shipping.
Few scholars profess certainty about the origins of the ancient script.
Both parties profess a commitment to clean energy while approving new coal plants.
She professed her love for him in a long letter she never found the courage to send.
tc: Although they ______ to care about the environment, the company's executives have repeatedly lobbied against pollution limits.
'Although' sets up a contrast with their actions, so the blank means to claim, perhaps falsely.
se: Many people ______ a deep love of classical music but have never attended a concert.
claim
Both 'profess' and 'claim' mean to state something about oneself that may not be true.

m: to put forward an idea, theory, or plan for others to consider
x: At dinner, my uncle propounded his theory that tea tastes better from a clay cup.
In the strategy meeting, the new analyst propounded a bold plan to enter the Indian market.
Darwin propounded the theory of natural selection after decades of careful observation.
The economist propounded a controversial model linking rainfall patterns to election results.
She propounded a simple rule for their marriage: never go to bed angry.
tc: Rather than merely criticizing existing models, the young physicist went on to ______ a theory of her own for colleagues to evaluate.
'Rather than merely criticizing' and 'for colleagues to evaluate' show the blank means to put forward.
se: In his final lecture, the philosopher went on to ______ a new theory of moral responsibility.
propose
Both 'propound' and 'propose' mean to offer an idea for consideration.
