m: to cut away unnecessary or unwanted parts in order to reduce or improve something
x: Every spring, my father prunes the mango tree so that it produces more fruit.
The new CEO pruned the product line, dropping a dozen items that rarely sold.
My supervisor told me to prune the literature review from forty pages to fifteen.
Lawmakers pruned the budget proposal, cutting spending on several unpopular programs.
After the move, she pruned her circle of friends to those who had truly stood by her.
tc: The essay was far too long, so the editor told her to ______ every sentence that did not support her main argument.
'Far too long' shows the blank means to cut away unnecessary parts.
se: To keep the meeting short, the chair decided to ______ the agenda to just three items.
trim
Both 'prune' and 'trim' mean to cut something down by removing extra parts.

m: to inquire too closely or nosily into other people's private affairs
x: I don't mean to pry, but are you and your sister still not speaking?
Employees complained that the new monitoring software let managers pry into their personal messages.
Researchers must not pry into participants' lives beyond what the study requires.
Tabloid photographers pried into the family's grief, camping outside their home for days.
She hated how her in-laws pried into every detail of her finances and plans.
tc: Respecting her colleague's privacy, Mina chose not to ______ when he returned from his long, unexplained leave looking upset.
'Respecting her colleague's privacy' shows the blank means to ask nosy questions.
se: Reporters were warned not to ______ into the private lives of the victims' families.
snoop
Both 'pry into' and 'snoop into' mean to investigate someone's private matters nosily.

m: to feel or show fear; to shrink back in fright
x: I quailed at the sight of the dentist's drill, even though the procedure was minor.
Junior staff often quail when the chairman storms into the office unannounced.
Many students quail at the thought of defending their thesis before a hostile committee.
Despite repeated threats, the reporters refused to quail and kept publishing their investigation.
He quailed under his father's stern gaze and confessed to denting the car.
tc: Although his officers expected the young recruit to ______ before the advancing enemy, he held his position bravely.
'Although' contrasts the expectation with 'held his position bravely', so the blank means to shrink back in fear.
se: Even seasoned negotiators would ______ at the thought of facing such a ruthless opponent.
flinch
Both 'quail' and 'flinch' mean to shrink back in fear or dread.

m: understood or enjoyed only by a small, elite group; also (of air) thin and low in oxygen
x: Despite years in the rarefied world of art auctions, my friend still prefers tea from a roadside stall.
Junior staff found the boardroom's rarefied discussions of financial theory hard to follow.
Her research on abstract number theory is so rarefied that only a dozen people can judge it.
Climbers suffer headaches and fatigue in the rarefied air above eight thousand meters.
He felt out of place in her rarefied circle of diplomats and opera lovers.
tc: Far from being popular entertainment, the poet's work circulated only in the ______ circles of a few academics.
'Far from being popular' and 'a few academics' show the blank means exclusive and elite.
se: The debate took place in the ______ world of theoretical physics, far from the concerns of ordinary voters.
esoteric
Both 'rarefied' and 'esoteric' describe something understood only by a small group of specialists.

m: to make a harsh, grating sound, or to speak in a rough, grating voice
x: After shouting at the cricket match all afternoon, my voice rasped like sandpaper.
'Shut the door,' the manager rasped, his throat sore from a week of back-to-back meetings.
During the lecture, the old projector's fan rasped so loudly that students could barely hear.
Doctors say a voice that rasps for more than three weeks should be checked by a specialist.
His breath rasped in his chest as he tried to tell her how much he had missed her.
tc: Her normally smooth voice had begun to ______ after three days of shouting at the protest rallies.
The contrast with 'normally smooth' and the cause 'three days of shouting' show the blank means to sound harsh and grating.
se: Hoarse from his cold, the old man could only ______ a few words to the nurse.
croak
Both 'rasp' and 'croak' mean to speak in a rough, hoarse voice.

m: a hidden, remote, or inner part of something, such as a building or the mind
x: She keeps her grandmother's jewelry in a small recess behind the bookshelf.
Old complaints buried in the recesses of the company's archive finally came to light.
The novel explores the darkest recesses of a soldier's memory after the war.
Divers explored the deepest recesses of the underwater cave for evidence of ancient life.
Even after years of marriage, there were recesses of his heart she had never reached.
tc: The thought was not conscious; it lurked somewhere in the deepest ______ of her mind, surfacing only in dreams.
'Not conscious' and 'deepest ... of her mind' show the blank means a hidden inner part.
se: The old letter had been hidden in a dusty ______ behind the fireplace.
nook
Both 'recess' and 'nook' mean a small, hidden space set back in a wall or room.

m: compensation or payment given for loss, harm, or effort
x: As recompense for the delayed flight, the airline offered us free meals and a hotel room.
The staff worked through the holidays without any recompense beyond a thank-you email.
Volunteers in the study received modest recompense for their time and travel.
Flood victims are still waiting for the recompense promised by the government two years ago.
She felt his apology was poor recompense for years of neglect.
tc: Having lost their homes to the new dam, the villagers demanded ______ from the authorities for everything they had given up.
'Lost their homes' and 'for everything they had given up' show the blank means compensation.
se: The court ordered the company to pay ______ to the workers injured in the explosion.
compensation
Both 'recompense' and 'compensation' mean payment for harm suffered.

m: able to be saved, improved, or made good; also exchangeable for money or goods
x: These vouchers are redeemable at any branch of the bookshop until December.
Our manager believes that even the worst-performing teams are redeemable with the right leadership.
Her supervisor told her the thesis was redeemable if she rewrote the second chapter.
Reformers insist that most young offenders are redeemable if given education and support.
She still believed their friendship was redeemable, despite the hurtful things he had said.
tc: Although critics wrote the novel off as a disaster, the editor saw it as ______ and spent a year helping the author rescue it.
'Although critics wrote it off' contrasts with 'helping the author rescue it', so the blank means capable of being saved.
se: The coach refused to give up on the struggling player, insisting that his career was still ______.
salvageable
Both 'redeemable' and 'salvageable' mean the career can still be saved.

m: to stagger or lose one's balance; to feel shocked, confused, or overwhelmed
x: I was still reeling from the taxi fare when the driver asked for a tip.
The company is reeling after losing its biggest client to a competitor.
Several first-year students reeled at the amount of reading assigned in the first week.
Coastal towns are reeling from the cyclone that destroyed thousands of homes overnight.
He reeled backward when she told him she was moving abroad without him.
tc: The boxer's punch was so powerful that his opponent began to ______ across the ring before collapsing.
'So powerful' and 'before collapsing' show the blank means to stagger.
se: Dizzy from the heat, the tourist began to ______ and grabbed the railing for support.
stagger
Both 'reel' and 'stagger' mean to move unsteadily as if about to fall.

m: the bending of light, sound, or other waves as they pass from one medium into another
x: Refraction makes a straw in a glass of water look as if it is bent.
Our optics team used refraction to design lenses that sharpen images in low light.
In the physics practical, we measured the refraction of light through a glass prism.
Rainbows appear when sunlight undergoes refraction and reflection inside raindrops after a monsoon shower.
She smiled at the rainbow on the wall, created by refraction through the crystal he had given her.
tc: Because of ______, a coin lying at the bottom of a pool appears closer to the surface than it really is.
The coin's misleading position shows that light is being bent as it leaves the water, which is refraction.
se: The ______ of starlight by the atmosphere makes stars appear slightly higher in the sky than they really are.
bending
'Refraction' is exactly the 'bending' of light, so both give the sentence the same meaning.

m: to restore someone or something to a former position, condition, or status
x: After the misunderstanding was cleared up, the gym reinstated my membership at no extra cost.
The tribunal ordered the company to reinstate the engineer it had unfairly dismissed.
The university reinstated the scholarship after donors protested its cancellation.
Voters pressured the city council to reinstate the night bus service.
Once he apologized sincerely, she reinstated him as her closest confidant.
tc: After an inquiry cleared her of all charges, the board voted to ______ the suspended principal in her former position.
'Cleared of all charges' and 'former position' show the blank means to restore.
se: Under pressure from parents, the school decided to ______ the music classes it had cut last year.
restore
Both 'reinstate' and 'restore' mean to bring back something that had been removed.

m: a small amount of something that remains after the main part is gone or used
x: The price sticker left a sticky residue on my new phone case.
Cleaners scrubbed for hours to remove the oily residue from the factory floor.
Chemists analyzed the residue at the bottom of the flask to confirm the reaction was complete.
Inspectors found pesticide residue on vegetables sold in several city markets.
Even after they made up, a residue of resentment lingered between the two brothers.
tc: Long after the floodwaters receded, a thick ______ of mud and silt covered every floor in the village.
'After the floodwaters receded' shows the blank means what was left behind.
se: The ______ of the estate, after all debts were paid, went to the dead man's niece.
remainder
Both 'residue' and 'remainder' mean what is left of the estate after payments.

m: to echo or be filled with loud sound; also to be widely noticed or celebrated
x: Laughter resounded through the house as the cousins gathered for Eid dinner.
Applause resounded through the conference hall when the team's results were announced.
The professor's booming voice resounded through the lecture theater, waking even the sleepiest students.
The verdict resounded across the country, sparking debates in homes and newspapers.
Her words of encouragement still resound in my mind whenever I face a difficult decision.
tc: The cathedral was so vast that even a single cough would ______ through its nave for several seconds.
'So vast' and 'for several seconds' show the blank means to echo.
se: Cheers began to ______ around the stadium as the home team scored the winning goal.
echo
Both 'resound' and 'echo' mean that the sound filled the stadium loudly.

m: to make someone angry or irritated
x: Nothing riles my mother more than guests who arrive late without calling.
The new attendance policy riled employees who were already working long hours.
Questions about his methodology clearly riled the speaker at the conference.
The proposed fuel price hike has riled commuters and transport unions alike.
He knew exactly which comments would rile his sister, and he used them often.
tc: Usually unflappable, the referee refused to let the players' constant taunts ______ him.
'Unflappable' and 'taunts' show the blank means to make angry.
se: Comments about her accent never failed to ______ the new manager.
irritate
Both 'rile' and 'irritate' mean to make someone annoyed or angry.

m: a quick, clever reply, especially to criticism or an insult
x: When my uncle mocked my haircut, my sister's witty riposte left the whole table laughing.
Her calm riposte to the client's complaint defused the tension in the meeting.
The professor's riposte to the hostile question earned applause from the audience.
In a sharp riposte, the opposition spokesperson accused the ministry of hiding the real figures.
He wanted to deliver a clever riposte, but he only stammered and blushed in front of her.
tc: Stung by the critic's insult, the playwright fired back with the clever ______ that newspapers quoted for weeks.
'Stung by the insult' and 'fired back' show the blank means a quick, clever reply.
se: Her quick ______ to the heckler drew laughter and applause from the crowd.
retort
Both 'riposte' and 'retort' mean a sharp, witty reply.

m: to hold someone's attention completely; also to fasten firmly with metal pins
x: The detective series riveted me so much that I watched all ten episodes in one night.
Her presentation riveted the board, and nobody checked a phone for forty minutes.
Students were riveted by the guest lecturer's account of surviving a winter in Antarctica.
The trial riveted the nation, with millions following every day of testimony.
During the final over of the cricket match, the whole family sat riveted to the television.
tc: Far from boring the audience, the documentary managed to ______ viewers from its opening scene to its final credits.
'Far from boring' signals the opposite, so the blank means to hold attention completely.
se: The magician's final trick was enough to ______ even the most restless children in the hall.
captivate
Both 'rivet' and 'captivate' mean to hold someone's attention completely.

m: a newcomer or beginner with little experience, especially in a job or sport
x: As a rookie driver, I stalled the car twice at the same traffic light.
The rookie on our sales team closed a bigger deal in his first month than any of us.
Every rookie researcher is tempted to collect data without a clear question in mind.
Police departments are struggling to train rookies quickly enough to replace retiring officers.
She made the rookie mistake of telling her new boyfriend about all her exes on their first date.
tc: Unlike the veterans who had played for a decade, the ______ was still learning the basic rules of the professional game.
The contrast with 'veterans' and 'still learning the basic rules' show the blank means a beginner.
se: Even after two months, the ______ still asked senior colleagues how to file a simple report.
novice
Both 'rookie' and 'novice' mean an inexperienced newcomer.

m: a heading or category under which things are grouped; also a set of rules or scoring criteria
x: Our teacher handed out a rubric showing exactly how each essay would be marked.
Under the rubric of 'efficiency savings', management quietly cut fifteen jobs.
The grant committee scores every proposal against a detailed rubric of five criteria.
Many unrelated programs were grouped under the broad rubric of 'urban renewal'.
She joked that their marriage needed a rubric so he would know exactly what she expected.
tc: So many unrelated policies were lumped together under the single ______ of 'reform' that the word lost all meaning.
'Lumped together under' shows the blank means a heading or category.
se: All of these projects fall under the general ______ of community development.
heading
Both 'rubric' and 'heading' mean the category under which the projects are grouped.

m: a noisy disturbance or commotion, often involving argument or fighting
x: The neighbors' dogs caused such a ruckus that nobody on our street could sleep.
A ruckus broke out in the meeting when the bonus figures were finally revealed.
Students raised a ruckus outside the exam hall after the results were delayed again.
The proposal to raise bus fares caused a ruckus in the city council chamber.
Their argument over the wedding guest list turned into a ruckus that woke the whole family.
tc: The library had been perfectly quiet until a group of fans burst in, chanting and shouting, and created the loudest ______ anyone could remember.
The contrast with 'perfectly quiet' and 'chanting and shouting' show the blank means a noisy commotion.
se: Police were called to calm the ______ outside the stadium after the final whistle.
commotion
Both 'ruckus' and 'commotion' mean a noisy disturbance.

m: sinking or drooping downward; declining or weakening in strength, value, or spirit
x: We finally replaced the sagging sofa that had swallowed our guests for years.
The manager organized a team lunch to lift sagging morale after the layoffs.
Economists attribute the sagging enrollment figures to sharply rising tuition fees.
The party hopes a new leader will revive its sagging popularity before the election.
He noticed his father's sagging shoulders and realized how much the illness had aged him.
tc: Desperate to revive the company's ______ sales, the board hired a new marketing director with a record of quick turnarounds.
'Desperate to revive' shows the sales were weakening, so the blank means declining.
se: A string of victories helped restore the team's ______ confidence after a terrible start to the season.
flagging
Both 'sagging' and 'flagging' describe confidence that has weakened.

m: a sudden, vigorous burst of attack, criticism, or gunfire, often the first in a series
x: My brother opened the family debate with a salvo of complaints about the food.
The rival firm fired the first salvo in a price war by halving its delivery fees.
The reviewer's opening salvo questioned whether the study's sample was large enough to mean anything.
Warships fired a salvo of missiles at the coastal radar station overnight.
Her letter was the opening salvo in a long, bitter dispute over their late father's house.
tc: The senator's harsh speech was only the opening ______ in what became a months-long campaign against the bill.
'Opening' and 'months-long campaign' show the blank means the first burst of attack.
se: The coach responded to the criticism with a fierce ______ of his own at the press conference.
volley
Both 'salvo' and 'volley' mean a burst of attacking words.

m: to satisfy a desire or appetite fully, sometimes to the point of excess
x: A single bowl of khichuri on a rainy evening is enough to sate my hunger.
No amount of overtime pay seemed to sate the young banker's appetite for money.
The museum's archives sated her curiosity about the city's colonial past.
Investor demand for the shares was so strong that the initial offering could not sate it.
After years apart, nothing could sate their longing to spend every moment together.
tc: Rather than whetting the guests' appetite for more, the enormous feast seemed to ______ them completely.
'Rather than whetting' signals the opposite, so the blank means to satisfy fully.
se: The documentary did little to ______ my curiosity about the deep ocean; if anything, it made me want to learn more.
satisfy
Both 'sate' and 'satisfy' mean to fulfill a desire, here curiosity.
